Iran's interior minister Mostafa Mohammad Najjar said at a press conference Saturday in Tehran that moderate candidate Hasan Rowhani has won the presidential vote. Najjar said Rowhani obtained more than 50 percent of more than 36 million votes cast in Friday's election. Rowhani was the lone moderate candidate in the race supported by reformists in a race that once appeared solidly in the hands of Tehran's ruling clerics. Rowhani's conservative and hard-line opponents were far behind the moderate Rowhani, who has vowed to follow a policy of detente and interaction with the outside world.

President Donald Trump denied knowledge of any attempt to hide the guided-missile destroyer USS John S. McCain during his visit to the Pacific, but said the attempt was "well-meaning." "I would never do a thing like that," he said. "Now, somebody did it because they thought I didn't like him. Okay? They were well-meaning, I will say. I didn't know anything about it. I would never have done that." The president commented on the story as he left the White House for a commencement speech at the Air Force Academy. Trump again confirmed that he never liked McCain, citing his vote to kill the Republican effort to repeal Obamacare and his effort to get America to go to war in Iraq. "I wasn't a fan of John McCain. I never will be, but certainly, I couldn't care less if there is a boat named after his father," Trump said. The Wall Street Journal reported an email from the White House Military Office to the U.S. Navy Seventh Fleet directing the guided-missile destroyer to be out of sight during Trump's visit. Trump did not deny the story. "I don't know who did it. We will probably be able to find out who did it," he said. "They thought they were doing me a favor because they know I am not a fan of John McCain."

Republican frontrunner Donald Trump posted on Twitter criticizing Mitt Romney after Romney, the 2012 Republican nominee, had asked for his endorsement. Romney had said on Fox News: "We have good reason to believe that there's a bombshell in Donald Trump's taxes." He also called on Sen. Marco Rubio (R-FL) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) to release their tax information. Romney said: "Either he's not anywhere near as wealthy as he says he is, or he hasn't been paying taxes we would expect him to pay or perhaps he hasn't been giving money to vets or to the disabled like he's been doing." An update noted that Trump posted on Twitter on Thursday: "Mitt Romney, who was one of the dumbest and worst candidates in the history of Republican politics, is now pushing me on tax returns. Dope! Why doesn't @MittRomney just endorse @marcorubio already. now! Just for your info, tax returns have 0 to do w/ someone's net worth. I have already filed my financial statements w/ FEC. They are great! I'm going to do what @MittRomney was totally unable to do- WIN!"

The government says it expects to receive $750 million more from the latest sale of stock held in American International Group. The sales are part of an effort to recoup taxpayer money from the largest bailout of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury Department says the banks underwriting the sale have exercised their option to buy 24.6 million AIG shares at the offering price of $30.50 each. That brings the total from the fourth round of sales in AIG stock to $5.75 billion. Treasury announced last week that it sold $5 billion in AIG stock. Treasury says it has received $23.3 billion from four sales of AIG stock. Treasury and the Federal Reserve stepped in with $182 billion to rescue New York-based AIG from collapse in September 2008. Treasury's portion of the bailout was $47.5 billion. With the latest sale, AIG still owes taxpayers about $24 billion on the original investment, according to Treasury estimates.

President Donald Trump wrote on Twitter Monday that former Vice President Joe Biden's son, Hunter, had stepped down from his role at a Chinese-backed investment firm. Hunter Biden's attorney confirmed Sunday that he would step down from the board. Trump wrote that the media would continue to protect Hunter, as ABC News conducted an interview with the former vice president's son late last week. The interview airs Monday. Trump wrote: "Now watch the Fake News wrap their greasy and very protective arms around him. Only softball questions of him please!" Trump increased his criticism of Hunter in back-to-back rallies last week. "Whatever happened to Hunter? Where the hell is he? Where's Hunter?" Trump asked last Thursday in Minneapolis. "Where's Hunter?" Trump also criticized establishment news broadcasts for repeatedly saying that Trump's claims of corruption were "totally unsubstantiated." "It's not unsubstantiated; he took a fortune out of Ukraine, knew nothing, took a fortune out of China," Trump said on Friday. The president posted on Twitter: "Now looks like he has raided and scammed even more countries! Media is AWOL."

A federal judge on Friday allowed Lev Parnas, an associate of Rudy Giuliani, to turn over documents to Congress as part of the impeachment proceeding against President Donald Trump. U.S. District Court Judge Paul Oetken granted Parnas' request to turn over House intelligence committee documents and data seized when Parnas was arrested in October. Parnas' attorney, Joseph Bondy, said in a court filing he expected to receive the materials from the U.S. Justice Department this week. Parnas and another man, Igor Fruman, played key roles in efforts by Giuliani, Trump's personal lawyer, to launch a Ukrainian corruption investigation against Democratic presidential contender Joe Biden and his son Hunter. Parnas and Fruman were indicted in October on federal campaign finance violations related to a $325,000 donation to a group supporting Trump's reelection. They have pleaded not guilty. Parnas has provided documents to the intelligence committee in response to a congressional subpoena. His attorney says he wants to provide more information that falls "within the scope" of the subpoena, including two batches of documents seized from his home and the contents of one of his iPhones, according to court filings. "Review of these materials is essential to the Committee's ability to corroborate the strength of Mr. Parnas's potential testimony," Parnas' attorney, Joseph Bondy, wrote in a filing.

Vice President Joseph R. Biden addressed Americans Saturday during the White House weekly address. He asked them to ask why they oppose raising the federal minimum wage. Biden said there is no reason why an American working 40 hours a week has to live in poverty. President Obama is working with congressional Democrats to increase the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10.10 per hour. Many Republican lawmakers oppose the action, pointing to a study that the move would eliminate about 500,000 jobs nationwide. Biden said there is proof that raising the minimum wage is good for the economy. He said there is clear data that shows fair wages generate loyalty of workers to their employers, which has the benefit of increasing productivity and leading to less turn over. Biden said raising the minimum wage would generate an additional $19 billion in additional income for people who need it the most. He also said it would help to close the gap in pay between men and women, because women make up the majority of minimum-wage employees. Biden said the president and he think they deserve it, and that a lot of you do too. He said it is time to act and give America a raise.

The top Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee plans to vote against Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor, citing concerns about her record of "judicial activism." Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., said in a USA Today column Monday that even though Sotomayor "renounced the pillars of activist thinking" during her testimony before the committee, he does not believe she will follow through. "I don't believe that Judge Sotomayor has the deep-rooted convictions necessary to resist the siren call of judicial activism. She has evoked its mantra too often," he wrote. Sessions aide Andrew Logan confirmed that Sessions will oppose Sotomayor. Sessions' decision comes the day before the Judiciary panel is scheduled to vote on President Obama's first high court nominee. Sen. Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, another Republican on the Judiciary Committee, also announced Monday afternoon that he would oppose Sotomayor. So far, South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham is the only Republican on the committee to vote in favor of the justice. Sotomayor is virtually certain to be confirmed by a vote of the full Senate by the end of next week, becoming the first Hispanic justice. Sessions acknowledged she probably had the votes in his column. He cited several decisions she has joined that were "contrary to the Constitution." He said each was "consistent with liberal political thought" and led him to doubt her "repudiation of judicial activism." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Eric Trump criticized George Conway, Kellyanne Conway's husband, over what he called "utter disrespect" toward his wife. Trump wrote on Twitter: "Of all the ugliness in politics, the utter disrespect George Conway shows toward his wife, her career, place of work, and everything she has fought SO hard to achieve, might top them all. @KellyannePolls is great person and frankly his actions are horrible." Earlier Monday, Trump accused Conway of jury- and witness-tampering. Trump had praised former campaign adviser Roger Stone for resisting to work with the special counsel's team. Trump tweeted: "I will never testify against Trump. This statement was recently made by Roger Stone, essentially stating that he will not be forced by a rogue and out of control prosecutor to make up lies and stories about 'President Trump.' Nice to know that some people still have 'guts!'"

White House aide Kellyanne Conway appeared on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday. During the exchange, host Jake Tapper asked Conway about a $130,000 payment to adult film actress Stormy Daniels. Conway said CNN had Daniels' attorney Michael Avenatti on the network over 65 times in less than two months. Conway said, "I know the president said he didn't know it when it occurred. Now, respectfully I know that CNN has invested a lot in this story and in Ms. Daniels' attorney. Mr. Avenatti He has appeared on your network over 65 times in less than two months. That a choice that you make. When I look at the CNN polling, I don't see this on there. I see the economy and immigration, health care. I see ISIS, historic talks on North Korea. We are on the precipice of ending decades of war between North Korea and South Korea in large part due to this presidents leadership." Tapper asked, "Do you think his job includes lying to the American people. Because he continues to do so." Conway responded, "You just want that to go viral. And you want to say President Trump and lie in the same sentence."

Before leaving for New York for a series of fundraisers, President Obama held a press conference at the White House to discuss his strategy on Syria. Obama told reporters that his strategy was still developing and that he would continue to consult with congress and the American people about any action in Syria. "I don't want to put the cart before the horse," he said. "We don't have a strategy yet." Obama said the news media were getting a little further ahead of where they were at than they currently are on confronting ISIL in Syria. "I think that's not just my assessment but the assessment of our military, as well," he said. Obama said that solution to the situation in Syria was not simply a military issue but also a political issue. He suggested that the United States would support a "moderate opposition" inside of Syrian to give the country's citizens a choice. "We have to give people inside of Syria a choice other than ISIL or Assad," he said, "And I don't see any scenario in which Assad somehow is able to bring peace and stability to a region that is majority Sunni." Obama also said he had no intention of taking military action against Russia, even though it was clear that Vladamir Putin was acting aggressively in Ukraine. "We are not taking military action to solve the Ukrainian problem," he explained.

President Obama addressed gun violence Friday at a White House press conference, urging Americans to pressure Congress to pass gun-control legislation after nine people were killed a day earlier at an Oregon community college. "Our inaction is a political decision that we are making," Obama said. "Every couple of months we have a mass shooting. This will not change until the politics change." On Thursday, 26-year-old Christopher Harper Mercer opened fire in a classroom at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Ore., killing nine people before being shot by responding officers. The president tried unsuccessfully to pass comprehensive gun-control legislation through Congress in 2012 after a gunman killed 26 people inside the Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newton, Conn. "The shootings will not go away until policies, elected officials change," Obama said Friday. "This is happening every single day in forgotten neighborhoods around the country." Obama called on Americans to "vote against" members of Congress who do not support efforts to control gun violence and to let them know "precisely why" they cast such votes. He also called on voters, gun-control groups and others to take on the gun rights lobby group the National Rifle Association, which was influential in blocking the Capitol Hill legislation several years ago. "The NRA is very effective," he said. Obama said the group knows how to "stir up fear" and raise money.

Senate Republicans will add the repeal of Obamacare's individual mandate to the tax bill, Senate leaders said Tuesday afternoon. President Donald Trump urged the Senate in a tweet Monday to add the repeal. Sen. Rand Paul said Tuesday morning he would push for the move. Sen. Tom Cotton also indicated he supported putting the repeal in the bill. Republican leaders confirmed the repeal will be part of the bill and have enough votes for it to pass through the Senate. "We're optimistic that inserting the individual mandate will be helpful," Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell told reporters Tuesday. Senate Majority Whip John Cornyn and Sen. John Thune also told reporters that the repeal would be included. The savings from the repeal would "be distributed in the form of middle-income tax relief," Thune said. Thune also said that the bill had 50 votes in the Senate, enough to pass with a tie-breaking vote by Vice President Mike Pence if done under rules that allow for the passage of certain bills by a bare majority. A repeal of the individual mandate would save $338 billion over the next decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office's analysis. "Repealing the mandate pays for more tax cuts for working families and protects them from being fined by the IRS for not being able to afford insurance that Obamacare made unaffordable in the first place," Sen. Cotton said in a statement, according to the Hill.

President Trump said Thursday that he did not forewarn the Russians and Syrians of an upcoming missile strike in his Wednesday tweet. In the tweet, Trump wrote: "Never said when an attack on Syria would take place. Could be very soon or not so soon at all! In any event, the United States, under my Administration, has done a great job of ridding the region of ISIS. Where is our 'Thank you America?'" On Wednesday, the president sent another tweet warning Russia that missiles "will be coming," earning criticism for tipping off the Russian-backed Assad regime. After new reports of chemical weapons by Syrian President Bashar Assad, the U.S. and other world leaders are trying to decide what to do next about the situation in Syria. Last spring, Trump ordered missile strikes after photos of children killed or severely injured by gas agents surfaced. The Assad regime and Russians both deny any use of chemical weapons. Russia vows to shoot down any and all missiles fired at Syria.

Sources told the New York Daily News that New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo met with Gov. David Paterson to discuss filling Hillary Rodham Clinton's seat in the U.S. Senate. Clinton has not resigned from the Senate yet, so Paterson will not appoint her successor until then. Caroline Kennedy is still a main contender for the appointment. The article states that Cuomo does not want it widely known that he is interested in the Senate seat because he does not want to appear that he is campaigning for it. The article also states that nobody should have to campaign for a Senate seat and that it is one thing to campaign for the Senate in an election and lose, but it is another thing to campaign for a Senate appointment and lose, because it means one guy cannot vote for you. The article also includes the question: "Will Congress pass the tax bill before Christmas?" Carleton Bryant is the assistant managing editor for strategic planning and development/special projects for The Washington Times. He previously served as The Times' Metropolitan desk editor, Features desk editor, assistant National desk editor, and a National and Metropolitan reporter. He currently writes a humor blog and weekly humor column, both titled "Out of Context."

Former FBI Director James Comey leaked memos of his interactions with President Trump. Ty Clevenger, a lawyer who filed a grievance against Comey, said in a letter Friday to the New York lawyers' disciplinary committee that if the fired director ended up leaking classified information it should bolster the case against him. Earlier this week, Sen. Charles E. Grassley revealed that Comey appears to have authored seven memos about his interactions with Trump. The government has deemed four of those seven memos to have classified information. Comey also leaked at least four memos to a law professor friend. Grassley said according to that math, at least one of the memos Comey leaked must have had classified information. Clevenger said that could run afoul of New York bar rules prohibiting a lawyer from engaging in "illegal conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer." Clevenger wrote: "If Mr. Comey deliberately leaked the documents, his breach of duty was analogous to willful breach of client confidentiality, and that reflects adversely on his 'honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer.'" Clevenger is also pursuing bar complaints against former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and her top lawyers, arguing their handling of Mrs. Clinton's secret emails breached standards for lawyers.

A Monmouth University/Gannett New Jersey poll shows Republican candidate Chris Christie with a 1-point lead over Democratic Governor Jon Corzine, well within the margin of error. Two days before the New Jersey gubernatorial election, the poll shows voters are split about evenly between Democratic Governor Jon Corzine and Republican challenger Chris Christie. The two candidates have been in a dead heat for weeks. The Monmouth University/Gannett New Jersey poll showed Christie with a 1-point lead over Corzine, well within the margin of error. Among likely voters, Christie pulled 43 percent and Corzine pulled 42 percent. The survey also showed Independent Chris Daggett dropping from 14 percent to 8 percent. The poll data suggests Daggett's supporters are drifting toward Christie. Corzine has low approval ratings. The survey showed 35 percent approve of the job he is doing. President Obama is heading to New Jersey Sunday to seek support for the Democratic incumbent. The poll of 1,041 likely voters was taken Wednesday through Friday and had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) tweeted a photo of House Budget Committee Chairman John Yarmuth (D-KY) taking a photo next to a cardboard cutout of her. The tweet showed Yarmuth taking a photo next to a cardboard cutout of her. Ocasio-Cortez then tweeted, "GOP: Let's pose our older male members next to cardboard cutouts of young female legislators." Twitter users noted the error and she deleted the tweet. Ocasio-Cortez has previously made similar errors on Twitter, including a tweet in which she mixed up the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Ocasio-Cortez said recently on Yahoo's Skullduggery podcast that she writes all her own tweets. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) recently said a "glass of water" with a "D next to its name" could have won Ocasio-Cortez's district.

The Trump administration on Friday announced new travel restrictions with Mexico and Canada. The restrictions suspend normal operations and processes for anything other than essential travel at land ports of entry along the U.S.-Mexico and U.S.-Canada border. President Trump said during a White House press briefing: "These measures will protect the health of all three nations and reduce the incentive for mass global migration that would badly deplete the health care resources needed for our people." The orders include: U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents returning to the United States; individuals traveling for medical purposes (e.g., to receive medical treatment in the United States); individuals traveling to attend educational institutions; and individuals traveling to work in the United States; and individuals traveling for emergency response and public health purposes (e.g., government officials or emergency responders entering the United States to support Federal, state, local, tribal, or territorial government efforts to respond to COVID-19 or other emergencies); individuals engaged in lawful cross-border trade; individuals engaged in official government travel or diplomatic travel; and individuals engaged in military-related travel or operations. At this time, the restrictions do not apply to air, freight rail, or sea travel but to passenger rail and ferry travel. The restrictions are in place until April 20.

The Justice Department is expected to oust the head of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, according to people familiar with the matter. The move toward the replacement of Kenneth Melson, acting ATF director since April 2009, could begin next week, although the precise sequence of events remains to be decided, these people said. The shakeup reflects political damage caused by the gun-trafficking operation called Fast and Furious, which used tactics that allowed suspected smugglers to buy large numbers of firearms. The agency has been without a Senate-confirmed director since 2006. The Bush and Obama administrations were unable to overcome opposition from gun-rights groups to win approval of nominees. In November, President Barack Obama nominated Andrew Traver, the head of the ATF's Chicago office, as permanent ATF director. The nomination stalled in the Senate after the National Rifle Association said Traver had a "demonstrated hostility" to the rights of gun owners. Traver is set to travel to Washington on Tuesday to meet with Attorney General Eric Holder and Deputy Attorney General James Cole, the people said. The administration is weighing whether to name Traver as acting director or choose another interim chief while awaiting Senate action on his nomination, they said.

Same-sex marriage won a second victory in two days in Pennsylvania, as Gov. Tom Corbett said Wednesday he will not appeal a court decision that struck down the state's ban. Corbett said in a statement: "The case is extremely unlikely to succeed on appeal. Therefore, after review of the opinion and on the advice of my commonwealth legal team, I have decided not to appeal." On Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge John Jones III struck down Pennsylvania's 1996 law banning recognition of gay marriage, calling it unconstitutional. One widow, 11 couples, and one couple's teenage daughters had sued. Corbett opposes same-sex marriage and supported unsuccessful efforts to amend the state constitution to ban gay marriage. "As a Roman Catholic, the traditional teaching of my faith has not wavered," Corbett said. "I continue to maintain the belief that marriage is between one man and one woman. My duties as governor require that I follow the laws as interpreted by the courts and make a judgment as to the likelihood of a successful appeal." Pennsylvania is the 19th state to recognize same-sex marriages. Hundreds of gay couples filed applications for marriage licenses after Jones' ruling Tuesday. Pennsylvania was the last northeastern U.S. state to legalize gay marriage.

President Obama nominates the first Latina for the Supreme Court. Judge Sonia Sotomayor will undergo the confirmation process. Speculation has been raised about how the Republican Party will handle the nominee. Questions have been raised about whether a case against Sotomayor's personal story will counter criticism, or whether her 20-year record on the bench will satisfy both conservatives and liberals. The confirmation process will be previewed with two key members of the Senate Judiciary Committee: Democratic Senator Arlen Specter and Republican Senator Lindsey Graham. The program will also air "Right Now," a series examining the Republican Party's future and who has what it takes to bring it back to prominence. This week, former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney will appear. North Korea test fires another short-range missile off its coast. The panel will discuss how the U.S. and the international community should respond. The panel includes Brit Hume, FOX News senior political analyst; Mara Liasson of National Public Radio; Bill Kristol of The Weekly Standard; and Juan Williams of National Public Radio. The program also presents Power Players of the Week wishing college graduates well and offering words of wisdom. Local listings will be updated.

On Tuesday, former United States Senator Bob Dole was assisted out of his wheelchair to salute former President George H.W. Bush as he laid in state at the Capitol Rotunda. Dole, who is 95 years old and served the state of Kansas in the U.S. House and Senate, faced Bush in the 1988 Republican primary for the presidential nomination. Bush ultimately defeated Dole, and the two remained friends for several years. Dole, like former President George H.W. Bush, served in World War II. Dole said Bush's passing marks the end of an era. "I believe there are certain qualities that veterans have and when Bush was president, I think about three-fourths of Congress were veterans and we would stick together and work together across the aisle," Dole told CNN on Saturday. "And President Bush was a bipartisan president. So we got quite a lot done." Both Dole and Bush had great respect for one another on a personal level. Dole served as Senate Majority Leader during the Bush administration and worked together on many different issues. "Many people doubted I could serve the president since we had a rather rough campaign, but it wasn't true — because of the man he was, not because of me," Dole said in 2016.

On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) called for Labor Secretary Alex Acosta to resign over the plea deal he gave billionaire Jeffrey Epstein on child sex trafficking charges in 2008 while serving as an attorney for the Southern District of Florida. Schumer said, "This week billionaire Jeffrey Epstein was indicted in New York on federal sex trafficking charges. The newly released evidence of Epstein's behavior involving dozens of children is sickening, is appalling, is despicable. Epstein should have been behind bars years ago, but unfortunately, Secretary of Labor Alex Acosta cut Epstein a sweetheart deal while Acosta was a U.S. attorney in Florida in 2008." He continued, "I am calling on secretary Acosta to resign. It is now impossible for anyone to have confidence in secretary Acosta's ability to lead the department of labor. If he refuses to resign, President Trump should fire him. Instead of prosecuting a predator and serial sex trafficker of children, Acosta chose to let him off easy. This is not acceptable. We cannot have as one of the leading appointed officials in America, someone who has done this, plain and simple." He added, "I am calling on the Department of Justice's office of professional responsibility to make public the results of its review of Acosta's handling of the Epstein case."

During a town hall with young people, President Obama addressed critics during a town hall promoting the White House "My Brother's Keeper" initiative. Obama said, "I just don't watch TV." He said he would listen to critics who had their interests at heart. "Who gives you constructive criticism because they're invested in the same things you are but maybe can see the things you can't, versus folks who are just -- what'd someone say -- hatin'? Somebody just hatin', just haters?" Obama said people should only focus on "constructive criticism." "One thing you should learn is, if somebody is being constructive in their criticism, usually they are not criticizing you, they're criticizing your actions and what you do and are giving you something specific," Obama said. Obama used a basketball metaphor to explain himself, comparing a coach who has specific goals for players versus a coach that tells a player they are no good. "If they can't, if all they're saying is, 'You're not worth nothin,' then that's probably not something that you want to pay a lot of attention to," Obama said. "Does that make sense?"

Democratic presidential candidate Joe Biden and a Michigan plant worker argued over AR-14s. The worker said, "You are actively trying to infringe our Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms." Biden responded, "You're full of shit." Upon further claims that he was trying to take their guns, Biden responded, "Don't tell me that," and suggested "going outside" to resolve the argument. The exchange occurred over a week after Biden tapped Robert 'Beto' O'Rourke to serve as his point-man on gun control. On March 2, 2020, Breitbart News reported that Biden brought O'Rourke during a campaign stop and told the crowd that O'Rourke would "be the one who leads" the gun control effort. An update to the article stated that a closer video angle of the incident contradicted early reports that Biden said, "I'm about to slap you in the face." The clearer audio at that moment, heard through crosstalk, sounded more like "I'm gonna go outside with you." The headline and text of the article were updated to correct the inaccurate early transcription.

Representative Liz Cheney (R-WY) said during a preview of an interview with NBC's Savannah Guthrie that aired Wednesday on MSNBC's "Andrea Mitchell Reports" that she intended to be "one of the leaders in a fight to help to restore our party." Cheney was addressing House Republicans voting to remove her as chair of the conference. Guthrie asked, "Are you the leader of the opposition in exile right now in the Republican Party?" Cheney said, "I intend to be the leader, one of the leaders in a fight to help to restore our party. In a fight to bring our party back to substance and principles, and in a fight to make clear that we won't participate in the really dangerous effort that's underway." Guthrie said, "A lot of people frame this as a battle for the soul of the Republican Party." Cheney replied, "This is the opening salvo, and it's a battle we have to win because it's not just about the Republican Party. It's about the country." Guthrie said, "The Trump political team is actively looking to coalesce around a primary challenger to you. What is your message to them?" Cheney said, "You know, bring it on."

A House and Senate GOP Budget Committee analysis of President Barack Obama's newly released budget says the plan achieves $119 billion in net deficit reduction, not the $1.8 trillion the White House claims. The GOP analysis finds that Obama's budget would generate $8.2 trillion in new debt, increasing total U.S. debt to $25.4 trillion over the next decade. The Republican budgetary analysis also finds that the Obama budget would mean a debt increase per household of $60,980. The budget would also raise taxes $1.1 trillion in addition to the $1 trillion in Obamacare taxes and the over $600 billion from Obama's recent tax increase. The Obama Administration claims its budget pays for every program without adding a dime to the deficit. "Every new initiative in the plan is fully paid for," says the White House, "so they do not add a single dime to the deficit." Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) says President Obama's budget is just more of the same, similar to the last two budgets he proposed that were unanimously rejected by the U.S. Senate. "We've been hoping that the president would finally learn that spending is the problem and make a meaningful attempt to rein in Washington's growth," said Boehner. "It doesn't seem that will happen either."

House Speaker John Boehner's office released a 68-second video criticizing President Obama for his willingness to negotiate with Russian President Vladmir Putin over Syria but not with the GOP over the budget. The video presents a series of recent clips showing Administration officials and the President stating flatly that there will be no negotiations with the GOP on the budget. The video then runs a series of clips showing Obama and Secretary of State Kerry's eagerness and pride regarding negotiating with Putin over ridding the world of Syria's chemical weapons. The video concludes with a question: "Why is the Obama administration willing to negotiate with Putin on Syria… but not with Congress to address Washington's spending problem?" The article states Boehner is likely using the video to change the media conversation, which has focused on Republicans. The article states the media have been completely on Obama's side with the debt debate and have given Obama a pass for his negotiating position, which it describes as extremist. The article states Boehner is asking a question media should have asked the first time Obama threatened a government shutdown with his refusal to negotiate.

Twitter apologized Monday for allowing a phrase that roughly translates as "Die Trump" to briefly trend in Turkey. The phrase "Mahvolursun Trump" started trending on Twitter in Turkey after President Trump threatened to destroy the country's economy if it did anything "off-limits" in Syria after U.S. troops withdrew from the region, Breitbart News first reported. "As I have stated strongly before, and just to reiterate, if Turkey does anything that I, in my great and unmatched wisdom, consider to be off limits, I will totally destroy and obliterate the Economy of Turkey (I've done before!),," the president wrote. "They must, with Europe and others, watch over the captured ISIS fighters and families." Doğu Perinçek, leader of Turkey's left-wing Patriotic Party, responded, "Mr. Trump you can destroy only USA," along with the hashtag "#MahvolursunTrump," which reportedly touched off the trend. Twitter apologized for the "mistake" and said it had removed the hashtag. "This phrase should not have appeared in trends, and we're sorry for this mistake. At times, we do prevent certain content from trending and we have now done so with this trend," the company said in a statement.

On Sunday, CNN's "State of the Union" host Jake Tapper played a clip from earlier in the week of 2020 Democratic presidential candidate former Vice President Joe Biden. Biden said President Donald Trump was the same sort of bully he would smack in the mouth. When asked how to beat Trump, Biden said, "I beat him by pointing out who I am and who he is and what we are for and what he is against. This is a divider-in-chief, acting with racist policies and moving to formant hate. That is the only way to sustain himself." He added, "I'm looking forward to this man. You walk behind me in a debate, come here, man. You know me too well. The idea that I'd be intimidated by Donald Trump? He's the bully that I knew my whole life. He's the bully that I've always stood up to. He's the bully who used to make fun when I would stutter, and I smacked him in the mouth. Look, this is not — I think the American people want a president who has some dignity, who has a value set, who is actually trying to restore the soul of this country. So when they turn on the television they look up, and their kids say, I want to be like that guy or that woman."

Former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush spoke on ABC's "Good Morning America" in Tampa, Florida, ahead of Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney's address to the Republican National Convention on Thursday evening. Bush said Romney will have to show more of himself, but that will be hard for Romney because he is not suddenly going to come across in a "new-age kind of way." Bush also said Republicans should not do anything "stupid." He said the party must acknowledge the nation's increasing diversity when addressing immigration and creating a climate of economic growth. He said if political parties ignore demographics, "you do it at your peril."

Former President Jimmy Carter on Sunday criticized the Obama administration's surveillance efforts, saying the country's use of drones has been "abused" and that he communicates by mail with foreign leaders because he believes his electronic correspondences are being monitored. "I have felt that my own communications are probably monitored," the former Democratic president told NBC's "Meet the Press." "And when I want to communicate with a foreign leader privately, I type or write the letter myself, put it in the post office and mail it, because I believe if I send an email, it will be monitored." Carter has dealt with a situation similar to the one Obama faces with Russia taking over the Crimea region of Ukraine. In 1980, he boycotted the Summer Olympics in Moscow after Russia invaded Afghanistan. However, Obama, unlike other U.S. presidents, has never consulted with him or his foundation, Carter said. The former president said he thinks the reason is that he and Obama have differing points of view on the Israel-Palestinian situation. "I can understand this is a sensitive issue," Carter said. "I can live with it." Carter also said the National Security Agency's collecting data on Americans' phone calls and Internet use and the United States' use of drones has become "extremely liberalized and I think abused by our own intelligence agencies."

A CNN/ORC national poll released Monday shows Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump at 49 percent, a 33-point lead over his nearest Republican competitor, Senator Marco Rubio of Florida at 16 percent and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas at 15 percent. Retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson was at 10 percent and Ohio Governor John Kasich was at 6 percent. In a CNN/ORC poll taken in late January, Trump was at 41 percent, with Cruz at 19 percent and Rubio at 8 percent. The poll assessed candidates on who would be most effective at solving the country's problems, who can best handle the responsibilities of being commander-in-chief, and who best understands the problems facing people like you. Trump was judged the most honest and trustworthy by a 13-point margin over Carson, 35 percent to 22 percent. Among Trump supporters, 78 percent said they are definitely supporting him, while 22 percent said they could still change their minds. Among people supporting other candidates, 57 percent said they are committed. On the Democratic side, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton led Sen. Bernard Sanders 55 percent to 38 percent.

On Monday, Donald Trump spoke at a rally in Springfield, Illinois. He said Americans should consider boycotting Starbucks for taking "Merry Christmas" off their coffee cups. He said if he wins the presidential election, "we're all going to be saying 'Merry Christmas' again." Trump said he is "speaking against myself" because "I have one of the most successful Starbucks in Trump Tower." He said he read about Starbucks's plain red cups earlier in the day. "Starbucks is taking Merry Christmas off. No more Merry Christmas on Starbucks. No More. I wouldn't buy," Trump said. "Maybe we should boycott Starbucks. I don't know. Seriously, I don't care. That's the end of that lease, but who cares." He then said Americans will be saying "Merry Christmas" again if Trump becomes President. "I will tell you — lots of big things, lots of little things, you can call this anything you want, but if I become President, we're all going to be saying 'Merry Christmas' again," Trump said. "That I can tell you."

On Sunday before an estimated crowd of 25,000 just outside Huntsville, Alabama, Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump received his biggest endorsement of the 2016 election cycle from Sen. Jeff Sessions (R-AL). Sessions, who has not endorsed a candidate in a GOP primary in his 20-year senatorial career, stressed Trump's pledge on border security, immigration and trade in his public endorsement. "I told Donald Trump this isn't a campaign, this is a movement," Sessions said. "The American people are not happy with their government." "There is an opportunity this year and we have the opportunity this Tuesday — it may be the last opportunity we have to fix illegal immigration. Donald Trump will do it," he added. Sessions also praised Trump for his stance on trade agreements, including the Trans-Pacific Partnership. "They trade agreements undermine our sovereignty and they shouldn't pass," Sessions said. "Donald Trump when he is elected president will make sure it does not pass." Trump welcomed Sessions' endorsement and praised his efforts on immigration. "He's really the expert as far as I'm concerned, on borders and so many other things," Trump said.

Presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump said on Tuesday's "O'Reilly Factor" on the Fox News Channel that taxes on "everybody" will go down, but "I may have to raise [taxes on the rich] it from that point." Host Bill O'Reilly said, "Finally, I was a little upset because my taxes are going to go up if you win. I'm going to be paying more now." Trump responded, "That's wrong. ... I have the biggest tax cut of anybody running, by far, and that includes the 16 people that are vanquished, okay? And nobody even came close. But, I may have to raise it from that point." O'Reilly asked, "So, your original statement in the debates you might have to go up a little for me? For me, I may have to pay more?" Trump then answered, "No, Bill, you're going to actually, perhaps go down. Actually, everybody's going to go down. But who's really going to go down is the middle class, who have been absolutely destroyed by taxes, and also businesses are going to go down."

During an event last week, Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas stated that the country would be better if more people could be described as "honorable." Thomas said, "If we could use that word about more people who are in public life, people who actually ask the questions at confirmation hearings, instead of 'Spartacus.'" He added, "Hey, look, '300.' But at any rate — but the — if we could use the word 'honorable' more often, think about the difference it'll make, then you'll have a legacy. We will have left the country in better shape, morally, structurally than we found it. But as long as we're looking at our interests, or scoring points, or looking cute, or being on TV, or the greenhouse effect, or what editorials we're getting, especially the legal system, how do we maintain it? If you can't debate hard issues honestly, with honor, with integrity, how do we keep a civil society?"

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton fainted due to a stomach virus that left her dehydrated and suffered a concussion in the fall last week, the State Department said on Saturday. As a result, Clinton is not expected to testify next Thursday at congressional hearings on the attack in Benghazi that killed four Americans, including U.S. Ambassador to Libya Chris Stevens. State Department spokesperson Phillipe Reines said Clinton "became dehydrated and fainted, sustaining a concussion" while suffering from a stomach virus that caused her to miss a scheduled trip to Mexico last week. "She has been recovering at home and will continue to be monitored regularly by her doctors," Reines said. Reines added that at the recommendation of Clinton's doctors, "she will continue to work from home next week, staying in regular contact with Department and other officials." He said she "is looking forward to being back in the office soon." Congress will hold hearings on Benghazi next week, and Clinton had been scheduled to testify. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice, after withdrawing her name for consideration to be the next Secretary of State on Thursday, said that Clinton had initially been asked to go on the Sunday shows immediately after the attacks. Rice said she took Hillary's place because Clinton was too worn down from her travels to do the interviews.

Rep. Chris Gibson (R-NY) signed the anti-tax "Taxpayer Protection Pledge" when he was running for Congress in 2010 to represent New York's 20th Congressional District. He now claims he is not bound by the pledge because, after redistricting, he now represents New York's 19th Congressional District. Gibson's office said: "Congressman Gibson doesn't plan to re-sign it for the 19th Congressional District, which he now represents (the pledge is to your constituents of a numbered district)." According to John Fund, this loophole does not hold up because the Taxpayer Protection Pledge is addressed "to the taxpayers of the ___ district," which the candidate fills in. Fund notes half of Gibson's new constituents were also in his old district. Further, the pledge is also made to "the American people" and not just solely to constituents in a particular district. Grover Norquist, president of Americans for Tax Reform, which administers the pledge, told Fund that "one would hope Representative Gibson would treat his constituents with more respect than he is showing." Gibson continues to insist that he can "consider all comprehensive packages brought forward as a result of bipartisan negotiations" without technically violating the pledge that helped get him the Republican nomination and win two elections.

Former New York City Mayor Ed Koch died early Friday morning at age 88, according to The Associated Press. Spokesman George Artz said he passed at 2 a.m. and the funeral was set for Monday. The AP reported that Koch was known as a feisty leader. His signature phrase, the AP reported: "How's I doing?" Another line, according to the AP: "You punch me, I punch back. I do not believe it's good for one's self-respect to be a punching bag."

Republican presidential candidate Dr. Ben Carson accepted the apology of Sen. Ted Cruz on behalf of his campaign for a "mistake" made during the Iowa caucus on Monday night. Carson's Communications Director, A. Larry Ross, stated: "Dr. Carson has accepted Senator Cruz's apology issued earlier this afternoon. These 'dirty tricks' political tactics are part of the reason Dr. Carson got into this race and reflect the 'Washington values' of win at all cost — regardless of the damage to the country — which he is trying to change. This incident further demonstrates that we need an individual who is not a politician to lead and to heal our nation, not someone driven by ambition." Carson said he will continue to work tirelessly toward reforming the system, restoring faith in the integrity of the electoral process, and giving government back to 'We the People.' He invited Senator Cruz and all candidates who profess to reject politics as usual to join him in conducting a race worthy of American ideals and respectful of the American people. Carson said he is looking forward to continuing his campaign in New Hampshire, South Carolina, and beyond. Dr. Ben Carson had alleged the Cruz campaign spread a rumor that Carson was suspending his campaign based on a false CNN report, which he said cost him some votes during Monday's caucus.

President Trump told Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell on Wednesday that it is "too soon to give up" on the election. The Kentucky Republican congratulated President-elect Joseph R. Biden on his win for the first time. The president retweeted a news story about Trump allies criticizing McConnell for congratulating Biden. "Mitch, 75,000,000 VOTES, a record for a sitting President (by a lot). Too soon to give up," Trump said. "Republican Party must finally learn to fight. People are angry!" Biden received more than 81 million votes. The president and his supporters say many of the Democrat's votes were illegal due to expanded mail-in balloting. McConnell also urged Senate Republicans on Tuesday not to join with House Republicans in a plan to object to Biden's electoral votes when Congress meets on Jan. 6. At the same time the president was telling McConnell not to give up on the election, Trump also retweeted a news story about the Rev. Franklin Graham saying Trump "will go down in history as one of the great presidents of our nation." "May God bless him, Melania, and their family, as God leads him to the next chapter in his life," Graham said.

Senator John Kerry called President Bush to concede the 2004 race for the White House late Wednesday morning. The program "Dayside" will present Senator Kerry's concession speech live. The program will examine what the Bush campaign did "right" to win and what happened to the Kerry campaign. Republican Governor Haley Barbour of Mississippi and Democratic strategist Dan Gerstein will examine why Ohio turned into Florida. Ohio is the election's Florida with John Kasich, former Ohio Congressman and host of FNC's "Heartland." The exit polls indicated Kerry ahead by Tuesday afternoon. John McIntyre, director and co-founder of RealClearPolitics.com, will explain why the numbers did not add up. The program "DaySide with Linda Vester" takes viewers beyond headlines for a closer look at the stories that newsmakers and neighbors are talking about. The live studio audience can be reached at 1-877-FOX-TKTS (1-877-369-8587). "DaySide with Linda Vester" airs weekdays at 1 p.m. ET.

As President Trump considers his 2020 re-election strategy, the "America First" agenda championed by former White House chief strategist Steve Bannon is in conflict with the "Economy First" agenda supported by most of Trump's current White House advisers on trade policy and the importance or lack thereof of the promised border wall, according to a report in Axios. In conversations at Mar-a-Lago and back in Washington, friends and advisers have begun giving President Trump advice about how to win reelection in 2020. Trump is getting conflicting advice. The Bannon purists want America First, and most of his friends want Economy First. So far, he has governed like a fairly conventional Republican, so the Economy First camp is winning. The next month, with pending decisions on immigration and trade wars, will show whether he reverts to his campaign norm in action, not just words. The Bannon-Breitbart-Stephen Miller wing believes Trump has to deliver on building a wall, curtailing immigration and cracking down on China. Moderating forces like Gary Cohn, Steven Mnuchin, James Mattis and Rex Tillerson are counseling against moves that could alienate allies and roil global markets.

Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts posted on Twitter Monday afternoon criticizing Republican Sen. Ted Cruz's coronavirus relief proposal that would give every person in the country $2,000 a month for a sustained period of time. Markey wrote: "Give every person in our country $2000/month for the duration of the pandemic, $2000/month for 3 months after that, and $2000/month retroactive to March." He also wrote: "Why be so cheap? Give everyone $1 million a day, every day, forever. And three soy lattes a day. And a foot massage. We have a magic money tree — we should use it!" Cruz responded: "It's not a god–- joke Ted. Millions of families are facing hunger, the threat of eviction, and the loss of their health care during a pandemic that is worsening every day. Get real." The exchange followed President Trump's announcement over the weekend of four executive actions to provide Americans financial relief from the pandemic after talks failed in Congress on Friday.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and David Letterman shared laughs about jokes Letterman has made about the lawmaker's girth. Christie has termed his plumpness "fair game" for comedians. During his first appearance on "Late Show with David Letterman" on Monday, the Republican and potential 2016 presidential contender read two jokes that he said were "some of my personal favorites." The governor pulled out a doughnut and started eating it while Letterman asked him if he was bothered by the digs that have been made about his weight. Christie said he was not, noting that he laughs at the jokes if he finds them funny. "Late Show" airs on CBS at 11:35 p.m. Eastern time.

On Monday, a winner emerged in the Senate race between former "Saturday Night Live" star Democrat Al Franken and incumbent Republican Norm Coleman. The Minnesota State Canvassing Board certified election results declaring Franken the winner. The recount process involved hand-inspection of several million ballots and a narrow margin of victory. The recount was subsequently endorsed by Minnesota's highest court. The article states that prolonged litigation undermines the integrity and validity of Minnesota's electoral system and adds to controversy surrounding the U.S. Senate as Congress returns to work. The article states that while these factors are significant, their prevalence does not diminish the importance of ensuring a fair election in which every eligible voter can cast a ballot and all ballots are counted. The article reports that Coleman's campaign claims that some ballots were mishandled and others wrongly excluded from the recount, which gave Franken an edge in the process. The article also states that the appearance of impropriety and the Board's refusal to consider several hundred additional votes warrant another look, especially given the narrow lead held by Franken. The article recommends that every vote be counted and counted accurately.

Republican incumbent Norm Coleman is seeking a total recount of all ballots in Minnesota's U.S. Senate race, which he narrowly lost to Democrat Al Franken, the Minneapolis Star-Tribune reported. Coleman had argued that about 12,000 ballots be rejected when he was leading during the initial recount. He now wants those ballots to be counted in a new recount. Franken, who won by 225 votes, was cool to the suggestion of a total recount. Franken was cool to the suggestion of a total recount. The article stated that another recount is what Minnesota needs — another recount, noting the first one took half a lifetime and should be done by the time his 17-year-old son is eligible for Social Security. The article also stated it would be almost ironic if Coleman's margin of victory lies among the 12,000 ballots he initially said should be rejected. The article included the question: "Should Sen. Al Franken resign?" Carleton Bryant is the assistant managing editor for strategic planning and development/special projects for The Washington Times. He previously served as The Times' Metropolitan desk editor, Features desk editor, assistant National desk editor, and a National and Metropolitan reporter. He currently writes a humor blog and weekly humor column, both titled "Out of Context."

In the closing days of a U.S. Senate race in Kansas, Independent Greg Orman was criticized for referring to Bob Dole, a 91-year-old living legend in that state, as a "clown." According to the Washington Examiner, when asked about the long line of Republican bigwigs who have campaigned for incumbent Senator Pat Roberts, including Dole, Orman replied: "It sort of seems like a Washington establishment clown car to me." The Roberts campaign responded: "In the final days of this campaign, Democrat Greg Orman is finally showing Kansans his true colors and revealing his arrogant disdain for Republicans. His liberal personal views aside, for Greg Orman to attack Senator Dole as a 'Washington establishment clown' is an outrage. Few leaders have done more for Kansas and this country than Senator Bob Dole, and Greg Orman should immediately apologize for his slimy attack on Senator Dole and other Republican leaders." Dole also released a short statement: "I don't think I've ever been called a 'clown' before. I'm disappointed by Mr. Orman's statement." According to the Real Clear Politics poll of polls, Orman leads by a single point with four days remaining.

A U.S. solider was killed in combat in eastern Afghanistan on New Year's Day, the first such death in 2018 the military announced. Four other U.S. service members were wounded during a combat engagement in Achin, Nangarhar province, officials said Tuesday. Two were in stable condition and the two others returned to duty. General John Nicholson, commander of the U.S. Forces-Afghanistan, said in a news release: "We are deeply saddened by the loss of one of our own. At this very difficult time our heartfelt sympathies go out to the families and friends of our fallen and wounded brothers." The name of the soldier has not been released pending family notification. The United States formally concluded its combat mission in Afghanistan at the end of 2014 but still carries out operations against the Taliban and an ISIS affiliate, both of which are active in Nangarhar. Vice President Pence made an unannounced trip to Afghanistan just before the Christmas holiday and thanked troops for their service while reiterating the "real progress" the U.S. is making in the country to "put the Taliban on the offensive." Pence said: "I believe victory is closer than ever before. I believe with all my heart that Afghanistan will be free."

President Obama said in an interview with radio host Tom Joyner on Wednesday that he was "too polite" during last week's presidential debate. Obama argued that Republican rival Mitt Romney changed his past positions. He said he would be more aggressive in the next two debates, scheduled for Oct. 16 and 22. Obama said: "Because, you know, it's hard to sometimes just keep on saying 'and what you're saying isn't true,' because it gets repetitive." Obama and his aides said he wanted to have "a conversation" with voters. After the debate, Obama said Romney was hard to pin down because he was two-faced. Obama told Joyner: "The good news is, is that's just the first one. Gov. Romney put forward a whole bunch of stuff that either involved him running away from positions that he had taken, or doubling down on things like Medicare vouchers that are going to hurt him long term. ... And, you know, I think it's fair to say that we will see a little more activity at the next one."

President Obama is set to announce San Antonio Mayor Julian Castro will be the new head of the housing administration. Castro gave a keynote address at the 2012 Democratic Convention. He has a twin brother who is also in politics. The current housing secretary, Shaun Donovan, will now run the budget office. Republican Senator Bob Corker described a meeting between top White House aides and republicans in Congress as "bizarre." The meeting was supposed to answer questions on President Obama's foreign policy, but republicans say they did not get answers they wanted. New home sales are reported today. Wall Street reaction is reported. Doug McKelway is reporting on train travel from Union Station. Laura Ingle is watching traffic on the road from the Port Authority bus station in NYC. Adam Housley is monitoring roads from the 405 freeway in Los Angeles. Mike Tobin is reporting on changes to air travel thanks to technology at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport. Jonathan Serrie is reporting today on the bacteria on airplane seats and door handles. The U.S. military commander in the Pacific is warning that the Pacific is a tinderbox right now and there is a high risk of "miscalculation" in a standoff between Vietnam and China over fishing rights in the ocean.

Florida Sen. Marco Rubio's 12-year-old daughter Amanda Rubio was injured in a car accident Saturday afternoon while visiting with classmates. The statement said Amanda Rubio was a passenger on a golf cart involved in a collision in a private gated community. She was airlifted to Miami Children's Hospital with a head injury and admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit. She is in fair condition. A Rubio spokesman said the senator and his wife are grateful for all the outpouring of support and prayers. The Rubio's are touched and grateful for calls from President Obama and Vice President Biden, and Governor Romney's personal message earlier today. The Senator was alerted to the accident after leaving a campaign rally in Kissimmee with Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney. At 6:44 p.m., the Romney motorcade pulled over to the side of I-4. Rubio was seen talking on a cell phone outside the campaign bus for several minutes, shaking hands with a few people, and driving away in a Florida State Trooper's vehicle. Rubio appeared at two events for Romney today and was scheduled to appear at a third tonight in Land O' Lakes, near Tampa.

President Obama visited Roseburg, Oregon, on Friday to meet with families of victims of last week's shooting at Umpqua Community College. The shooting led the president to renew his call for gun-safety measures. Protesters in the small Oregon town held signs reading "Gun free zones for sitting ducks," "Obama is wrong," "Nothing trumps our liberty," and other anti gun-control slogans. Reporters traveling with the president said several hundred people greeted Obama at the airport, and roughly half of them were protesting his calls for more gun legislation. The meeting with victims' families Friday afternoon was closed to the press, and details of their discussions were not expected to be released. Following the meeting, Obama said he will continue pushing for new gun-safety measures. "We're going to have to come together as a country, but today is about the families," he said.

President Barack Obama danced and took in baseball games during a day-long event in Brussels, Belgium, that killed over 30 people, including some Americans. Hours after the attacks, Obama gave the attack 50 seconds of time in a speech that was described as praising communist Cuba and condemning the United States. An hour later, Obama participated in the same event planned by his hosts. During the event, Obama did not have the 50 seconds of his time to discuss the attacks. He was seen doing the wave at a Cuban baseball park. Following the event, the press was shown scenes of the president doing the tango with a Cuban woman. This occurred despite Obama's claim that defeating ISIS was his "number one priority." The optics of the event drew criticism. Obama said on the presidency: "It's not promotion, not marketing. It's hard." One of the hosts of ABC's The View, a normally liberal woman, said the optics of seeing Obama do the wave at a communist ballpark were a bad sight for the American people and for the world.

Mitt Romney will announce his running mate at 8:45 a.m. ET Saturday in Norfolk, Virginia, according to an official press release from the Romney campaign. The announcement comes roughly two weeks before the start of the Republican National Convention in Tampa. The campaign has not yet confirmed who the running mate is. Speculation has centered lately on Rep. Paul Ryan of Wisconsin. Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, Ohio Sen. Rob Portman and former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty have all been mentioned as possibilities in recent days. The Romney campaign could also announce an outside-the-box selection Saturday morning. The announcement comes as some polls, including a recent Fox News survey, show the Republican presidential candidate losing some ground to President Obama. In a statement issued Friday night, the Romney campaign said the running mate would be revealed at 9 a.m. EDT at the Nauticus Museum. Romney is beginning a four-day bus tour through swing states. The vice presidential selection will dominate headlines, and Romney's team has been teasing the announcement for weeks.

The White House declined to confirm whether President Barack Obama took a 5 percent pay cut due to sequestration last year. Obama promised last April to take a 5 percent pay cut in solidarity with federal employees furloughed as a result of the automatic budget cuts known as the sequester. The cut was meant to equate to the level of spending cuts imposed on nondefense federal agencies. A White House official said at the time: "The president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester, he will contribute a portion of his salary back to the Treasury." According to his tax returns, Obama is still receiving the presidential salary of $400,000 per year. Last year, he earned $394,796 in wages from the Defense Financing and Accounting Service (DFAS-CIVPAY), which handles the salaries for civilian members of the Defense Department. Obama's income was commensurate to his salaries in recent years. He took in $395,188 in 2010, $394,821 in 2011, and $394,840 in 2012. The salary is also comparable to what former President George W. Bush received in 2007, when he earned $397,839.

A delegation of congressional Democrats began a three-day visit to Cuba on Saturday to discuss expectations for normalization of relations between the United States and the island nation. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo added his name to other high-ranking politicians planning a trip to the island. The delegation's leader, Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, said in a statement Saturday that the lawmakers want to explore opportunities for greater cooperation and to encourage Cuban officials to address issues of concern to Americans and their representatives in Congress. Traveling with Leahy were Sens. Dick Durbin of Illinois, Debbie Stabenow of Michigan and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and congressmen Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Peter Welch of Vermont. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo is planning a trade mission to Cuba to promote the state, spokeswoman Melissa DeRosa said Saturday. She did not say when the Democratic governor would travel, adding that details would be announced later. DeRosa says the trip to Cuba would be part of a "Global NY" initiative. Cuomo has previously announced that he plans trips to Israel, China, Mexico and elsewhere during his second term as governor. Last month, President Barack Obama announced plans for renewed economic ties and other administration-led initiatives aimed at re-establishing relations with Cuba. Many congressional Republicans have been cool to the effort.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that accusations of Russia meddling in the 2016 United States presidential election were "simply rumors." U.S. intelligence officials said they have definitive evidence linking Moscow to the Democratic Party email hacks. Putin made the comment during a news conference with German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who was visiting Russia for the first time in two years. The Russian president added that the claim was being used as part of the political fight in Washington. "We never interfere in the political life and the political processes of other countries and we don't want anybody interfering in our political life and foreign policy processes," Putin said. U.S. intelligence agencies claim Russia hacked email account with the aim of benefiting Donald Trump's campaign and harming his Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. On Tuesday, the former Democratic presidential nominee also blamed part of her loss on Russia's role in hacking into her campaign's internal emails and subsequently coordinating their release on WikiLeaks. "He [Putin] certainly interfered in our election," Clinton said during the Women for Women International's annual luncheon in New York. "And it's clear he interfered to hurt me and help his opponent." Merkel said Germany would take "decisive measures" if it believed there was foreign meddling in its upcoming election. Relations between Germany and Russia remain strained, mostly over the unresolved conflict in eastern Ukraine.

A senior White House adviser on Sunday said President Obama's forthcoming budget would not resemble the House Republican proposal, which Americans have already rejected. "The American people rejected it," Obama adviser Dan Pfeiffer said on "Fox News Sunday." "And (Republicans) shouldn't be doubling down on it." The president is scheduled to release a budget Wednesday that is expected to include a mix of tax increases and cuts to entitlement programs such as Social Security and Medicare. "You can do both," Pfeiffer said. "That's what you'll see." Pfeiffer also told ABC's "This Week" that Obama will not "enact a Romney economic plan," which he said was essentially drastic cuts to entitlement programs with tax breaks for the wealthiest Americans. "What we won't do is cut our way to prosperity," he said. On Saturday, the president said his budget was not his "ideal plan," but it was a compromise he would be willing to accept. House Speaker John Boehner said last week that the Obama budget blueprint holds reforms "hostage" to tax increases.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Monday shows former Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge at 43 percent and Sen. Arlen Specter at 46 percent in a hypothetical general election matchup. The poll was conducted in a hypothetical general election. Specter is not a declared candidate. Over the weekend, speculation arose that Ridge is considering a bid to be the Republican nominee after Specter switched from Republican to Democrat last week. The current front-running Republican candidate in the race, former Rep. Pat Toomey, is trailing Specter by a wide margin. The latest poll showed Specter leading Toomey 53-to-33 percent in a Pennsylvania general election. Polls recently showed Toomey trouncing Specter in the GOP primary, which contributed to Specter's decision to switch parties. In a statement, Quinnipiac pollster Clay Richards said Ridge is probably the only figure in Pennsylvania who could pose a significant challenge to Specter. The poll also found that Ridge would lead 47-to-37 percent among independents if he enters the race. If the GOP nominee is Toomey, the poll showed independents backing Specter by 45-to-36 percent.
