Liberal pundits are searching for explanations as to why Herman Cain's poll numbers have not been affected by sexual harassment allegations. With additional allegations coming, they are hoping that something will drop the poll numbers of a candidate who could plausibly defuse accusations of racism by the Obama campaign. The timing of Anita Hill's accusations made the public suspicious from the start and aware she was being brought forward because liberals could not win in the marketplace of ideas. The same reaction may be happening now, since all of these women were brought forward when Cain rose in the polls. Polls indicate the public does not buy into the accusations. The polls may still remain the same, courtesy of Bill Clinton. During the Lewinsky scandal, Clinton's poll numbers remained the same because the economy was then booming. Herman Cain is judged as having the best prescription for turning the economy around. Polls may again stay the same. Clinton's remarks may have gotten the public used to philandering politicians.

Peter Navarro responded to President Obama's coronavirus criticism during remarks for an online event honoring students graduating from Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Obama said the pandemic had "torn back the curtain on the idea that so many of the folks in charge know what they're doing. A lot of them aren't even pretending to be in charge." Last week, in a private call with former members of his administration, Obama described the response as a "chaotic disaster." The former president has mostly refrained from directly criticizing President Trump or his administration during the past three years of his tenure, but that has shifted as the 2020 campaign ramps up with Obama's former vice president leading the Democrats. Navarro said he did not see any mention of China or manufacturing in Obama's "kumbaya of incompetence" speech Saturday, arguing that is what the American public is concerned with. "We're going to go back to the future here: by American, deregulate and innovate," he said. "Bring the jobs home and make it here."

President Obama held a campaign rally in Camden, New Jersey, for Governor Jon Corzine's re-election bid. During the rally, Obama repeated repeated statements that Republican opponent Chris Christie is "wrong when matters most." Obama said: "We're two days away from making sure that NJ has the quality leadership it deserves. We're two days away from making sure we've got fairness in our economic system. Jon knows these are challenging times. That's why he got into public service. He didn't do it for the paycheck. There's a lot of silliness in the campaign season; a lot of distortion. I want to make sure you understand the Corzine record: he has provided more property tax relief than any other Governor in NJ history. He was the first Governor in 60 years who reduced the size of the government. Yes, YOU are going to vote Tuesday, but I'm going to need you to knock on doors." Some 5,500 people were in attendance, according to Kurt Voss, General Manager of the Susquehanna Bank Center.

In Michigan, Santorum supporters planted hundreds of campaign signs in Shelby Township prior to Mitt Romney's appearance today. Some of these signs were planted alongside sidewalks and roadways across from and surrounding the Romney campaign stop. Approximately two hours before the scheduled event, Romney campaign staffers, including Dennis Lennox of Topinabee, MI, began planting Romney signs in front of the location. Around the same time, several other people, who refused to identify themselves, began uprooting hundreds of Santorum signs along the roadway leading to the event. Signs placed at a commercial intersection were also removed. When asked to explain his actions, Santorum supporters were confronted with obscenities from one person removing signs. He claimed to be unaffiliated with the Romney campaign. One officer on the scene, Lou Francis, refused to assist in retrieving stolen campaign signs valued at over $1500. Jonathan Burgos reported: "Every Asian market outside Sri Lanka retreated after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben S. Bernanke yesterday said a premature withdrawal of quantitative easing would put the U.S. economic recovery at risk."

Rep. Chris Cannon lost the Republican primary for his congressional seat. Jason Chaffetz, a former chief of staff to Utah Governor Jon Huntsman Jr., defeated Cannon. Chaffetz is serving his sixth term in the House and has a conservative record on nearly every other issue. This was the third time Cannon faced a primary challenge centered on the immigration issue. Cannon has been a study on immigration. He was one of President Bush's closest allies in pushing for a guest-worker program. He has kept a fairly hard-line voting record on bills calling for a crack-down on illegal immigration. His defeat comes as House Democrats have found candidates willing to run in conservative districts professing their own get-tough message. That has helped take the sting out of the Republican-Democratic fight on the issue. Immigration is still a roiling issue but so far, it appears to be best used to unseat Republicans. That is not the effect Republicans had hoped for.

During his appearance on "Jimmy Kimmel Live" on Thursday, host Jimmy Kimmel asked former President George W. Bush about jokes made against him while he was president, specifically Will Ferell's impression of him on "Saturday Night Live." Bush responded, "I love humor and the best humor is when you make fun of yourself." Kimmel responded, "Tell that to the president." Bush also recalled a dinner he had with "SNL" executive producer Lorne Michaels during which they discussed who came up with the fake word "strategery." Bush recalled, "I said, 'Well let me ask you this? Did you come up with misunderestimate.'" Kimmel asked Bush if his father, George H. W. Bush, was faking being sick to avoid the inauguration. Bush said, "You're a funny man," to which Kimmel said, "That wasn't a joke."

On Thursday, a federal appellate court ruled on Texas' right to abortion, upholding a law that requires all abortion clinics to meet the same building, equipment, and staffing standards as hospital-style surgical centers. The ruling requires all abortion clinics in the state to meet the same building, equipment, and staffing standards. According to providers, the standards were unnecessary and costly. The state argued they improved patient care. The thirteen clinics are closing overnight, leaving the state with eight abortion clinics — all in major metropolitan areas. Texas has 5.4 million women of reproductive age, which is the second most in the country. Nancy Northup, president and chief executive of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said the ruling has gutted Texas women's constitutional rights and access to critical reproductive health care and stands to make safe, legal abortion essentially disappear overnight. In July 2013, Texas passed an abortion law despite a filibuster by Democratic state senator Wendy Davis. Davis is now running for governor.

President-elect Donald Trump on Saturday wished a "Happy New Year" to friends and enemies on Twitter. "Happy New Year to all, including to my many enemies and those who have fought me," Trump began the tweet. He ended the tweet by wishing everybody "Love," but not before making sure that all those who "lost so badly" to him knew the New Year's message was also intended for them. "They just don't know what to do," he wrote. The speaker was unclear. Trump and supporters have since Election Day argued that backers of defeated Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton and others continue to search for excuses and others to blame for her defeat. Trump tweeted again at midnight, wishing all Americans a "Happy New Year." Trump has roughly 18 million Twitter followers and continues to use the social media site to bypass conventional media outlets like television and newspapers to send messages to Americans. Trump spent his New Year's Eve at his private Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that President Obama plans to give back 5% of his salary to the Treasury, retroactive to March 1. The president's salary is $400,000 per year, so the 5% reduction will amount to $20,000 annually. The move was taken "in solidarity with federal workers who are going to be furloughed as part of the automatic budget cuts known as the sequester," according to the official, who added that "the president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester." The administration official noted the president's support for federal workers but did not mention the president's concern for taxpayers. Starting in April, the president will write a monthly check to the Treasury for $1,667.67, according to the unnamed official. The payment will be in addition to the amount withheld from the President's monthly salary for federal income taxes. It was unclear if President Obama plans to continue this practice for the remaining three and a half years of his term or only for the next twelve months.

Jon Stewart has released a race card deck for the November election. The card addresses Rick Santorum, Rick Santorum, and other candidates. The card includes candidates. Stewart cannot point to President Barack Obama's record and state his candidacy. The card is labeled "White Man's Sampler." The article notes that Stewart has not used the race card in public spaces for weeks. The article references the Occupy Wall Street crowd in the context of the election. Republicans were eager to cast their vote for Herman Cain before sexual-charged allegations shut down Cain's campaign. The article states that Stewart must play the full race card deck before the final vote is tallied.

President-elect Donald Trump criticized Democratic Congressman John Lewis after Lewis said he does not believe Trump is a "legitimate president." Lewis said this is the first inauguration he will not attend. A Washington Post report reported that Lewis skipped President-elect Bush's inauguration because he did not believe Bush was the true elected president. Trump wrote on Twitter: "John Lewis said about my inauguration, 'It will be the first one that I've missed.' WRONG (or lie)! He boycotted Bush 43 also because he 'thought it would be hypocritical to attend Bush's swearing-in....he doesn't believe Bush is the true elected president.' Sound familiar!" Lewis said he will skip Trump's inauguration because the President-elect is "wrong" for America. Lewis said: "I don't plan to attend the inauguration. It will be the first one that I miss since I've been in Congress. You cannot be at home with something that you feel that is wrong."

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Wednesday that he supports Barack Obama's nomination of Samantha Power as the new U.N. ambassador. McCain stated, "I believe she is well-qualified for this important position and hope the Senate will move forward on her nomination as soon as possible." Obama, who pushed the Senate to endorse Power, said, "To ensure that we have the principled leadership we need at the United Nations. I would strongly urge the Senate to confirm her without delay." The article reports that McCain claims to be a strong supporter of Israel but apparently wants to ignore Power's 2002 call for a possible U.S. invasion of the Jewish state. Power said in 2002 that "external intervention" using a "mammoth protection force" was necessary to keep Israelis and the Palestinians apart. She said such a move would be "unfortunate," asserting, "Unfortunately, imposition of a solution on unwilling parties is dreadful. I mean, It's a terrible thing to do, it's fundamentally undemocratic."

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence accepted the nomination to serve as Republican nominee Donald Trump's vice president. Pence said the 2016 general election is about "change versus status quo." "I'm a Christian, a conservative and a Republican in that order," Pence said as he introduced himself. "I thought I'd be spending this evening with all my friends from the great state of Indiana, yet there I was a few days ago in New York City with a man who won 37 states." Pence was officially announced Trump's running mate last weekend in New York City. The Indiana governor introduced his family and spoke about his conservative record. "We will always stand with those who stand on the thin blue line of law enforcement in America," Pence stated, which was the top moment discussed on Facebook during the speech. "Hillary Clinton will never become President of the United States of America," he said, saying she "essentially offers a third Obama term." "Conservative principles work every time you put them in to practice," he said.

President Barack Obama attributed the election results to Donald Trump's successful personality. During a press conference in Greece, NBC's Chris Jansing asked Obama whether he felt responsible for his party's loss of the presidency. Obama said, "Presidential elections always turn on personalities. They turn on how campaigns are run," and said Clinton lacked both. Obama said some in America might want change after eight years of his presidency, but noted he still has high approval ratings. He said, "Last I checked, a pretty healthy majority of the American people agree with my world view on a whole bunch of things." Obama said Americans probably wanted to "shake things up" after eight years and try something new. He said, "I do think, as I've said before, that history doesn't move in a straight line, it zigs and zags, and sometimes goes forward, sometimes moves back and sideways."

A gun discharged inside a 5-year-old kindergartener's backpack at a Tennessee elementary school cafeteria on Thursday, officials said. No one was hurt. A statement from the Shelby County school district said the gun went off inside the kindergarten student's backpack as students waited for the opening bell. There were no injuries. School staffers immediately took control of the backpack. School security officers and the Memphis Police Department responded quickly, the district said. The child was detained and was still being questioned by officers Thursday afternoon, with the child's mother present. Police spokeswoman Karen Rudolph said investigators were trying to determine how the gun ended up in the backpack. Students were kept safe and calm while the matter was handled, the district said. There was no evidence of harmful intent, the district said. "However, weapons of any kind are prohibited on campuses, and this student will be disciplined in accordance with the state's zero tolerance policy," the statement said. The zero-tolerance policy calls for "certain, swift and reasoned punishment" for students who bring drugs or guns to school, which could include expulsion.

Some television media personalities arrived at Trump Tower in New York City Monday afternoon to meet with President-elect Donald Trump. NBC's Lester Holt, Chuck Todd, and president Debora Turness were among the attendees. CNN's Jeff Zucker, Erin Burnett, and Wolf Blitzer were also present. Fox News executives Bill Shine, Jack Abernethy, Jay Wallace, Suzanne Scott, CBS's John Dickerson, Norah O'Donnell, Gayle King, and Charlie Rose entered the building. ABC's George Stephanopoulos, Martha Raddatz, and David Muir were also present. MSNBC's president Phil Griffin was also reportedly in attendance. The meeting was reportedly "Off the Record." Some reporters and executives did not speak to their press colleagues outside elevators or waved. When a reporter asked Chuck Todd what he was doing there, he shrugged his shoulders and said, "I wish I knew!" He added, "Here's what I'm going to fight for. A protective pool."

President Donald Trump on Friday blamed Iran for attacks on two oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman. "Iran did do it, and you know they did it because you saw the boat, I guess one of the mines didn't explode and it's probably got essentially Iran written all over it," Trump said during a phone interview on Fox and Friends on Friday morning. He said it was obvious Iran was covering up their role in attacking the tankers by trying to secretly remove the unexploded mine. "They're a nation of terror," Trump said. "They've changed a lot since I've been president, they were unstoppable and now they're in deep, deep trouble." Trump said Iran was flourishing in the Obama administration, actively involved in 14 different conflicts in the Middle East, but they were "pulling back." "I'm not looking to hurt that country, but they can't have a nuclear weapon, it's very simple," he said.

British officials voiced suspicions that a bomb destroyed a Russian plane over the Sinai Peninsula, killing 224 people. An American official said U.S. intelligence also has "a definite feeling it was an explosive device planted in luggage or somewhere on the plane." CNN reported that other U.S. officials also said their analysis is pointing toward a bomb attack. Based on this intelligence, CNN's source said ISIS, or a group affiliated with them, is most likely responsible for the attack. American officials noted their conclusions were tentative and a formal consensus had not been reached. The British government is holding an emergency meeting Wednesday afternoon on the plane crash and the safety of aviation in Egypt. The Russians believe there was an explosion aboard the plane, although they have so far been reluctant to declare it a terrorist attack or name ISIS as the likely perpetrator. The UK Telegraph reported that Russian president Vladimir Putin's political situation could be delicate, with he may gain more public support for action in Syria due to public outrage, or his government might be criticized for allowing the destruction of the plane.

Former CIA Director John Brennan appeared Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." Brennan, whose security clearance has been revoked by President Donald Trump, said he believed Trump's behavior was "treasonous." Brennan said, "I called his behavior treasonous which is to betray one's trust and to aiding and abet the enemy and I stand very much by that claim." He continued, "I think these are abnormal times and I think a lot of people have spoken out against what Mr. Trump has done. And maybe it's my warning, training as an intelligence professional. I have seen the lights blinking red in terms of what Mr. Trump has done and is doing and is bringing this country down on the global stage and fueling and feeding divisiveness in our country." He added, "He continually lies to the American people. The type of things he is doing, I need to speak out. I don't believe I'm being political at all. I am not a Republican. I am not a Democrat."

All three judges that will hear Tuesday's arguments on the constitutionality of President Obama's health care law were appointed by Democratic presidents, including Obama himself. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit made the announcement shortly before the trial started, even though the case has been scheduled for months. Judges Diana Motz, the senior member of the panel, was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1994. Andre Davis and James Wynn were appointed by Obama. The hearing in Richmond is the first appellate review of Obama's signature legislation passed last year, and combines two cases. The first case was brought by Liberty University, and the second case was brought by the government after losing to Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinell. The judges were randomly selected by computer a couple of months ago. They have presumably been reading briefs in the case ever since. The full 14 member Fourth Circuit is evenly split between Republican and Democratic judges, but only three judges hear any given case. The fact that the judges are Democratic appointees does not mean they will decide to uphold the law in the end, but this has been one of the most partisan issues around the country in recent memory.

White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said on Tuesday's broadcast of the Fox News Channel's "Hannity" that President Trump accepted House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's invitation to give the State of the Union address at the House. Sanders said, "Nancy Pelosi invited the president. He accepted. She cited security concerns as a potential reason to delay that. The United States Secret Service and DHS have addressed those concerns. And we're moving forward until something changes on that front." Sanders also discussed the possibility of having the speech take place elsewhere, stating, "I don't know if there would be a place that all of those members would attend, but the president's focus is on speaking to the American people. ... And if Nancy Pelosi chooses to go in that direction, the president will continue to speak to the American people, and I'm sure that he'll do that on that evening as well."

Sarah Palin appeared on Sean Hannity's airwaves this week to discuss her 2008 predictions that Russia's Vladimir Putin would take advantage of President Obama's weak overseas policies. Palin said the Russian invasion of Crimea shows her prediction to be true. "Anybody who carries the common-sense gene knows that Putin doesn't change his stripes," she said. Palin also said a weak United States opens the door for other nations, like Russia, to take the international stage, a scenario that leads to bold foreign strikes, such as the one going forth in Ukraine. Palin said Putin is seen as a leader who "wrestles bears and drills for oil," while Obama is perceived as one with serious "weakness," and as a man who "wears mom jeans and equivocates and bloviates." Palin also said Obama's foreign policy is "leading from behind," and other nations will soon be "taking advantage of that weakness in America at this point," Mediaite reported.

President Donald Trump said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that he felt betrayed by his former campaign strategist Steve Bannon after Bannon made unvarnished comments about the president's family were published in a book about the presidency. "I feel betrayed because you're not supposed to do that," Trump said. When asked if the relationship was over permanently, Trump replied, "We'll see what happens. I don't know what the word permanent means." Trump made the comments after news broke that Bannon would testify to Congress about the Russian collusion investigation. The president had criticized Bannon, accusing him of unfairly taking credit for his election win. "Steve's greatest asset is that he was able to convince a corrupt media that he was responsible for my win," Trump said. He asserted that his former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and his deputy campaign manager David Bossie deserve more credit than Bannon. "Steve had nothing to do with my win, or certainly very little," he said.

A letter to the editor stated that Hillary Rodham Clinton is not the best Democratic presidential candidate. The writer said they are tired of wordsmithing and hair-splitting regarding her emails and the issue of classification. The writer said information fed by her campaign and its supporting pedants is nonsense. The writer cited several points that the writer said are germane. First, the writer said it is unimportant to learn whether Clinton's email communications were marked with some classification. The writer said Clinton was the secretary of state at the time and as such she should have known that virtually all her official communications had some classification, including her schedule. The writer said mixing personal and official communications is not a very smart thing to do, and that mixing them on a personal server located in a private, non-governmental residence is dumb. The writer said that when listening to what Clinton says about anything, her explanations are akin to a ball in a pin-ball machine: They never seem to be consistent or true. The writer said Bernie Sanders is consistent and truthful, and asked why the country is ignoring a fine person like Martin O'Malley.

Freedom Industries, a West Virginia company at the center of a chemical spill that left 300,000 residents without water for days, has won a $4 million bankruptcy deal with a lender that will help it continue operations. The terms of the arrangement allow that Freedom Industries' 51 employees will continue to get paid and so will vendors. The company will start concerted clean-up efforts at the site of the Elk River spill, said Freedom Industries attorney Mark Freelander to The Associated Press. Freedom Industries President Gary Southern testified in bankruptcy court that the Jan. 9 chemical spill has left his company and the community "completely chaotic," AP said. He also said his company has already spent $800,000 to fix environmental damages in the past week. The chemical company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protections, a move that immediately halted dozens of lawsuits that were filed by businesses and residents. Meanwhile, state and federal investigators are still trying to determine what led to the spill of the coal-cleaning chemical into the water. The company's biweekly payroll amounts to about $172,000, AP reported.

US President Donald Trump said Friday following his summit with Kim Jong Un that he has "largely solved" the North Korean nuclear problem. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump said President Barack Obama told him before he took office that the "most dangerous problem" for the United States was North Korea's nuclear weapons program. "I have solved that problem," Trump said. "Now we're getting it memorialized and all but that problem is largely solved." "We signed a very good document," he said. "But more importantly than the document I have a good relationship with Kim Jong Un. That's a very important thing. I can now call him. I gave him a very direct number. He can now call me if he has any difficulty. We have communication. People are shocked. They thought Trump was going to get in, he's going to start throwing bombs all over the place. It's actually the opposite."

The article reports that the Supreme Court justices will not uphold or strike down Proposition 8, citing a Kennedy-related concern that the issue is too soon to rule on the same-sex marriage issue. The article states that Proposition 8 will stay invalidated. The article states that the nine justices are "very uncomfortable striking down" Proposition 8 and suggests dismissing the case, which would leave in place a 9th Circuit ruling favoring same-sex marriage. A subsequent update states Proposition 8 is unlikely to be upheld or struck down, and that the Court will decide the case in 30 minutes. The article also states that in the past, the site has been quoted favorably in mainstream media. The article argues that the unbiased, objective, not-at-all-liberal media should stop criticizing the site. The article asserts that there is nothing the unbiased, objective, not-at-all-liberal media hates more than a buzz-killing party pooper.

On June 5, the U.S. Senate voted 78 to 17 to confirm Sylvia Burwell, Obama's appointee for secretary of Health and Human Services. The confirmation process proceeded through a fast-tracked process with bipartisan support. All Republican presidential contenders voted "no" on the confirmation. With Senate approval, Burwell will replace retiring Kathleen Sebelius as head of HHS. Her most difficult responsibility will be to push regulations for President Obama's Obamacare law. Burwell's confirmation was swift and devoid of protracted debate over her suitability. All three Republican senators considered for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016 cast no votes. Her most significant government experience was as an economic adviser to Bill Clinton. She led his economic transition team in 1992 and went on to stints at agencies including the National Economic Council and the Office of Management and Budget during the Clinton years. After Clinton left office, one of Burwell's longest-held jobs was at the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.

Roger Stone, a longtime confidant of President Trump, late Monday formally apologized for posting a picture on Instagram of U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson with what appeared to be crosshairs next to her face. Stone's attorneys said in a court filing: "Roger J. Stone hereby apologizes to the Court for the improper photograph and comment posted on Instagram today." Earlier in the day, Stone posted a picture of Jackson on his Instagram with what appeared to be crosshairs in the background. The photo was quickly deleted. A caption below the photo depicted Judge Jackson as a partisan judge who has targeted conservatives. Stone was arrested last month during an FBI raid of his Florida home. He is charged with obstruction of justice and lying to Congress. He posted a statement on Instagram later Monday saying that "any inference that this was meant to threaten the judge or disrespect the court is categorically false." The statement also said the image next to Judge Jackson's head was not crosshairs but the "logo of the organization that originally posted it."

A Pew Research Center survey shows the Supreme Court's favorability rating remains close to an all-time low. Among Americans overall, 52 percent view the court favorably and 31 percent unfavorably. Forty-seven percent of Republicans have a favorable opinion, up from 38 percent in July, following discussions about health care reform. The favorable sentiment among Democrats fell from 64 percent to 56 percent. The survey also found that about as many conservative Republicans say the Supreme Court is liberal as middle of the road (39 percent). Very few conservative Republicans, 9 percent, say the court is conservative. Nearly half of liberal Democrats say the Supreme Court is conservative; 31 percent say it is middle of the road, and 15 percent view the court's ideology as liberal.

New York Democrats flipped a Republican-held New York State Assembly seat Tuesday that had been in Republican control for nearly 40 years. Steve Stern, a former Suffolk County legislator who ran as the Democrat candidate, defeated Republican candidate and civil litigator Janet Smitelli in the race to represent the 10th Assembly District in Long Island. Stern won with 59 percent of the vote, while Smitelli had 42 percent of the vote in the special election to fill a seat vacated by Republican Chad Lupinacci. The district had been in Republican hands since 1978. Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton and former President Barack Obama carried the district in the 2016 and 2012 elections. Voter registration in the state shows more Democrats are registered to vote in the district than Republicans. The Albany Times Union reported that Democrats had 6,000 more registered voters in the district than Republicans. In 2016, the Democrat candidate for New York Assembly in the 10th Assembly District lost by 9,000 votes. Two labor unions, the New York AFL-CIO and New York State United Teachers (NYSUT), supported Stern's candidacy, which Stern's campaign claimed caused higher turnout in a special election.

North Korea's state-run newspaper Rodong Sinmun reported that Kim Jong-un has been taking tours of meteorological buildings and complaining that weather forecasters are giving "too many incorrect" predictions, CNN reported. The news agency did not explicitly state that Kim threatened to take action against those responsible for the faulty forecasts. The photographs showed Kim appearing to criticize and chastise officials cast by the newspaper as meteorological experts. Kim said outdated weather equipment was partly to blame. He also said forecasters' scientific method could stand some improvement, CNN reported. He relayed the importance of providing accurate weather reports to protect citizens' lives and property from "abnormal climatic phenomenon," and to help agricultural and fisheries industries stabilize their production, the state-run news outlet reported, CNN said.

President Obama will issue an executive order on Thursday reversing the Bush administration policy that bans the use of federal dollars by non-govermental organizations that discuss or provide abortions outside the United States. The order will be signed on the 36th anniversary of the Roe v. Wade Supreme Court ruling that legalized abortion in all 50 states. The policy, known in governmental circles as the "Mexico City policy," requires any non-governmental organization to agree before receiving U.S. funds that they will "neither perform nor actively promote abortion as a method of family planning in other nations." The language was announced at the United Nations International Conference on Population in 1984 and was approved by President Reagan and originally drafted by his assistant secretary of state, Alan Keyes. Keyes ran unsuccessfully as the GOP nominee against Obama for the U.S. Senate in 2004. President George Herbert Walker Bush continued Reagan's Mexico City policy. President Bill Clinton issued an executive order lifting the ban on Jan. 22, 1993. President George W. Bush issued an executive order re-instating the ban on federal dollars for NGOs that discuss or provide abortions on Jan. 22, 2001.

President Trump posted a short video Friday afternoon that was based on a TIME Magazine cover from October 2018. The magazine's cover showed a series of "Trump" election signs, with the years extending until 2044. The cover read "How Trumpism outlasts Trump." In the president's version of the video, it zoomed in on one of the signs, superimposing a picture of himself hovering over it. Instead of stopping at 2044, the years continued to climb at a rapid rate until the sign read: "Trump 4EVA." The video was originally created by Twitter user Carpe Donktum. The president's comments received wide-ranging reviews, many from journalists and his most ardent supporters. Some critics have speculated whether Trump would leave office voluntarily after an election defeat. "Real Time" host Bill Maher, who is convinced he will not leave the White House if he loses in 2020, has speculated that Trump would leave the White House voluntarily after an election defeat.

The United States is threatening to cut aid, holding back approximately $800 million, nearly a third of the $2 billion that the country gives annually. Pakistan has responded by declaring it rejects conditional aid from the United States. Corps Commanders in the Pakistani Army say they will rely on their own resources instead. They also say they will pull troops from the Afghan border if the U.S. cuts aid, which they say will mean the Taliban will have free reign in the border region. Pakistan's Defense Minister said: "If Americans refuse to give us money, they okay. I think the next step is that the government or the armed forces will be moving from the border areas. We cannot afford to keep military out in the mountains for such a long period." The White House announced cutting aid. China declared it pledged to continue its support for Pakistan, calling it "a close ally."

Donna Brazile, the Democrat strategist who ran Al Gore's campaign, said Republican candidates who ignore the Tea Party do so at their peril. On ABC's This Week, Brazile said, "The Tea Party is still highly caffeinated," and acknowledged that the "Tea Party is the energy inside the Republican Party." Brazile said Cantor ignored Tea Party conservatives who also rose up in part to protest George W. Bush's expansion of the federal government, and he paid for it with his political career. Brazile said, "You ignore them, you ignore the base and that's a problem. And he ignored the base." Breitbart News reported that only after Brat began criticizing Cantor on amnesty did his broader message tying Cantor to crony capitalism resonate. Palin has been hammering this message for years and throughout her political career, including in a 2011 speech in Iowa.

In a preview clip of an interview set to air on Fox News Channel's Tuesday broadcast of "Fox & Friends," President Donald Trump said Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were "outplayed" by North Korea. Trump said, "I don't want to telegraph what I'm doing or what I'm thinking. I'm not like other administrations, where they say we're going to do this in four weeks. It doesn't work that way. We'll see what happens. I hope things work out well. I hope there's going to be peace, but they've been talking with this gentleman for a long time. You read Clinton's book and he said, 'Oh, we made such a great peace deal' and it was a joke. You look at different things over the years with President Obama. Everybody has been outplayed. They've all been outplayed by this gentleman and we'll see what happens. I just don't telegraph my moves."

Democratic and Republican members of Congress sat together for President Obama's State of the Union speech Tuesday night. Rep. Paul Broun, a medical doctor by profession, posted on Twitter at the end of Obama's address to the nation. In a tweet at the end of the address, Broun wrote: "Mr. President, you don't believe in the Constitution. You believe in socialism." Other Broun tweets included: * Corporate tax rates should be zero. Those were only a sampling of Broun's State of the Union tweets. Broun has previously criticized the administration. In 2009, he criticized the president and Democrats for their health care reform proposal. He said that if the proposal became law — which it did — then "when mama falls and breaks her hip, she'll just lie in her bed in pain until she dies with pneumonia because her needed surgery is not cost efficient."

U.S. Park police revealed a shooting outside the White House complex near West Executive Drive on 17th Street on Monday at 3:15 p.m. According to CNN, a suspect brandished a firearm outside the White House complex before being shot by Secret Service agents and taken into custody. Further reports indicated the shooting took place at 3:15 p.m. The shooter was a man. According to the DC Fire and Emergency Services, the man was transported with critical injuries to a local hospital. Reporters at the White House were told to seek shelter in the basement and remain in the building while Secret Service cleared the North Lawn. ABC News reported Vice President Joe Biden was at the White House at the time but was immediately secured. President Barack Obama was golfing at the time, having left earlier in the afternoon for the golf course at Andrews Air Force Base. A White House official said the situation is under control. "No one within or associated with the White House was injured, and everyone in the White House is safe and accounted for," the official said. "The president has been made aware of the situation."

In a preview clip of an interview set to air on Fox News Channel's Tuesday broadcast of "Fox & Friends," President Donald Trump said Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were "outplayed" by North Korea. Trump said, "I don't want to telegraph what I'm doing or what I'm thinking. I'm not like other administrations, where they say we're going to do this in four weeks. It doesn't work that way. We'll see what happens. I hope things work out well. I hope there's going to be peace, but they've been talking with this gentleman for a long time. You read Clinton's book and he said, 'Oh, we made such a great peace deal' and it was a joke. You look at different things over the years with President Obama. Everybody has been outplayed. They've all been outplayed by this gentleman and we'll see what happens. I just don't telegraph my moves."

Billionaire Microsoft founder and philanthropist Bill Gates visited Trump Tower on Tuesday afternoon for a visit with President-elect Donald Trump. Earlier in the day, Gates praised Trump on CNBC for his message to make America a better place economically and compared him to former President John F. Kennedy. Gates said: "In the same way President Kennedy talked about the space mission and got the country behind that, I think whether it's education or stopping epidemics, other health breakthroughs, finishing polio and in this energy space, there can be a very upbeat message that his administration is going to organize things, get rid of regulatory barriers, and have American leadership through innovation." Gates said he spoke with the president-elect on the phone after the election and appeared upbeat that he would pursue "the power of innovation." Gates spent most of his interview promoting his new initiative to move the world into a "green" clean energy future. Gates said: "I think this administration likes a good deal," signaling his hope that Washington D.C. would increase the research and development spending for cheap sources of clean energy.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) appeared Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union." Warner said President Donald Trump has "parroted" the policies of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Warner said, "That's the defining question of our investigation and the Mueller investigation; was there collusion? I'm not going to talk about what we may have been briefed in the gang of eight when these investigations opened. But I do think it's curious that throughout that whole summer when these investigations started, you had Vladimir Putin policies almost being parroted by Donald Trump." He added, "You had Trump say only nice things about Putin. He never spoke ill about Russia. The Republican campaign doctrines softened on Russia. And decreased their willingness to defend Ukraine. There was a series of outside actions. We all remember when Trump and his bluster basically said to the Russians, 'if you've got more e-mails, bring them on.' These are not actions of a traditional president for the United States."

State Law Enforcement Division Chief Reggie Lloyd said Thursday that Gov. Mark Sanford did not improperly use state funds for visits with his Argentine mistress. Lloyd said Sanford did not break any laws. The governor's spokesman said he does not intend to resign. South Carolina's attorney general asked police to investigate the governor's travel after Sanford revealed to The Associated Press he had spent time with Maria Belen Chapur more often than previously disclosed. Sanford has given two personal checks totaling $3,300 to the state treasurer as reimbursement for part of a taxpayer-funded trip to South America last year. He says the money covered lodging, meals and airfare to Buenos Aires, where he saw Chapur. Top South Carolina Republicans have called for Sanford to step down.

Republican Senate candidate Joni Ernst, a native of Iowa, said in an advertisement released in 2014 that she knows how to cut pork in Washington because she grew up castrating pigs on her farm in Iowa. In the advertisement, Ernst states: "I grew up castrating hogs on an Iowa farm, so when I come to Washington, I'll know how to cut pork. Washington is full of big spenders. Let's make 'em squeal." The advertisement features Ernst wearing a vest and flannel shirt and shots of pigs in pens. Ernst, currently an Iowa state senator, will face a Republican primary field in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin. She is one of five GOP candidates competing against Rep. Bruce Braley, who is running unopposed on the Democratic side.

Secretary of State Mike Pompeo plans to travel to Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Speaker of the Knesset Benny Gantz, the department said Friday. The two leaders will discuss efforts to fight the COVID-19 pandemic, security issues, and threats from Iran. Pompeo will depart for Israel on Wednesday. The department said he will meet with Netanyahu and Gantz, who last month agreed on a unity government after three close elections. The three leaders will discuss efforts to fight the COVID-19 pandemic, security issues, and threats from Iran. State Department spokeswoman Morgan Ortagus said: "The U.S. commitment to Israel has never been stronger than under President [Donald] Trump's leadership. The United States and Israel will face threats to the security and prosperity of our people together." Pompeo's trip will be his first since March 23, when he traveled to Afghanistan amid efforts by leaders there to form a new government. After discussions with President Ashraf Ghani and Chief Executive Abdullah Abdullah, Pompeo announced the United States' plan to cut $1 billion in assistance.

Rep. Tim Murphy, a Pennsylvania Republican, said Tuesday that both General Motors and the nation's highway safety body "messed up pretty bad" in failing to recall cars with an ignition-switch problem linked to more than a dozen deaths. Murphy, a member of the House Oversight and Commerce Committee, will hear from GM CEO Mary Barra on Tuesday before his subcommittee. Murphy said something terrible went wrong within the company. He said the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration "also knew something was wrong" and will have to answer for its oversight. NHTSA acting administrator David Friedman is also set to testify before Murphy's subcommittee. GM is accused of knowing about the switch problem since 2005 but doing little to rectify the situation. Since then, relatives of motorists who died in car crashes linked to the problem have come forward and demanded answers from the company, which also received billions in bailout money from the U.S. government after the 2008 economic recession. GM has recalled millions of vehicles because of the revelations.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a 2020 presidential hopeful, appeared Sunday on CBS's "Face the Nation." She said the anti-abortion laws being passed in several states was a result of President Donald Trump starting "a war" on women's reproductive freedoms. Gillibrand said, "This is nothing short of all-out assault on women's reproductive freedoms. An effort to take away our human rights and civil rights make no mistake. Make no mistake, the 30 states that are trying to unwind abortion rights are trying to get rid of Roe v. Wade. It's nothing more complex than that. They do not believe that women should have the right to make the most intimate, personal, life, and death decision, and I think it's untenable. I hope American people are paying attention because President Trump has started a war on America's women if it's a fight he wants to have it's a fight he's going to have, and he's going to lose."

Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI) appeared on CNN's "New Day" on Friday. She responded to a report that President Donald Trump has his eyes on former Attorney General William Barr to serve as attorney general and State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert to serve as United Nations ambassador to replace outgoing Nikki Haley. Hirono questioned Barr's nomination as Jeff Sessions' replacement, arguing that Trump is looking for people who will "protect him" and "cover for him." Barr has defended former FBI Director James Comey's firing and has been critical of FBI special counsel Robert Mueller's team. Regarding Nauert's nomination, Hirono said she would have "difficulty" supporting her due to her lack of experience. "I do not know that being loyal to the president is the uppermost qualification. It is for the president, but it isn't for me," Hirono said. She added that Trump "very clearly" struggles to find experienced and qualified people for jobs within the administration.

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that National Security Agency Director Gen. Keith Alexander offered to resign earlier this year following leaks by former contractor Edward Snowden. The Journal said the Obama administration declined Alexander's offer because it did not want Snowden to win a political victory and calculated that Alexander's resignation would not fix the NSA's problems. A former senior defense official said some top administration officials found their confidence in Alexander shaken because he presided over a grave security lapse. The officials also did not think his resignation would solve the security problem and were concerned that letting him leave would wrongly hand Snowden a win. There was speculation throughout the summer as to why the administration had not asked Alexander to resign. President Barack Obama had dismissed senior military leaders for less serious lapses, as in 2010, when he fired Gen. Stanley McChrystal, then the head of U.S. forces in Afghanistan, for negative comments about the President and Vice President attributed to his staff by a reporter for Rolling Stone magazine.

Jeb Bush's mother, Barbara Bush, has expressed support for a potential presidential campaign. Barbara Bush previously said publicly that "we've had enough Bushes" in the White House. In a Monday interview on Bloomberg's "Street Smart" program, Neil Bush said he did not know if Jeb Bush would decide to enter the race but emphasized that Barbara Bush is "starting to swing a little bit" in favor of running. Neil Bush said Jeb Bush has to decide whether he wants his family to go through this and enter the campaign fray with joy. Jeb Bush has said his support for amnesty legislation and Common Core will turn off conservatives. He has also said a candidate must be willing to lose the primary in order to win the general and said he would decide "in short order" whether to run for president.

On Thursday, former Florida Governor Jeb Bush appeared on Fox News Radio's "Kilmeade and Friends" and was asked whether former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton should voluntarily turn over the Clintons' private server, which stored all her email from her tenure as secretary of state. Bush replied, "I don't know." When asked whether he thought Clinton should turn over her server, Bush said, "I don't know. I don't know what the laws are. I think being clear and transparent in a world of deep disaffection where people don't trust folks is the right thing to do. That's why we unveiled 200, and whatever it was, and 80 thousand emails." Former President George W. Bush jokingly referred to Clinton as his "sister-in-law." Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-SC) and House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) have asked Clinton to turn over the server.

Walker is expected to formally enter the Republican presidential race on Monday. A social media message read "Scott is in. Are you? Join our team today." The tweet included a photo of the governor with "Scott Walker is running for president" superimposed on it. The tweet has since been deleted. A Twitter spokesman said in a statement to Fox News: "We're looking into today's issue, and we've determined the Walker team was not at fault." Throughout the day, Walker aides remained adamant about his upcoming announcement Monday. Rick Wiley, another aide, replied to a message about Walker's announcement: "Set your DVR for 5pm on Monday bro, it will be epic." Walker is expected to enter the race. He has spent months touring the country, trying to court voters on his way to entering the race.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, and Sen. Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, discussed a lifetime ban on former members of Congress who become lobbyists. Ocasio-Cortez wrote on Twitter: "If you are a member of Congress + leave, you shouldn't be allowed to turn right around&leverage your service for a lobbyist check. I don't think it should be legal at ALL to become a corporate lobbyist if you've served in Congress." Cruz said he would work across the aisle to get the ban done. "The Swamp would hate it," Cruz tweeted. Ocasio-Cortez said she wanted a "clean" bill deadline specifically addressing the lobbying issue. It is not clear what Cruz has in mind legislatively, but he sounded eager to try something.

The Justice Department released a 20-page opinion Wednesday outlining why Matthew Whitaker can legally serve as the interim Attorney General. President Donald Trump appointed Whitaker following the resignation of Attorney General Jeff Sessions last Wednesday. The department argues Whitaker's appointment was lawful under a statute called the Vacancies Reform Act. The department's Office of Legal Counsel offers advice to the executive branch but its guidance does not carry the force of law. Department officials had previously advised the White House that Trump could designate Whitaker as acting attorney general, a senior Justice Department official said Wednesday. The department wrote in its opinion: "As all three branches of government have long recognized, the President may designate an acting official to perform the duties of a vacant principal office, including a Cabinet office, even when the acting official has not been confirmed by the Senate."

On Friday, NBC's "Meet the Press" host Chuck Todd criticized Fox News for not taking action against host Sean Hannity when he did not disclose he was a client of Trump's attorney Michael Cohen while commenting on FBI raids on Cohen's office. Todd said, "Sean Hannity can do what he wants to do, but I'm surprised Fox isn't making him, at a minimum, disclose a conflict every time he talks about this." Todd also criticized a post on Hannity's website titled "The Utter Hypocrisy of Chuck Todd," which highlighted Todd's wife, who was a Democratic consultant. Todd said, "What I take offense to on that is — that's my wife, that's not me. I think it's a ridiculous place that we're in society that it's guilt by association."

Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a 50-year-old mother of two, has decided to run for governor in 2014, sources confirmed to Fox News. Davis intends to file paperwork for the race Wednesday or Thursday of next week. The filibuster at the Texas Capitol temporarily blocked new statewide abortion restrictions from being passed in June. The abortion bill, signed into law by Gov. Rick Perry, requires doctors to have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, allow abortions only in surgical centers, limits where and when women may take abortion-inducing pills, and ban abortions after 20 weeks. Davis' filibuster drew hundreds of supporters to the Texas state capitol and drew a mention from President Obama's campaign Twitter account. No other Texas Democrats have entered the governor's race. Republican Attorney General Greg Abbott announced his candidacy this summer and is the early favorite to succeed Gov. Rick Perry. Perry is not seeking re-election after 14 years in office.

Broadway's Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda joined President Obama in the Rose Garden on Monday and performed a rap song about civic terminology. The two-minute freestyle session showed Obama holding up cards with the words "Constitution," "Obamacare," and "NASA" written on them. As Obama flipped the cards, Miranda sang lyrics off the top of his head about the key words. "Constitution, the POTUS, I'm freestylin.' You know this," he sang as seen in a video clip posted to the White House Facebook page. The Grammy-winning Hamilton cast also mingled with first lady Michelle Obama. The first lady had the cast perform for a group of high schoolers visiting the White House. Monday was not Miranda's first visit to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. Six years ago, Miranda performed the song "Alexander Hamilton" in the East Room of the White House.

Mitt Romney's campaign borrowed $20 million before the Republican convention to stay competitive until federal rules allowed it to tap general election campaign funds, according to a report by the National Review that was confirmed to Fox News by the campaign. The National Review article notes that Federal Election Commission rules barred the campaign from using general election funds until Romney was officially nominated, even though his nomination was a foregone conclusion leading up to the late-August convention in Tampa, Fla. Borrowing the money to improve cash flow in the meantime is permitted by the FEC, a campaign aide told the National Review, saying similar arrangements have been made by past campaigns. The campaign was able to "collateralize this debt with $20 million of general-election funds that were already sitting in our bank account," the aide said. A senior campaign advisor told Fox News the campaign is not in debt because of the loan as its cash on hand exceeds its liability. "Basically, this shows how we smartly took advantage of the finance law to stay competitive during the primary," the adviser said. The campaign has paid back $9 million, the conservative magazine reported.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie responded to a former White House physician who said on national television earlier this week that his health could not handle the rigors of being president. Dr. Connie Mariano, an ex-Navy physician who headed the Medical Unit in the White House during President Bill Clinton's administration, said on CNN that Mr. Christie — who had appeared on "Late Show With David Letterman" on Monday — could die in office if he were elected president, United Press International reported. Mr. Christie responded at a Wednesday news conference, saying, "This is just another hack who wants five minutes on TV," and explaining that the doctor had never even examined him, according to UPI. Dr. Mariano had already addressed that line of argument in her CNN appearance, during which she said that in cases involving body types such as Mr. Christie's, up-close examinations were not necessary. "When I see someone who looks like him, you don't have to be a White House doctor to be concerned about health issues," she said during her CNN appearance, UPI reported.

President Donald Trump said federal authorities are making progress on discovering the motives of the Las Vegas shooter. "They're learning a lot more, and that'll be announced at the appropriate time," Trump said as he was leaving the White House for a trip to Las Vegas to visit with victims and first responders to the country music festival shooting that killed 59 people and wounded hundreds. "It's a very sad thing. We're going to pay our respects and to see the police who have done really a fantastic job in a very short time," Trump said. First Lady Melania Trump is also traveling with the president on the trip. "It's a very, very sad day for me, personally," President Trump told reporters. The president plans to meet with victims and medical staff at a Las Vegas hospital later this afternoon as well as some law enforcement officials and first responders who responded to the shooting.

Stormy Daniels has filed a lawsuit against President Trump alleging defamation. According to a document filed Monday with the U.S. District Court for Central California, Daniels, an adult-film star whose real name is Stephanie Clifford, claims that Michael Cohen insinuated, falsely, that she lied when claiming she had a sexual affair in 2006-07 with Trump, then a reality-TV star and real-estate mogul. The document amends a lawsuit that sought to declare null and void a non-disclosure agreement that Clifford signed in 2006. The amended lawsuit also says the $130,000 Cohen paid Clifford as "hush money" out of his own funds in October 2016 was a campaign contribution that, because the amount and the fact it was not disclosed publicly, violated federal laws. Earlier on Monday, Cohen filed a cease-and-desist order against Clifford over her "60 Minutes" interview, in which she made explicit her longtime claims of an affair with Trump in 2006-07.

On Wednesday, during NBC's "Megyn Kelly Today," audience members booed and laughed at Lanny Davis after she asked for donations to continue to tell the truth about Michael Cohen. Davis said, "Could I take one opportunity to remind everyone that Michael Cohen has suffered a tragic and difficult experience with his family. He's without resources, and we've set up a website called michaelcohentruth.com, that we're hoping that he will get some help from the American people so he can continue to tell the truth." After the audience jeered and laughed, host Megyn Kelly said, "The audience, they don't appear ready to donate Lanny." The audience booed again after Davis said, "I would say the reaction of your audience maybe they are not as interested in getting the truth out about Donald Trump as many other people in the country. Approximately 60 percent of the country would not have the reaction of your audience."

President Barack Obama canceled White House tours due to the sequester but hosted a steak dinner for twelve Republican senators on Wednesday. According to the White House, the dinner included steak, salad, sautéed vegetables and coconut sorbet. On Wednesday, RNC chairman Reince Priebus said that since the president has been complaining loudly about the cutbacks they have had to make at the White House—including tours for schoolchildren—due to the sequester, it would be more appropriate if the country's leaders also dined on a budget. Priebus said he would like to order pizza for them and have it delivered to the White House. Priebus said if the pizza will illuminate an important economic point for President Obama: instead of redistributing the slices, the best way to make everyone happy is to make the pie bigger, which is as true for dinner as it is for economic growth and opportunity. The senators reportedly discussed gun control, immigration reform, and the debt with Obama.

President Trump on Sunday suggested that thousands of Tax Day protesters in cities across the country over the weekend were paid and called for "someone" to investigate who funded the effort. The president tweeted about the rallies about 9 a.m. on Easter Sunday. Saturday's Tax Day protests included rallies in New York City; Chicago; Washington, D.C.; and near his golf course in West Palm Beach, Florida, and elsewhere. The protests were aimed at pressuring Mr. Trump to release his federal income tax returns, which he has refused to do despite questions about his financial ties around the world. In criticizing the protests, Mr. Trump questioned the motives of the demonstrators and said the question of his tax returns was settled in the November election. "I did what was an almost impossible thing to do for a Republican — easily won the Electoral College! Now Tax Returns are brought up again?" Mr. Trump tweeted before following up seven minutes later with accusations about the protests themselves. "Someone should look into who paid for the small organized rallies yesterday. The election is over!" he tweeted.

President Donald Trump commented on the disqualification of Maximum Security at the Kentucky Derby on Saturday. The horse had led from the start and was initially awarded the victory. On Sunday, Trump wrote on Twitter: "The Kentucky Derby decision was not a good one. It was a rough and tumble race on a wet and sloppy track, actually, a beautiful thing to watch." The stewards ruled that Maximum Security interfered with other horses in the final turn, disqualifying the horse. The decision made Country House the winner, the first time it occurred in the history of the Derby. Trump wrote: "Only in these days of political correctness could such an overturn occur. The best horse did NOT win the Kentucky Derby – not even close!"

Former GOP presidential candidate John McCain gave his support Monday to fellow party member Robert Ehrlich in his attempt to retake the Maryland governorship. McCain said after a meeting at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, Md., that Ehrlich is a "fine guy" and has his endorsement, according to the Associated Press. In the state's Republican primary Tuesday, Ehrlich faces business investor Brain Murphy, who has been endorsed by Sarah Palin, McCain's running mate in 2008. Ehrlich is expected to win the primary, then continue in what polls show is a tight race with incumbent Democratic Gov. Martin O'Malley, who defeated Ehrlich in 2006.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani tweeted for his own RouhaniCare initiative. The president's account tweeted: "Gov will extend medical insurance to all Iranians. First step will be to cover 5mn uninsured Iranians by the social safety net #RouhaniCare." One Twitter user asked: "Will the website work?" The Huffington Post's Mehdi Hasan wrote: "Obama must sue for trademark violation." The Daily Caller's Jim Antle wrote: "Now the Iranians are just trolling." MSNBC's Christopher Hayes wrote: "#RouhaniCare is the hashtag of the day. Not even close." Wall Street Journal columnist Sadanand Dhume tweeted: "In spirit of cooperation, feel free to copy US website." BuzzFeed's Andrew Kaczynski said: "If you like your plan you can keep it." Rouhani's account is not verified by Twitter and is thought to be run by his aides.

The Republican National Committee criticized the CNBC debate moderators' performance. RNC Chairman Reince Priebus released a statement stating, "the performance by the CNBC moderators was extremely disappointing and did a disservice to their network, our candidates, and voters." A source inside the RNC told The Daily Caller they are discussing options for the future, adding, "nobody in the building is happy with what happened right now." RNC insiders said there are limits to how much control the party can exert over topics and questioners. Priebus said he will fight to make future debates more about issues than the moderators. Priebus said he is proud of his team for standing up against what he called an improper and unprofessional display put on by CNBC. CNBC responded that a candidate should be able to handle such questions. CNBC said: "People who want to be President of the United States should be able to answer tough questions."
