Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, said Tuesday on the Senate floor that President Trump should thank his predecessor, President Obama, for the economy's booming growth. Schumer said the president would be eager to defend the accomplishments of his nascent administration and take credit for a healthy American economy, pointing to low employment, job growth, and a soaring stock market. Schumer said these trends were present before Trump took office. Schumer said Trump was handed an already healthy economy by his predecessor, and like many things in his life, he inherited the healthy economy. Schumer said Obama created more jobs in the last year of his term than Trump created in the first year. Schumer said if Trump were going to pat himself on the back, give a shout out to Barack Obama.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said during an interview with Yahoo News' Skullduggery podcast that a Joe Biden presidential run "doesn't particularly animate me." She said she understands why people would be excited by the idea of Obama being vice president, but there is an emotional element to that. "I understand why people would be excited by that, this idea that we can go back to the good old days with Obama, with Obama's vice president. There's an emotional element to that, but I don't want to go back. I want to go forward," she said. Ocasio-Cortez said she does not have a candidate in the 2020 election field. She mentioned her support for Sens. Bernard Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. "I'm very supportive of Bernie's run. I haven't endorsed anybody, but I'm very supportive of Bernie. I also think what Elizabeth Warren has been bringing to the table is truly remarkable, truly remarkable and transformational," she said. Biden has not announced his candidacy to face President Trump in the 2020 presidential election despite being the frontrunner in many polls.

Caitlyn Jenner used the women's restroom at the Trump International Hotel and Tower in Manhattan without incident. The Republican presidential candidate said last week that transgender people should be able to use whichever bathroom they choose. Trump said North Carolina's "bathroom law," which directs transgender people to use the bathroom that matches the gender on their birth certificates, has caused unnecessary strife. Trump said that if Jenner, who won an Olympic gold medal as Bruce Jenner, were to walk into Trump Tower, she could use whichever bathroom she wanted. Jenner used the women's room without incident.

House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) said Thursday that he believes Alabama's latest move against abortion, which bans almost all abortions in the state, goes too far. "It goes further than I believe, yes," McCarthy stated during a press conference after being asked about the new abortion law. He continued by reaffirming his position on abortion, stating, "First of all, I believe the most precious gift God gives us is life. And I defended my pro-life position my whole political career." McCarthy also stated that he has believed in three exceptions to abortion, which include "rape, incest, and life of the mother." He added, "That's exactly what Republicans have voted on in this House. That's what our platform says." McCarthy also said he believes many of his Republican colleagues stand in agreement with him. Gov. Kay Ivey signed the bill, which does not include exceptions for rape and incest, into law Wednesday evening. The new law also seeks to criminally punish any doctor who performs an abortion.

West Virginia Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin said Friday he will vote to confirm Republican Sen. Jeff Sessions as attorney general. Sessions needs a simple majority in the Senate to confirm him. Republicans will control 52 Senate seats by December if the GOP wins Louisiana's special election. Manchin's state voted for President-Elect Donald Trump, with every single county voting Republican and giving him 68.7 percent of the vote. Manchin is one of several Democrats in vulnerable seats, with Democratic seats in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Florida, and Ohio also up for grabs. All five states voted for Trump, with Pennsylvania turning red for the first Republican presidential candidate since 1988. Republicans could hold a filibuster-proof majority after mid-term elections if they win those 10 seats in the states which Trump won. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has also announced he supports Sessions for attorney general. Sessions was the first Senator to endorse Trump.

White House counselor Kellyanne Conway accused CNN's Anderson Cooper of sexism on Thursday after an appearance on his show earlier in the week. Conway said on Fox News: "Let me tell you something, Hillary Clinton is in search of sexism as an excuse for why her disastrous candidacy and campaign lost six months ago. I face sexism a lot of times when I show up for interviews like that." Cooper rolled his eyes while interviewing Conway on Thursday. Conway was responding to a reel of past video clips of President Trump praising former FBI Director James B. Comey, who was recently fired by Trump. Conway said the clips were "conflating two things" but mentioned she was grateful for "the trip down memory lane." She reminded Cooper that Trump won Michigan, which prompted his eye roll. Conway said: "Could you imagine having a male anchor on a network roll [his] eyes at Hillary Clinton or a female representative spokeswoman for President Obama or President Bill Clinton? I think not."

A U.S. District Court judge issued a temporary block on Monday to North Dakota's new ban on abortions in cases where a heartbeat is detected in the fetus. The new state law could have an impact on those who are as early as six weeks pregnant. Judge Daniel Hovland in Bismarck called the law "clearly invalid and unconstitutional," The Associated Press reported. He issued the temporary injunction that prevents the law from taking effect until at least Aug. 1. "There is no question that [the law] is in direct contradiction to a litany of United States Supreme Court cases addressing restrains on abortion," the judge wrote, AP reported. "[It] is clearly an invalid and unconstitutional law based on the United States Supreme Court precedent in Roe v. Wade from 1973 … and the progeny of cases that have followed." The law cleared the Republican-controlled legislature and was signed into law by Gov. Jack Dalrymple earlier this year. The ban makes North Dakota one of the most restrictive in terms of abortion, AP reported.

According to a Monday evening Washington Post report, Mark Zuckerberg, the company's co-founder and CEO, has reportedly told close colleagues he would rather run Facebook than be president of the United States. The report states that Zuckerberg believes in Facebook's "unprecedented role in the world" and would rather lead the company than be president. When reporters recently questioned Zuckerberg during a conference call about whether someone else should lead Facebook, Zuckerberg was reportedly "adamant" that he was the right person to run the company. Zuckerberg had previously raised speculation about a potential presidential run in Iowa during photo opportunities and at Harvard commencement speeches, where he called for universal basic income and teared up while speaking about Dreamers and DACA recipients. He also said the fight against nationalism is the "struggle of our time." Zuckerberg will testify before the Senate Commerce and Judiciary Committees on Tuesday. On Wednesday, he will appear before the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

Two Democratic congressmen, Ted Lieu and Don Beyer, called on the Justice Department on Tuesday to criminally investigate Jared Kushner for omissions made during his security clearance process. Lieu, a member of the Judiciary Committee, and Beyer urged Attorney General William Barr to investigate whether Kushner made false statements on his security applications. "Ultimately, the President and his son-in-law have made a mockery of the security clearance process," they wrote. "Their actions put U.S. national security at risk and offend the thousands of dedicated career officials who both grant and receive clearances the correct way." Recently, reports surfaced that President Trump granted security clearance for his son-in-law and senior advisor despite concerns from other top officials in the administration, including former White House Counsel Don McGahn and former chief of staff John Kelly. In previous interviews, the president, his daughter Ivanka Trump, and an attorney for Kushner have all denied that Trump intervened in the security clearance process.

President Obama has extended his summer vacation on Martha's Vineyard to two weeks this year but will interrupt the golfing, biking and beaching with two days back at work in Washington. Mr. Obama and his family depart Saturday for Martha's Vineyard and he will fly back to the White House a week later, on Sunday Aug. 17, for two days of meetings before jetting back to the island Tuesday, Aug. 19, CNN reported. The return trip could signal that Mr. Obama will make a policy announcement, such as his anticipated moves to ease immigration laws, that would benefit from a backdrop that is more stately than a summer resort. Mr. Obama and his family have vacationed on the Massachusetts island every summer since he became president, except during his 2012 re-election campaign. In the past, it was always a one-week stint at the affluent summer colony. Similar to past presidents, Mr. Obama has faced criticism for taking vacations during crises at home and abroad. White House aides have insisted that the president is always on the job, keeping informed and issuing directives using secure communications equipment.

Margot Gerster, a mother of Hillary Clinton, went through the woods near Clinton's New York home on Tuesday after the Republican nominee Donald Trump defeated Hillary Clinton. Gerster wrote on Facebook that she was "heartbroken" about Clinton's defeat and decided to take her daughter Phoebe for a stroll to clear her head. Gerster said: "As we were leaving, I heard a bit of rustling coming towards me and as I stepped into the clearing there she was, Hillary Clinton and Bill with their dogs doing exactly the same thing as I was." Gerster said she hugged Clinton and talked to her and told her that one of her most proudest moments as a mother was taking Phoebe with her to vote for her. Clinton then posed for a picture, which Gerster confirmed to a Facebook commenter was taken by the 42nd President. Gerster said: "I do wish I'd asked [the Secret Service] to take one so he could be in it."

President Donald Trump signed a bill to create a national historic park in Atlanta honoring Martin Luther King Jr. The new law expands an existing historic site commemorating King to include the Prince Hall Masonic Temple. The temple served as the headquarters of an organization once headed by King, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The site currently includes King's childhood home and a church where he was a pastor, Ebenezer Baptist Church. Trump signed the legislation aboard Air Force One on Monday after arriving in Georgia to attend the college football championship game. He is being joined by King's niece Alveda King. White House spokesman Hogan Gidley says King made America "more just and free."

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll shows President Donald Trump with a job approval rating of 45 percent. In the same poll at this same point in his presidency, former President Obama's approval rating was 45 percent and the exact same disapproval rating of 52 percent. The poll also shows that Obama received coverage from establishment media during his presidency, comparing this to two-year hate campaigns the media launched against Trump. Among Republicans, Trump has an 86 percent approval rating. Independents approve at 34 percent, and Democrats approve at 11 percent. In the generic ballot that looks at the 2018 midterm elections, the lead for Democrats over the GOP has dropped to two points, 41 percent to 39 percent. One week ago, in the same poll, Democrats held a six-point lead. This drop in support for Democrats is in keeping with other polls released this week, which average out to just a two-point lead, down from seven points three weeks ago.

Florida Sen. Marco Rubio defended Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder on Thursday, stating the Republican governor took responsibility for the Flint water crisis. Rubio said Democrats were trying to politicize the issue. "I give the governor credit," Rubio said during the Fox News Republican debate held in Detroit. "He took responsibility for what happened and he's talked about being held responsible for it." Rubio criticized Democrats for the way they portrayed the situation in the media. Thursday's debate took place in Detroit, about 70 miles from Flint. The water crisis in Flint started after the city left the Detroit water system as part of a cost-saving measure in 2013. Despite warnings, officials did not treat the water from the Flint River, which caused lead to leach from pipes into the drinking water. Independent tests in August showed the water contained high levels of lead. In September, a pediatrician, Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha, compared blood tests and found a spike in lead poisonings in Flint.

White House physician Dr. Sean Conley said Tuesday that President Trump was reporting no symptoms after returning home on Monday night after receiving treatment for the coronavirus. Conley wrote in a memo that the president's team of physicians met with him in the residence. Conley said Trump had a restful first night at home and reported no symptoms. Conley said the president's vital signs and physical exam remained stable, with an ambulatory oxygen saturation level between 95 and 97 percent. Conley concluded that overall he continues to do extremely well and would provide updates as they know more. The president returned home from Walter Reed hospital Monday night after spending the weekend being treated for the virus. Doctors will monitor his ongoing recovery for the next several days. Conley told reporters on Monday afternoon that if he can get through to Monday with him remaining the same or improving better, they will all take that final sigh of relief.

An anonymous senior official in Donald Trump's administration confirmed the existence of the "deep state" resistance in the presidency. The official told Axios, "I find the reaction to the NYT op-ed fascinating — that people seem so shocked that there is a resistance from the inside." The official said some of them wished they had written the piece. The source added, "I hope he knows — maybe he does? — that there are dozens and dozens of us." On Thursday, Trump wrote on Twitter, "The Deep State and the Left, and their vehicle, the Fake News Media, are going Crazy – and they don't know what to do." Trump also wrote that he would continue to "drain the swamp" despite resistance to his important changes. On Wednesday night, he wrote, "I'm draining the Swamp, and the Swamp is trying to fight back. Don't worry, we will win!"

Microsoft founder Bill Gates appeared on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday and said he had a phone conversation with President-elect Donald Trump in recent days. Gates said part of the conversation dealt with Trump seeing areas where things could be improved. Gates compared Trump to former President John F. Kennedy, who Gates said had a similar "upbeat message" to that of Trump's. Gates said: "[I]n the same way President Kennedy talked about the space mission and got the country behind that, I think whether it's education or stopping epidemics, other health breakthroughs, finishing polio and in this energy space, there can be a very upbeat message that his administration is going to organize things, get rid of regulatory barriers, and have American leadership through innovation be one of the things he gets behind." Gates added: "Of course, my whole career has been along those lines. And he was interested in listening to that. And I'm sure there will be further conversation."

ABC canceled Roseanne Barr's top-rated "Roseanne" show after she tweeted an insult about Valerie Jarrett, a former aid to President Barack Obama. Barr said Jarrett, who is black, was from the movie franchise "Planet of the Apes." She tweeted: "muslim brotherhood & planet of the apes had a baby=vj." The president did not discuss Barr's tweet at a rally Tuesday in Tennessee. The White House declined to address it when asked repeatedly by reporters. Some news outlets, including CNN and MSNBC, have blamed Trump for fueling racism in the U.S. Barr has supported Trump, as did her character on the reboot this year of her sitcom. The backlash on Twitter and the cancellation move by ABC was fast and furious.

On Wednesday, CNN political commentator Symone Sanders appeared on CNN's "The Lead" and discussed President Donald Trump's decision to revoke former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) director John Brennan's security clearance. Sanders said the president sent his White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders "out there today to basically poop on the people." Sanders said, "You know, I think someone wants to muck up the news cycle, Jake. Look, I definitely—I think this is ridiculous. This is nothing short of extraordinary, and we should all be scared about the state of our democracy. The president sent his White House press secretary out there today to basically poop on the people from the press secretary podium." She added, "Not only threaten, like they didn't make a threat, it was a promise. They are snatching John Brennan's national security clearance. John Brennan was in the Situation Room when American heroes took out Bin Laden. Like what is happening here?"

Six weeks before the special election, Democrat Rep. Ed Markey leads former Navy Seal Gabriel Gomez by 6 percentage points in the Massachusetts Senate race. A WBUR poll of 497 likely voters found Markey at 41 percent and Gomez at 35 percent. Steve Koczela, president of the MassINC Polling Group, told WBUR: "Either way you look at it — with leaners or without leaners — you've got a race within single digits coming out of the primary. You've got a competitive race." Markey and Gomez, who has never held elected office, are running for the seat that former Sen. John Kerry, a Democrat, vacated to become secretary of state. Gov. Deval Patrick of Massachusetts appointed a former top aide, William "Mo" Cowan, earlier this year to fill the seat and set up a June 25 special election.

Australian police monitoring social media say the gunman holding hostages inside a Sydney cafe is demanding a telephone audience with Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Deputy Police Commissioner Catherine Burn said the demands are forming a part of the tactical response. Burn declined to confirm or comment further on the demands or on another claim made by two female hostages who called authorities to warn the gunman that two other bombs were planted at different sites in the city, Network 10 reported. Abbott has publicly announced that the hostage situation may be politically motivated but has not labeled it a terrorist assault. Witnesses at the scene of the Lindt Chocolat Cafe reported seeing a black flag with white Arabic writing being flown inside — the same flag that Islamic terrorists use to promote their messages. New South Wales State Police Commissioner Andrew Scipione said, "We have not yet confirmed it is a terrorism-related event."

Former first lady Barbara Bush, 84, was hospitalized Saturday in Houston to undergo routine tests but doctors do not suspect anything serious, family spokeswoman Jean Becker said late Saturday. Bush, who has not been feeling well for about a week, was being treated at Methodist Hospital and should be released in a day or two, Becker said. Becker said: "She hasn't been feeling well for about a week, and the doctors thought she should come in and undergo a battery of tests. It's not serious. She just hasn't been feeling herself and they're just trying to figure out why." Becker declined to provide details but said former President George H.W. Bush drove his wife to the hospital Saturday morning after consulting with her doctors. A hospital spokeswoman declined comment, saying information was only being released through the family. Mrs. Bush was hospitalized for nine days after undergoing heart surgery in March 2009 for a severe narrowing of the main heart valve. Doctors at the time said the condition was common among people her age. She also was hospitalized in November 2008, when she underwent surgery for a perforated ulcer. Doctors said the two ailments were unrelated.

Doug Ducey criticized Fox News for calling Arizona for Joe Biden. Ducey said, "Election Day votes are not fully reported, and we haven't even started to count early ballots dropped off at the polls. In AZ, we protected Election Day. Let's count the votes—all the votes—before making declarations." Miller tweeted, "We believe over 2/3 of those outstanding Election Day voters are going to be for Trump. Can't believe Fox was so anxious to pull the trigger here after taking so long to call Florida. Wow." Fox News defended the decision and refuted rumors that the network had retracted its Arizona projection. Anchor Bret Baier said, "We do not retract that."

President Donald Trump spoke to reporters after meeting with officials to survey damage in Georgia from Hurricane Michael on Monday. He said, "We have the worst immigration laws and the dumbest immigration laws in the history of the world." Reporters questioned the president about family separation policies for illegal immigrants caught at the border. "There's no country in the world that has such stupid laws as we do," he replied. Trump said the laws allow illegals to go through a court process, citing the practice of "catch and release." "They put one foot on our land and we have to bring them through a long court process," Trump said. Trump said he would continue working to change the laws but blamed Democrats for blocking any reforms. "We have the dumbest laws in history, and it's because of the Democrats," he said, "because they want to have these laws that way."

Obama administration officials are meeting this week to decide whether the United States should arm rebels in Syria with lethal weapons. According to a Fox News report, part of the issue is whether opposition forces can be trusted once weaponized. The administration has sought to arm rebels but has feared weapons could fall into the hands of "Al Qaeda-linked fighters or other extremists" fighting against Bashar al-Assad. The Free Syrian Army stands the best chance of receiving arms from the United States. The military group claims "no political or religious agenda"simply the overthrow of Assad. Assad's forces have recently received a boost from Hezbollah's support of Syrian forces. Best guesses suggest the administration is close to saying yes to weapons for small groups of opposition forces that are least likely to be Al Qaeda-linked.

Corey Lewandowski, former campaign manager for Donald Trump, said he has no professional regrets about his campaign. "I have no regrets when it comes to this campaign," Lewandowski said. "My biggest regret in the campaign is not being able to have my family more involved." Lewandowski did not disclose any reason behind his firing. "I think what's fair to say is anybody that knows me...knows that I'm a very straight shooter," he told CNN's Dana Bash on Monday afternoon following the announcement of his removal when asked about people questioning his advice to Trump. "I tell people the way it is." "I'm not smart enough to lie," he added, remaining loyal to Trump during the interview. Lewandowski said his job was to give his best advice and opinion, saying, "That's my duty and my obligation to anybody."

President Obama reacted to the death of Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia after wrapping up his golf game in California this afternoon. Obama said, "Tonight we honor his extraordinary service to our nation and remember one of the towering legal figures of our time," describing him as a "brilliant legal mind with a pugnacious style, incisive wit, and colorful opinions." The president made his statement at Rancho Mirage, California. Obama said he would nominate a replacement to the Supreme Court and expected the Senate to confirm his choice. "I plan to fulfill my constitutional responsibilities to nominate a successor in due time," he said. "There will plenty of time for me to do so and for the Senate to fulfill its responsibility to give that person a fair hearing and a timely vote." Obama said he took his constitutional responsibilities "seriously." "They're bigger than any one party," he added. "They're about our democracy."

President Donald Trump posted on Twitter in all caps: "THE SECOND AMENDMENT WILL NEVER BE REPEALED!" He wrote that overturning the Second Amendment "would be simple and would do more to weaken the N.R.A.'s ability to stymie legislative debate and block constructive gun control legislation than any other available option." He added: "As much as Democrats would like to see this happen, and despite the words yesterday of former Supreme Court Justice Stevens, NO WAY." He also wrote that overturning the Second Amendment "would be simple and would do more to weaken the N.R.A.'s ability to stymie legislative debate and block constructive gun control legislation than any other available option."

A New York federal appeals court ordered Monday that the US government must make public secret papers justifying drone attacks against suspected terrorists, including American citizens. The case was brought by The New York Times and two journalists in a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) case supported by the American Civil Liberties Union. Their request followed drone attacks in Yemen that killed Anwar al-Awlaki and Samir Khan in September 2011 and al-Awlaki's teenage son, Abdul Rahman, in October 2011. All three victims were United States citizens either by birth or naturalization. Judges based their decision on the fact that the information had already been the subject of numerous public statements and speeches, particularly by President Barack Obama, Attorney General Eric Holder and CIA chief John Brennan. Judge Jon Newman wrote, "Whatever protection the legal analysis might once have had has been lost by virtue of public statements of public officials at the highest levels and official disclosure of the DOJ White paper." The decision reverses a judgment of January 2013, which had sided with the US government.

A Wall Street Journal/NBC poll shows Hillary Clinton, the likely Democratic presidential nominee, has not addressed the controversy over her private email server and the fundraising controversy surrounding the Clinton Foundation in an interview or with the public. The poll finds Democrat support for Clinton remains strong, but the percentage of people who view Clinton negatively has increased six percent since last month's poll. Last month, roughly 36 percent of individuals surveyed said they viewed Clinton negatively, but now that number is 42 percent. The Wall Street Journal reports 25 percent of voters say they think Clinton is honest, down more than 10 percent from a poll last summer. It has been 24 days, more than three weeks, since Clinton announced her bid for president. She has not spoken to national media about her campaign or to address the controversies she is facing. Breitbart News previously reported this is a record for presidential candidates in recent history.

Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson canceled the remainder of his campaign events Tuesday after a fatal car crash involving staff and volunteers. According to the campaign, a van carrying three volunteers and a campaign staff member slid on an icy Iowa road and flipped on its side near Atlantic, Iowa. It was then hit by another vehicle. One volunteer, 25-year-old Braden Joplin, was transported to the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Obama, Neb. where he died Tuesday around 4:30 p.m., according to a statement from the campaign. "Carson plans to meet with Joplin's family members once he arrives in Omaha later this evening to offer his condolences," the campaign said. Three of the other passengers in the van are being examined at Cass County Memorial Hospital in Atlantic, Iowa, Carson's campaign said in a written statement. The accident comes less than two weeks before the Iowa caucuses, where Carson is polling fourth behind Donald Trump, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, according to polling data from RealClearPolitics.

Democrats have frequently cast President Trump as trapped in his own Watergate. On Wednesday, Trump posted on Twitter criticizing CNN and Carl Bernstein, for which Bernstein co-wrote the Trump Tower story that has been repudiated by one of its sources. Last month, CNN reported based on anonymous sources that Trump lawyer Michael Cohen was willing to testify that Trump knew in advance that Donald Trump Jr. was going to meet with Russians to get dirt on Hillary Clinton — a claim the president and his son both deny. In the past week, Cohen lawyer Lanny Davis said he did not know this was true, and his client told federal prosecutors under oath as part of a plea deal that he did not know that either. In addition, Davis was identified by name in CNN's story as having no comment on the report.

On Thursday, President-elect Donald Trump's senior adviser Kellyanne Conway appeared on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends." Conway said White House press secretary Josh Earnest's claim yesterday at the daily press briefing that Trump knew about Russia hacking the 2016 presidential election was "incredibly irresponsible." On Wednesday, Earnest said Trump was "obviously aware" of the Russian interference when referencing Trump's joke during a campaign rally inviting Russian hackers to find Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton's missing emails. Conway said, "That is just remarkable. That is breathtaking. I guess he's auditioning to be a political pundit after his job is over soon. That is incredibly disappointing to hear from the podium of the White House press secretary. Because he basically — he essentially stated that the president-elect had knowledge of this, maybe even fanned the flames. It's incredibly irresponsible and I wonder if his boss, president Obama agrees."

On Wednesday at American University in Washington, D.C., President Barack Obama spoke about the Iran nuclear deal. He said hardliners chanting "death to America" were the ones opposed to the deal and were making common cause with Republicans. Obama said, "I recognize that resorting to force may be tempting in the face of the rhetoric and behavior that emanates from parts of Iran. It is offensive. It is incendiary. We do take it seriously. But superpowers should not act impulsively in response to taunts, or even provocations that can be addressed short of war. Just because Iranian hard-liners chant 'death to America' does not mean that that's what all Iranians believe. In fact, it's those hard-liners who are most comfortable with the status quo. It's those hard-liners chanting 'death to America' who have been most opposed to the deal. They're making common cause with the Republican caucus."

Fox News star Kimberly Guilfoyle is leaving the cable network to join the America First Action Super PAC that supports President Donald Trump for president, according to a source close to Guilfoyle who confirmed reports to Breitbart News. Guilfoyle has worked for Fox News for 12 years and is a co-host of The Five. A spokesperson for Fox News confirmed in a statement to Breitbart News that Fox News has parted ways with Kimberly Guilfoyle. Guilfoyle is currently dating Donald Trump Jr. after his wife Vanessa filed for divorce in March. In a recent interview on Breitbart News Daily, she praised Trump Jr. as "number one up-and-coming political figure on the right." She said: "I've seen him at these political rallies, and I went to Montana with him, and I've known him for over a decade and saw him at the convention speech. He commands the room. He's a compelling political figure."

Hillary Clinton reacted to Donald Trump's press conference with military veterans on Friday, calling his actions "disgraceful." Clinton said in a statement: "Trump's actions today were disgraceful. After five years of pushing a racist conspiracy theory into the mainstream, it was appalling to watch Trump appoint himself the judge of whether the President of the United States is American." The Trump campaign said the Republican presidential nominee would address questions about the President Obama "birther" storyline at the campaign event, but he waited until veterans supporters finished speaking before making a statement. Trump said: "President Barack Obama was born in the United States, period. Now we all want to get back to making America strong and great again." Clinton said: "This sickening display shows more than ever why Donald Trump is totally unfit be president."

On Sunday, Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) appeared on CNN's State of the Union and called President Obama's Friday comments on Trayvon Martin and race "very impressive." McCain said, "I think we should continue to make progress," but added that "we still have a long way to go," and declined to "second guess" the verdict in the George Zimmerman case. McCain stated that "we were probably too optimistic" about race relations in the aftermath of the election of the country's first black president. "I think old prejudices die hard," McCain said. "We have made significant progress, but I think recent events highlight the differences that remain." McCain also said he believed that "Stand Your Ground" laws should be reconsidered in light of the Martin case, despite the fact that "Stand Your Ground" was never invoked by Zimmerman and he was acquitted on grounds of self-defense.

Charles Krauthammer appeared Tuesday on "Special Report with Bret Baier" and said, "Who is going to step out now and defend the president in these denials?" He said that when it comes to breaking allegations about President Trump by the New York Times, "I think what is really stunning is that nobody, not even from the White House, has come out under their own name in defense of the president here." Krauthammer continued, "Who is going to step out now and defend the president in these denials?" Late Tuesday, the New York Times published a story stating that Trump asked then FBI Director James Comey to end a federal investigation into former national security advisor Michael Flynn in a February Oval Office meeting. Comey reportedly detailed the meeting in a memo, writing that Trump told him, "I hope you can let this go." The White House has denied the report.

President Obama will deliver a speech Thursday urging Congress to pass a comprehensive immigration reform bill, the White House said Wednesday night. After the budget crisis ended last week, Obama called on Congress to pass an immigration reform bill, saying it was one of his top priorities moving forward. The Senate passed a bipartisan bill on immigration earlier this year, but it has stalled since being handed to the House. Most House Republicans prefer a piece-by-piece approach. House Speaker John Boehner expressed optimism on Wednesday about House action by year's end on efforts to overhaul immigration. "I still think immigration reform is an important subject that needs to be addressed. And I'm hopeful," Boehner told reporters at a Capitol Hill news conference when asked if the House can act in the remaining weeks. The House has five legislative weeks left, though lawmakers indicated that could change. Business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, labor unions and religious organizations including U.S. Catholic bishops and evangelicals are pressing for immigration legislation. Many of their members plan a lobbying effort on Capitol Hill next week.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant, the Russians are considering granting political asylum to Edward Snowden, the NSA whistleblower and whistleblower. Snowden, a government contractor, revealed the existence of a National Security Agency surveillance operation last week. Kommersant quoted President Vladimir Putin's press secretary as saying, "If we receive such a request, we will consider it." Snowden was previously staying in Hong Kong, where he fled to on May 20, but has since changed his location. Yesterday, Regina Ip, Hong Kong's top official overseeing security, said it would be in Snowden's "best interest to leave Hong Kong." China has an extradition treaty with the United States. Ip said, "He won't find Hong Kong a safe harbor. Those agreements have been in force for more than 10 years. If the US submits a request, we would act in accordance with the law." The US is preparing charges against Snowden and will most likely try to have him extradited once those are filed.

At Business Insider, Michelle Mark covered Donald Trump's response to Hillary Clinton's foreign policy speech. Trump's remarks followed a foreign policy speech Clinton gave earlier that day, during which she denounced Trump's policy proposals as "a series of bizarre rants, personal feuds, and outright lies" and declared that electing him would be a "historic mistake." Trump did not detail the arguments Clinton made in her speech, calling them "phony" and a "Donald Trump hit job." He also criticized her for the email matter that has affected her campaign for more than a year. Clinton has sought to address concerns that her private email account posed security risks to government business and classified material. Last Wednesday, the State Department released a report stating she "did not comply" with department policies regarding her email.

In an interview that aired on Monday, Ramos mentioned a speech Cruz's father, Rafael, made in which he compared President Barack Obama to Fidel Castro. Cruz told Ramos his father was referring to a statement Obama made at the State of the Union where Obama said "if Congress doesn't act to enact his agenda that he will do it anyway on his own." When Ramos pressed Cruz on whether he felt Obama was a dictator like Castro, Cruz said there were differences but said he was concerned about the "explosion of power in the federal government" under Obama. Cruz specifically cited the NSA surveillance program scandal and Obama's expansion of "presidential power in a way that is contrary to the constitution." When Ramos asked Cruz if he thought Obama was abusing his power, Cruz said Obama "absolutely" was. Cruz said: "I think he has absolutely been abusing his power and when you have a president who says 'regardless of whether Congress acts I'm going to force my agenda on the American people,' that's wrong, that's not consistent with our constitutional protections."

Sen. Kamala Harris (D-CA) said Sunday in an interview with The Des Moines Register that President Donald Trump did not "pull the trigger" at the mass shooting at a Walmart store in El Paso, Texas, but he had been tweeting out ammunition. Harris said, "I, as a prosecutor, I prosecuted hate crimes. As the Attorney General of California, where I ran the second largest Department Justice in the United States, I on an annual basis published the Hate Crime Report. So I will tell you this stuff is not new in our country. It certainly predates the election of Donald Trump, but it has also increased under Donald Trump. He has been fueling the flames of hate. I said recently on the issue of El Paso, you know, no, when people ask me is he responsible for these killings? Well no he obviously didn't pull the trigger but he sure been tweeting out the ammunition."

The White House announced Tuesday that it was canceling all public tours of the president's home because of the sequester spending cuts. In an email, the White House said: "Due to staffing reductions resulting from sequestration, we regret to inform you that White House Tours will be canceled effective Saturday, March 9, 2013 until further notice. Unfortunately, we will not be able to reschedule affected tours." The notice comes as both the White House and Congress try to find cuts to their own budgets as part of $85 billion in cuts to the entire government. As President Obama was returning from visiting wounded veterans at Walter Reed Medical Center, a reporter shouted a question about the decision to cancel the tours as Mr. Obama was walking from Marine One to the Oval Office. He smiled and waved. At the Capitol, staffers who use the building's West Front entrance that looks out on the National Mall were told Tuesday that door would be closed as of next week to save money. Susan Crabtree contributed to this report.

President Donald Trump's economic adviser Gary Cohn will hold a meeting next week at the United Nations to discuss climate change, according to a New York Times report. The breakfast will include climate and energy ministers from around the world, according to the Times. The Times cited an invitation describing the event as "an opportunity for key ministers with responsibility for these issues to engage in an informal exchange of views and discuss how we can move forward most productively." Cohn advocated for the Trump administration staying in the Paris Climate Agreement, describing the president in May as "evolving" on the issue. "His views are evolving, which is exactly what they should be," Cohn told reporters during a press briefing in Sicily at the G7 summit. Trump announced his decision to withdraw from the Paris agreement. "I was elected to represent the citizens of Pittsburgh, not Paris," Trump said during a speech at the White House explaining his decision.

A YouGov poll shows that Republican primary voters believe Donald Trump is a bold and strong Washington outsider. Of Marco Rubio, Donald Trump, and Ted Cruz, Trump led the categories in which respondents weighed various qualities. Seventy-five percent said Trump was bold, 62 percent said he was strong, and 64 percent said he was a Washington outsider. Twenty-three percent felt Rubio was bold, 29 percent thought he was strong, and five percent believed he was a Washington outsider. The only categories Rubio led were "typical politician" and "establishment candidate." Cruz received 54 percent support. He also received the highest rating for being religious and for being partisan. His honesty rating was 42 percent. When offered a choice between Trump, Rubio, and Cruz, the support split as follows:

The Obama administration would not comment Monday on claims that a German intelligence employee arrested last week was spying for the United States. The man was taken in custody amid allegations he passed documents to a foreign nation, rumored to be the United States. Germany Chancellor Angela Merkel, who has criticized U.S. surveillance and intelligence-gathering efforts, said the incident, if true, would amount to a "clear contradiction" of trust between the two countries. White House press secretary Josh Earnest would not comment on the specifics of the case but said the United States and Germany remain close-knit partners. "We're going to work with the Germans to resolve this situation appropriately," he told reporters. "We highly value the close working relationship we have with the Germans on a wide range of issues but particularly on security and intelligence matters. ... As of right now, I'm not in a position to comment any further on this matter."

After deadly mass shootings in El Paso and Dayton last weekend, Democrats and other Trump supporters demanded that President Trump denounce white nationalism, which they said propelled the alleged Texas gunman. Trump said Monday: "The shooter in El Paso posted a manifesto online consumed by racist hate. In one voice, our nation must condemn racism, bigotry, and white supremacy. These sinister ideologies must be defeated. Hate has no place in America. Hatred warps the mind, ravages the heart, and devours the soul." The article's page-one online headline read: "TRUMP URGES UNITY VS. RACISM." The article stated that the article's accurate words enraged Democrats and disproved the leftist lie that Trump is a divisive bigot.

Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) appeared on MSNBC's "Andrea Mitchell Reports" on Wednesday. Blumenthal stated that Paul Manafort "caught a break" in the overall sentence he received. Blumenthal further stated that Judge Amy Berman Jackson did not commit a "miscarriage of justice" like Judge T.S. Ellis did, but that Jackson could have been harder on Manafort. Blumenthal said, "Looking at the totality of what he did, and the totality of the sentences, both last week and now, Paul Manafort caught a break. This overall sentence is exceedingly lenient, probably excessively so, in my view." He added, "[T]he miscarriage of justice, as I've called it repeatedly, really occurred in the Eastern District of Virginia, not today in her courtroom. She did her best to be fair and factual. … But, she could have been tougher, and she tried to be balanced and fair."

Steve Kroft told Piers Morgan Monday night that President Obama keeps coming back to "60 Minutes" because "we're not going to go out of our way to make him look bad or stupid." The comments followed criticism that Kroft gave a softball interview instead of asking hard-hitting questions following Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's Benghazi hearings. "We have a format that suits him. It's long. We can do 12 minutes or 24 minutes," Kroft said. "We do a good job of editing." Kroft added that he has covered President Obama since his candidacy, and that it is a "question of fairness." Obama "knows that we're not going to play 'gotcha' with him." Morgan commented on the "remarkable bonhomie and long-lasting friendship" between the president and Clinton, and Kroft described the interactions between the two as revealing of the positive nature of their relationship.

President Barack Obama said he hoped President-elect Donald Trump would consider helping illegal immigrants brought to the United States as children who were granted amnesty by his 2012 executive order. "I will urge the president-elect and the incoming administration to think long and hard before they are endangering the status of what for all practical purposes are American kids," Obama said. Obama's 2012 DACA and DAPA executive orders were criticized for lacking permanent protection for children of illegal immigrants and their parents. Activists said they were hopeful Obama would be succeeded by a Democrat or a Republican more sympathetic to their plight. Obama defended them, asserting that they belonged in the country. "By definition, if they're part of this program, they are solid, wonderful young people of good character," Obama said. He suggested that the majority of Americans still supported his decision. "It is my strong belief that the majority of the American people would not want to see suddenly those kids have to start hiding again," he said.

Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump said Monday that his life has not always been easy. He said he was given a "small loan" of about $1 million to start his business, frequently being told no along the way. "My whole life really has been a 'no,' and I've fought through it," Trump said at a town-hall meeting sponsored by NBC's "Today Show." "It's not been easy for me. ... I started off in Brooklyn. My father gave me a small loan of a $1 million ... and I had to pay him back, I had to pay him back with interest." Trump said he went to Manhattan with the money and started buying properties and "did great," despite being told by many, including his father, that straying from Brooklyn and Queens real-estate may not lead to success.

President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro met and shook hands at the Palace of the Revolution today in Cuba. Obama arrived with the U.S. delegation and shook hands with Castro for about 30 seconds in front of the cameras. The two leaders spoke for a few moments in front of the press. "We had a great tour yesterday," Obama told Castro, referring to the First Family's sightseeing trip in Havana on Sunday. "Enjoyed it." "And we had a great dinner," he added. Susan Rice was also present as well as Secretary of State John Kerry, Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack and Secretary of Commerce Penny Pritzker who also shook hands with Castro. Both leaders listened as the national anthems of Cuba and the United States were played and reviewed the Cuban troops. The leaders expect to meet and deliver statements to the press later this afternoon. It is unlikely that the press will be allowed to ask questions.

A roundup of results from Tuesday's primary contests in New Hampshire included U.S. SENATE: Former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown won the GOP primary in his bid to return to the Senate, topping former U.S. Sen. Bob Smith and former state Sen. Jim Rubens. Brown faces first-term incumbent Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in November, a race that could help determine control of the Senate. Former U.S. Rep. Frank Guinta defeated businessman Dan Innis and two others in the race for the GOP's nomination in the 1st Congressional District. He will take on incumbent Democrat Carol Shea-Porter in another rematch between the two political foes. State Rep. Marilinda Garcia topped former state Sen. Gary Lambert and former state Rep. Jim Lawrence in the race to take on incumbent Democrat Annie Kuster in the 2nd Congressional District.

A proposal to name a new community in the Golan Heights after President Donald Trump will go before the Israeli government Sunday. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently suggested he wanted to name a new community after Trump because of his recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. The community would be called Ramat Trump, or Trump Heights. The Government Naming Committee said in their introduction of the proposal, according to Haaretz.com: "The initiative to establish a new community in the Golan Heights, named after President Donald Trump, is an expression of gratitude for his actions for the good of the State of Israel as a whole and the Golan Heights in particular." The committee continued: "There is importance in advancing the aforementioned decision at this time in order to strengthen the political ties between the State of Israel and the United States." In March, Trump signed a proclamation recognizing Israel's sovereignty over the disputed Golan Heights, reversing years of U.S. policy on the matter.

Former Navy Secretary Richard Spencer discussed President Trump's intervention in the review of Navy SEAL Eddie Gallagher's Trident on Tuesday. Defense Secretary Mark Esper asked Spencer to resign on Sunday for going behind his back in removing Gallagher's pin. Spencer in an interview with CBS News' "This Morning" defended his actions, saying they were an effort to maintain "good order and discipline" among the troops. "The special operating community has been put under amazing pressure to do amazing things, and they're amazing performing people," Spencer said. "But there's ramifications that happen with that. And we have to build a system around it that has discipline, people look up to us and go, 'Yes, they actually stick by what they say, and they take the higher ground.'" He added, "[A]n action like this erodes that."

Congressman Joe Sestak, a Pennsylvania Democrat, spoke to reporters on Friday about the White House memo revealing former President Bill Clinton as the individual who asked him to drop out of the Pennsylvania Senatorial primary in exchange for a job. The article asked Sestak if he ever thought what was happening could have risen to the level of a misdemeanor or felony. Sestak said, "If I ever thought anything had been wrong about this, I would have reported it." Congressman Darrell Issa, a California Republican and ranking member on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, stood on the Capitol steps behind Sestak and watched the Pennsylvania Congressman's presser. Issa has been investigating bribery allegations between the White House and Sestak for a number of months. Following Sestak's press conference, Issa appeared before reporters and made sure he had the last word before the Memorial Day recess.

More Republican senators have opposed Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell's plan to fund the Affordable Care Act using a procedural rule in the Senate. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) has been fighting this strategy. Sen. David Vitter (R-LA) has endorsed the strategy. The endorsement follows a report on Breitbart News that McConnell and Sen. John Cornyn, Cruz's Texas colleague, are withholding votes against Cruz. In a statement provided to Breitbart News, Vitter said: "Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid has indicated one of his first amendments after that will be to gut the provision in the bill that defunds Obamacare. I'll continue to fight President Obama & Senate Majority Leader Reid's efforts to fund Obamacare." Vitter's spokesman added that he will vote "no" on cloture.

Presidential candidate Hillary Clinton's campaign emailed supporters Wednesday saying the campaign raised more than $45 million in the first quarter, a record for this early in a campaign. Campaign Manager Robby Mook wrote that people had doubted whether Clinton could get grassroots supporters, but the hundreds of thousands of donations proved critics wrong. Mook said the campaign was still running the numbers and would be in touch again soon to tell a little more about the incredible group of people who had chipped in to support the campaign. Mook requested more donations to Clinton's campaign. He said some Republican candidates are rumored to have raised roughly $100 million dollars, which he said would be used to tear down the campaign and strengthen it. Mook said the campaign needed to keep working.

White House Counselor to the President Kellyanne Conway posted on Twitter on Tuesday night after Republican Karen Handel defeated her challenger Jon Ossoff. Conway wrote, "Laughing my #Ossoff." She also criticized pundits who predicted a loss for Trump and Republicans in Georgia. Conway wrote, "Thanks to everyone who breathlessly and snarkily proclaimed GA06 as a 'referendum on POTUS.' You were right." Conway thanked Handel for "being a grownup" and "running on the issues" while actually living in the district she was running to represent. She wrote, "Welcome to Congress," and highlighted Handel's call to "lift up this nation so that we can find a more civil way to deal with our disagreements."

President Donald Trump ordered a new round of economic sanctions on Iran on Monday. At the signing ceremony in the Oval Office, Trump said, "We do not seek conflict with Iran or any other country. I can only tell you we cannot ever let Iran have a nuclear weapon." The sanctions are expected to target Iran's supreme leader as part of the response to the country shooting down an American surveillance drone in international waters. Trump had ordered a military strike on Iranian targets in response to the attack. Trump called it back. The president warned Iran not to expect similar military restraint in the future. "I think a lot of restraint has been shown by us, but that doesn't mean we're going to show it in the future," Trump said. He added that he respected the Iranian people, despite what he called a dangerous governing regime. "I know many Iranians living in New York, and they're fantastic people," Trump stated.

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) said that if the Republican establishment has a brokered convention to "steal the nomination from the people," it would "cause a revolt." Cruz told reporters in Orono, Maine, according to the Washington Times: "If the Washington deal-makers try to steal the nomination from the people, I think it would be a disaster. It would cause a revolt." He added: "Instead, the answer is real simple. We've got to win this nomination. I'm the only candidate who has the delegate count, who has the state wins, who is in a position to beat Donald Trump. And if you want to beat Donald Trump, the way to do it is to come together behind this campaign. But Donald Trump embodies that Washington corruption that we are angry about. The answer to that corruption is not go with someone who has been funding liberal Democrats for decades, who has been enmeshed in that corruption."

In an interview with Fox News Channel's Sean Hannity, his first since former special counsel Robert Mueller testified before the House Intelligence and Judiciary Committees, President Donald Trump criticized the Mueller investigation. Hannity asked Trump about the importance of determining the origins of the special counsel probe. Trump argued this should not be allowed to happen to another president and likened it to "treason." "This should never happen to another president of the United States again," Trump said on Thursday's broadcast of Fox News Channel's "Hannity." "This is an absolute catastrophe for our country. This was a fake witch hunt, and it should never be allowed to happen to another president again. This was treason. This was high crimes. This was everything as bad a definition as you want to come up with. This should never be allowed to happen to our country again."

Former House Majority Leader Dick Armey has endorsed Midland University President Ben Sasse for the U.S. Senate in Nebraska, departing from FreedomWorks, the tea party-affiliated organization he helped found. The tea party-affiliated FreedomWorks endorsed former State Treasurer Shane Osborn days earlier. The two other conservative groups, the Senate Conservatives Fund and the Club for Growth, also endorsed Sasse. Armey is former chairman of FreedomWorks, which he left last year after a dispute. The former House majority leader assisted Republicans in taking control of the House in the 1990s, helping write the conservative Contract with America before retiring in 2002. He then became involved with the tea party movement, becoming co-chairman of Citizens for a Sound Economy, which merged with Empower America to become FreedomWorks in 2004. In his endorsement, Armey criticized Osborn, saying, "We don't need career politicians running because this is just the next rung on the ladder for them."

Vice President Joe Biden spoke at a Black History Month event in Washington on Tuesday and told about 150 attendees, "I may be a white boy, but I can jump." Biden, who hosted the reception at the Naval Observatory with his wife, Dr. Jill Biden, said he wanted to team up with former NBA star and Sacramento Mayor Kevin Johnson to take on President Obama, The Washington Post reported. "I told the president, next game, I've got him," Biden said. Biden also expressed disappointment with Voter ID laws passed in Southern states, including North Carolina, Alabama, and Texas, saying such laws are evidence of "zealotry" and "hatred," according to a White House pool report. "These guys never go away. Hatred never, never goes away," Biden said. "The zealotry of those who wish to limit the franchise cannot be smothered by reason." Fox News' Ed Henry contributed to this report.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump posted a video on Instagram criticizing fellow GOP presidential candidate former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush for saying illegal immigration is an "act of love." Bush said, "Yeah, they broke the law, but it's not a felony. It's an act of love." The video shows three mug shots of immigrants who all committed violent crimes during their stay in the United States. The screen then displays the phrase "Love? Forget love, it's time to get tough!" Trump previously said Bush would be easily influenced regarding illegal immigration because Bush's wife is from Mexico. "I mean, look, I would say that he would," Trump told CNN. "If my wife were from Mexico, I think I would have a soft spot for people from Mexico."

President Donald Trump signed a six-month waiver to delay moving the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem. The White House said Trump was still committed to his promise but made the decision to delay the move for the sake of peace negotiations between Israel and Palestine. The statement read: "As he has repeatedly stated his intention to move the embassy, the question is not if that move happens, but only when." The decision follows the precedent set by former presidents Clinton, Bush, and Obama who all signed a six-month waiver of the 1995 law. The delay will disappoint supporters of the president who hoped for bold action, separated from years of political rhetoric on the issue. The statement read: "[N]o one should consider this step to be in any way a retreat from the President's strong support for Israel and for the United States-Israel alliance."

President Donald Trump responded to rapper Kanye West after West expressed support for the president. West wrote: "You don't have to agree with Trump but the mob can't make me not love him. We are both dragon energy. He is my brother. I love everyone. I don't agree with everything anyone does. That's what makes us individuals. And we have the right to independent thought." West posted on Twitter after receiving backlash from liberal fans for positive things about the president. Trump wrote: "Thank you Kanye, very cool!" Trump responded on Twitter shortly after Breitbart News asked Press Secretary Sarah Sanders at the White House press briefing whether the president had communicated recently with West. In response to Trump, West posted a picture of a Trump MAGA campaign hat autographed by the president and a screen image of the president's tweet.

White House chief of staff Gen. John Kelly said it was a "mistake" to judge historical figures by modern standards. Kelly said, "It's inconceivable to me that you would take what we think now and apply it back then – I just think it's very very dangerous. It shows you how much a lack of an appreciation of history and what history is." Kelly made the comments during an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham, who asked him about the controversy over monuments of historical figures. Kelly said that Lee was an "honorable man" who chose to fight for his state, and that the loyalty to one's state was more important to Americans in that era. Kelly said, "The lack of an ability to compromise led to the Civil War and men and women of good faith on both sides made their stand where their conscience had them make their stand."

Rahm Emanuel, President-elect Obama's chief of staff, had direct discussions with Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich about Obama's vacant Senate seat, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. Sources with knowledge of the conversations told the Sun-Times that Emanuel spoke with the governor and pushed for the appointment of Valerie Jarrett in the days after the presidential election and asked that it be done by a certain date. The sources said Blagojevich told aides about conversations with Emanuel and sometimes gave them directions afterward. Some conversations between Blagojevich and Emanuel were likely caught on tape, the sources said. An Obama source strongly denied Emanuel spoke with the governor directly about the seat, the Sun-Times reported. Sources did not indicate that a deal was brokered in the conversations between Emanuel and Blagojevich. Blagojevich was arrested on corruption charges involving an alleged scheme to sell or trade Obama's vacant Senate seat.

The White House told Ukraine's President Viktor Yanukovich to withdraw security in Kiev as protests worsen and the death toll rises. White House spokesman Jay Carney said in a statement: "We are outraged by images of Ukrainian security forces firing automatic weapons on their own people. Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich should immediately withdraw his security forces from downtown Kiev an respect the right of peaceful protest, and we urge protesters to express themselves peacefully." The violence caused the US State Department to issue a travel alert to Ukraine and place visa bans on 20 Ukrainian officials. Protesters have been in Independence Square since late November when Yanukovich turned down a European Union trade deal in favor of a $15 billion bailout from Russia. The violence escalated on Tuesday after 25 people were killed. The total death tolls between Tuesday and Thursday vary between outlets. Reuters reported 50, but Thursday morning CNN reported more than 100 were killed. Yanukovich announced a truce between him and opposition leaders Wednesday night, but it failed as protesters thought it was a stunt.

On November 4, Vice President Joe Biden suggested Kansas Senate candidate Greg Orman (I) will caucus with Democrats if he defeats Republican incumbent Pat Roberts. Fox News's James Rosen relayed the news during the Election Day airing of The Real Story w/ Gretchen Carlson. Rosen said: "This is a late breaking development involving the White House that is threatening to shake up this very close race in its final hours, with Vice President Joe Biden telling WPLR Radio in Connecticut that Greg Orman 'will be with us.'" Rosen said Orman is "a pro-choice, self-made multi-millionaire businessman running his first political race, and he has been coy about which party he would caucus with in the Senate, if elected." Biden suggests he will caucus with Democrats. Senator Roberts' campaign responded to Biden's statement to voters today, arguing that "Orman is a Democrat masquerading as an Independent."

Sen. John McCain, the Arizona Republican who lost his bid for the White House to President Obama, criticized the new president for allowing what he described as pet projects into the $787 billion stimulus bill. McCain spoke to CBS News' Katie Couric on her webcast after Obama's speech to Congress. He criticized Democratic leadership for allowing what he said were over 9,000 earmarks into an omnibus spending bill over more than $400 billion that is set for a vote this week in the House. McCain also criticized Obama's claim that he had passed a stimulus that contained no pork, calling it technically true but false in reality. "In actuality it had billion[s] of dollars of earmarks in it," McCain said. McCain also expressed doubt about Obama's ability to "increase all these spending programs" and still cut the deficit by 2013, which the president has promised to do by half.

Russian President Vladimir Putin sent a telegram to President Trump in the Russian capital on Saturday stating that constructive dialogue between the two nations is essential for global stability. The Kremlin announced the message. Putin wrote that the two nations could develop a "pragmatic cooperation aimed at long-term perspective" on the basis of "equality and mutual respect." He noted that "the development [of] a constructive Russian-U.S. dialogue is particularly important for strengthening strategic stability in the world and finding the optimal answers to global threats and challenges." Ties between Moscow and Washington have declined following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and allegations of its meddling in the U.S. presidential election last year. In an interview with The New York Times on Thursday, Trump denied Russia colluded in the 2016 presidential election, adding "even if there was, it's not a crime." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Baltimore Mayor Catherine Pugh announced Tuesday she has resigned after being charged with failing to pay his taxes. The U.S. attorney's office alleged that Darryl De Sousa "willfully failed to file a federal return for tax years 2013, 2014 and 2015." De Sousa was a salaried employee of the Baltimore Police Department in each of those years. He faces up to one year in prison and a $25,000 fine for each of the three misdemeanor counts. De Sousa's attorney, Steven Silverman, said federal prosecutors did not give his client a chance to offer an explanation or to file late tax returns before bringing criminal charges against him.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said Tuesday during a press conference on the steps of the Supreme Court that President Donald Trump's Supreme Court nominee Judge Brett Kavanaugh must agree to recuse himself from cases involving "Trump's personal financial dealings" and special counsel Robert Mueller's probe. Blumenthal said, "I'm a no on this nominee. My colleagues should be a no on this nominee unless Judge Kavanaugh specifically commits that he will recuse himself on any issues that involve President Trump's personal financial dealings or the special counsel." He added, "He would be the swing vote. Judge Kavanaugh, if he is a justice, would be the swing vote in deciding whether he can pardon himself—get out of jail free pass. That's the accountability that will be lost if Judge Kavanaugh is confirmed. Likewise, whether he can be called before a grand jury—whether he can be indicted while he is still president."

U.S. Sen. Mark Kirk underwent surgery today at Northwestern Memorial Hospital after suffering a stroke, his office said. On Saturday, Kirk checked himself into Lake Forest Hospital, where doctors discovered a carotid artery dissection in the right side of his neck. He was transferred to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, where further tests revealed he had suffered an ischemic stroke. Early this morning, the senator underwent surgery to relieve swelling around his brain stemming from the stroke, the surgery was successful. Doctors are very confident in the Senator's recovery over the weeks ahead. The office released no other details. Kirk, 52, captured President Barack Obama's old U.S. Senate seat in a close 2010 election against Democrat Alexi Giannoulias.

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) said he will not punish the staffer who spread a report that Ben Carson was dropping out of the race. "I don't make it a practice of disciplining people for passing on public news reports," Cruz said on Mike Gallagher's radio program. Cruz reiterated that his political staff circulated a CNN report on Monday night during the caucus indicating Carson was returning to Florida instead of going to New Hampshire or South Carolina, the next primary states. The Texas senator said his aides did not circulate a follow-up report clarifying that Carson was simply returning home to Florida for a brief break from the campaign trail but was in fact continuing his presidential campaign. "The news turned out to be accurate — he did indeed return to Florida. That was news that the voters were interested in," Cruz said Wednesday, apologizing to Carson if his staff passing on the news report caused Carson "discomfort."

President Trump said the jacket first lady Melania Trump wore while boarding a plane to Texas to visit illegal-immigrant detention camps was a gibe at the media. The jacket had graffiti-like lettering spelling "I really don't care, do u." Media types called the jacket insensitive in light of their insistence that the Trump administration was torturing children. Trump tweeted Thursday evening: "I REALLY DON'T CARE, DO U? The back of Melania's jacket, refers to the Fake News Media. Melania has learned how dishonest they are, and she truly no longer cares!"

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) released an advertisement in South Carolina stating, "When it comes to appointing a Supreme Court justice, 'We cannot trust Donald Trump.' " The advertisement also references life, marriage, religious liberty, the Second Amendment, and states, "We're just one Supreme Court justice away from losing them all." The advertisement addresses President Trump on the issue of abortion. The advertisement plays a 1999 interview in which NBC anchor Time Russert asked Trump whether a hypothetical President Trump would "ban partial-birth abortions." Trump responded, "Well, look, I'm very pro-choice. But you would not ban it?" Russert asked again. Trump said, "No, I am pro-choice in every respect." The ad concludes with, "We cannot trust Donald Trump with these serious decisions."

Fox News co-moderator Megyn Kelly asked former Florida governor Jeb Bush a question about "your brother's war" at the Republican presidential debate in Cleveland on Thursday evening. Bush had already fielded one question from co-moderator Bret Baier about George W. Bush and whether he was his "own man." Kelly's questions on Thursday included a question about frontrunner Donald Trump's past statements about women. The article characterized the Iraq War as "your brother's war." The article stated that this description was odd because Bush had already answered one question about his brother, and was insensitive to those who proudly served and believed in the cause. Later, co-moderator Chris Wallace also asked Bush a question in which he referred to "your father and your brother."

North Korea denied reports it had cooperated with Syria on chemical weapons, dismissing them as a fabrication by the United States to pressure the country, state media reported late Thursday. State-run KCNA news agency cited a spokesman at the foreign ministry's research institute of American studies arguing that the United States made a "nonsensical argument" that it helped Syria produce chemical weapons. "As we have clearly said several times, our republic does not develop, produce and stockpile chemical weapons and opposes chemical weapons themselves," the spokesman said, via KCNA. Robert Wood, US disarmament ambassador to the Conference on Disarmament, said on Wednesday that there has been a history of a relationship between the two countries with regard to missile activity, chemical weapons components. Two North Korean shipments to a Syrian government agency responsible for the country's chemical weapons program were intercepted in the past six months, according to a confidential UN report on North Korea sanctions violations.
