President Trump's campaign arm launched a new advertisement Monday celebrating Trump's first 100 days in office, highlighting his achievements in office and dismissing negative media coverage. The $1.5 million ad buy, featuring a television ad and a series of targeted digital ads, comes as the administration seeks to counter criticism that the president's first days in office have not been as productive or as successful as had been hoped. A voiceover says, "America has rarely seen such success," but later adds, "You wouldn't know it from watching the news." The ad highlights the confirmation of Justice Neil Gorsuch to the Supreme Court, greater energy independence, de-regulation, and Trump's plan to cut taxes as examples of Trump's 100 day success. The narrator says, "America is winning again and President Trump is making America great again."

Reporters and some Republicans discuss Obama's economic policies in private, Obama told the Hill following his economic speech in Illinois. Republicans publicly criticized the president for giving an address that offered the same ideas. Obama said they and the media often praise his ideas. "It's interesting, in the run-up to this speech, a lot of reporters say that, well, Mr. President, these are all good ideas, but some of you've said before; some of them sound great, but you can't get those through Congress. Republicans won't agree with you," Obama said. Obama said some Republicans privately agree with a lot of his ideas. "I know because they've said so. But they worry they'll face swift political retaliation for cooperating with me," he said.

An Illinois judge on Tuesday dismissed a lawsuit that challenged the eligibility of Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX). The lawsuit was filed by Lawrence Joyce, a lawyer who challenged Cruz's eligibility to be president because he was born in Canada to an American mother. Joyce told USA Today: "What I fear is that Ted Cruz becomes the nominee, come September, Congressman Alan Grayson of Florida will go forward with his threats and probably several other Democrats will file suit to prevent Ted Cruz from being on the ballot." Grayson said in a radio interview in November: "I'm waiting for the moment that he gets the nomination, and then I will file that beautiful lawsuit saying that he's unqualified for the job because he's ineligible. Call me crazy, but I think the president of America should be an American."

A tea-party-backed conservative congresswoman, Rep. Michele Bachmann, a Minnesota Republican, said on Wednesday that President Obama has failed to demonstrate a vital U.S. national security interest for going into Libya. Bachmann said, "I would not have gone" into the country where Col. Moammar Gadhafi is fighting to cling to power against a resistance force. Bachmann is considering whether to seek the 2012 presidential nomination. She told NBC's "Today" show she does not support intervening regularly in humanitarian crises. She said the "Obama Doctrine" would provide a rationale for the United States "to enter into one country after another." Bachmann said she opposes military assistance to the rebels fighting Col. Gadhafi, saying she fears there are al Qaeda elements among their numbers.

Thousands of Australians are tweeting the hashtag #illridewithyou in support of the Muslim community after an Islamic State sympathizer took several people hostage at a Sydney chocolate shop. Police stormed the downtown Lindt chocolate cafe Tuesday where a gunman had been holding an unknown number of people hostage for more than 16 hours. An Islamic State flag was reportedly raised in the shop's window during the crisis, prompting fears among Sydney's Muslim community. More than 40 Muslim groups condemned the siege, saying in a statement that they rejected "any attempt to take the innocent life of any human being or to instil fear and terror into their hearts," Agence France-Presse reported. An Australian woman started the #illridewithyou campaign to show solidarity with Muslims who might feel targeted on public transportation.

Hawaii filed an amended federal lawsuit Tuesday night challenging President Donald Trump's revised travel ban. The state filed the suit with updates on its existing challenge to Trump's previous order. The lawsuit states the order will harm the Muslim population of Hawaii. The new order, announced Monday, bars new visas for people from six Muslim-majority countries and temporarily shuts down America's refugee program, affecting would-be visitors and immigrants from Iran, Syria, Somalia, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Hawaii's lawsuit says it is suing to protect its residents, businesses and schools, as well as its "sovereignty against illegal actions of President Donald J. Trump and the federal government." Hawaii's lawsuit had been on hold while a nationwide injunction on the initial ban remained in place.

Turkey's foreign minister Mevlut Cavusoglu said American forces in Syria are intentionally stalling the fight against Islamic State militants as an excuse not to cut ties with Syrian Kurdish fighters as Ankara has demanded. Cavusoglu said U.S. forces are leaving "pockets" with IS militants intact to justify continued cooperation with the Kurdish militia. Cavusoglu said ties with the U.S. are "at a critical stage" and that Washington needs to take concrete steps to regain Turkey's trust. Ankara is upset over Washington's support for the Syrian Kurdish People's Protection Units, or YPG — the top U.S. ally in the anti-IS fight. Turkey considers the YPG a "terrorist" group linked to Kurdish insurgents within Turkey. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson is due in Ankara later this week.

President Obama and presumptive Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney are in a statistical tie in Ohio, and the potential addition of home-state Sen. Rob Portman as Romney's running mate makes no difference, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released Thursday. Obama receives 45 percent support to Romney's 44 percent. The same poll on Feb. 15 showed Obama leading Romney 46 percent to 44 percent. The latest poll found Portman would not move the needle in Ohio as Romney's running mate, showing a 45-45 tie between the tickets with the senator included. Fifty-nine percent of Ohioans said they do not know enough about Portman to form an opinion. Republicans never have won the White House without capturing Ohio.

House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) said in a closed-door meeting Wednesday that "people say a lot of things about [me]" but he just lets "that s–t roll off [my] back." According to The Hill, Boehner was meeting with GOP lawmakers when he said these things. He reportedly also explained that he knew GOP lawmakers were among the critics. Thus, he said, those criticizing him included "people outside this room [and] people inside this room." Conservative Republicans do not think Boehner has fought hard enough for fiscal constraint, while Democrats say he is too closely aligned with the Tea Party. Boehner said he puts both sets of criticism behind him and that he did not take the position of Speaker to get a "big office," but to get things done.

The body of Boston bombing suspect Tamerlan Tsarnaev was reportedly buried in a Muslim cemetery in a small town in central Virginia, about 15 miles from Richmond, according to the Boston Globe. Al-Barzakh Cemetery in Doswell, the first Muslim resting place in the region, has interred Tsarnaev's remains, according to the Globe. Tsarnaev, 26, died during a shootout with police in Watertown, Mass. His brother and fellow bombing suspect Dzhokhar, 19, is recovering from gunshot wounds at Fort Devens. The interment came after a Virginia woman saw protests outside a Worcester, Mass., funeral home that was storing Tsarnaev's body. The woman said nobody wanted him buried locally, and she decided to help. The woman contacted the Islamic Society of Greater Richmond and asked if members could help find a burial ground for the body. Society members found the Doswell cemetery and moved Tsarnaev on Wednesday evening, the Globe reported.

Former President Bill Clinton defended corporate inversions during an event at the Clinton Global Initiative. He said the United States is now the only country that also taxes overseas earnings. Steel said the United States has broken tax code to bring jobs home. President Obama said the companies were exploiting a "loophole." The Treasury Department announced new rules this week designed to reduce benefits available through inversion. Corporate inversions became news this summer after Burger King announced plans to merge with foreign companies, including a Canadian chain called Tim Hortons. Inversion does not allow companies to escape taxes on money earned within the United States but does allow them to avoid U.S. taxes on money earned abroad.

A spokeswoman for Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau confirmed Monday that Trudeau will not attend the funeral of Cuban leader Fidel Castro. Andree-Lyne Halle, a spokeswoman for Trudeau, confirmed the decision. On Saturday, Trudeau described Castro as a "legendary revolutionary and orator" and "a remarkable leader." Trudeau's reaction prompted criticism on Twitter from two Republican U.S. senators, Marco Rubio of Florida and Ted Cruz of Texas, both Cuban-Americans. Rubio called Trudeau's remarks "shameful" and Cruz called them "disgraceful." Castro attended the funeral of Trudeau's father, former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, in Montreal in 2000. Governor General David Johnston, Queen Elizabeth's II representative as Canada's head of state, will attend Castro's funeral.

Police in the Dominican Republic said they determined that three women who said they had sex with a U.S. senator for money were paid to make false claims by an attorney in the Caribbean country. Police spokesman Maximo Baez said officers traced the payments to attorney Melanio Figueroa. Baez said two women received about $425 each and the other was paid about $300 to falsely state on camera that they had sex with U.S. Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey. Baez said at a news conference Monday that authorities were seeking to interrogate Figueroa about the payments. Figueroa did not respond to messages left at his office. The women's videotaped statements were published on a conservative U.S. website. Menendez denied the allegations.

A top Democrat in New Jersey's Legislature, Assemblyman John Wisniewski, said Sunday it is "far too early" to conclude whether Gov. Chris Christie knew about toll-lane closings that caused traffic problems near the George Washington Bridge and sparked a political scandal that could roil the 2016 presidential race. "We haven't had a chance to talk to some of the key players," Wisniewski, a Democrat who is leading legislative probes into the issue, told ABC's This Week with George Stephanopoulous. His comments came on the heels of an internal review that cleared Christie of wrongdoing and placed blame on top deputies in his office and at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey for the lane closings in Fort Lee, N.J., for several days in September.

Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) appeared on CBS' Face the Nation and asked for Vice President Joe Biden to step in and help broker a deal over the government shutdown. McCain said, "maybe we need to get Joe Biden out of the witness protection program." He said, "I'm glad that negotiations are going on. I'm disappointed that twice...we were close to a deal and the Democrats moved the goalposts, in light of the polling data." McCain criticized President Obama for not being as active as President Clinton was during the 1995 shutdown, stating he was "disappointed" in Obama. McCain said Democrats needed to be "magnanimous and get things done... I know what it's like to be in the majority and in the minority, and it won't be forgotten."

President Obama's meeting on comprehensive energy legislation with bipartisan members of Congress originally scheduled for Wednesday has been cancelled. A White House official said the meeting has been postponed due to scheduling conflicts. Hill sources told Fox the reason for the scheduling slide is to allow the president to focus on his meeting with Gen. Stanley McChrystal, who is under fire for remarks he made in a series of interviews with Rolling Stone magazine. The White House and Congressional Democrats have been trying to use the Gulf Coast oil spill as an impetus to pass an energy bill that transitions America away from its dependence on fossil fuels, increases the use of renewable energy sources, and places a price on carbon pollution. Republicans say the Democrats' legislation amounts to an energy tax. A White House official told Fox the meeting will be rescheduled for next week.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Lindsey Graham said Sunday that the idea of Senate Republicans voting to dismiss immediately the House impeachment articles was "dead for practical purposes." Graham said on "Fox News Sunday" that the GOP majority lacked the votes. He said there are a lot of senators who he thinks will acquit the president but believe that the committee needs to hear the House's case, the president's answer to the House's case, and ask questions, and that is when witness requests will be heard. His response ended speculation that Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell would hold a vote Tuesday to delay the trial without hearing the House impeachment managers make their case or the president's legal team respond.

A witness to the attacks at Nairobi's Westgate shopping mall said Saturday that gunmen with AK-47s and grenades told Muslims to stand up and leave and that non-Muslims would be targeted. Elijah Kamau said attackers with AK-47s and grenades made the statement about Muslims as they began their attack around midday. Gunmen threw grenades and opened fire during the attack. Associated Press reporters at the scene said they saw about 10 dead bodies and dozens wounded more than two hours after the attack began. Officials did not yet give an official death toll. Somali's rebel group al-Shabab vowed in late 2011 to carry out a large-scale attack in Nairobi in retaliation for Kenya's sending of troops into Somalia to fight the Islamic insurgents.

Former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty said Saturday on "America's News Headquarters" that he has regrets regarding his 2012 presidential bid. Pawlenty said his regrets are related to "tactical decisions." "We took it as far as I could with my race and our resources," Pawlenty said. "We didn't get it done, obviously." The former presidential candidate ended his campaign last August after finishing third in the Iowa straw polls. Shortly after that third-place finish, Pawlenty endorsed Governor Mitt Romney despite his earlier criticisms on Romney's healthcare law. During an appearance on "Fox News Sunday" last June, Pawlenty told Chris Wallace, "President Obama said that he designed Obamacare after Romneycare and basically made it Obamneycare." Pawlenty now actively campaigns for Romney. He says Romney is the most capable, knowledgeable, and electable candidate.

The U.S. Treasury Department will begin taking steps this week to delay hitting the government's $16.4 trillion borrowing limit. Without those steps, the debt limit would be hit on Dec. 31. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said in a letter to congressional leaders that the department will take several accounting measures to save approximately $200 billion beginning next year. The government borrows about $100 billion a month, so that would keep the government from reaching the limit for two months. Geithner said it is harder to predict how long the delay will last because ongoing negotiations over tax and budget policies make it hard to forecast what tax revenue and government spending will be next year. The debt limit is the amount the government can borrow to help finance its operations.

U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch said one of her top priorities remains alleviating an "epidemic of distrust" between minority communities and law enforcement. Lynch discussed tensions between minority communities and police agencies during a speech Monday at the national convention of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc., the country's largest African-American women's organization. Lynch did not mention specific incidents related to this tension, including the in-custody death in nearby Waller County, Texas, of Sandra Bland, a black woman who authorities say hanged herself earlier this month in her cell after a traffic-stop confrontation with a white officer. Lynch said she is determined to take on the tension between minorities and law enforcement as well as other issues "not only to build a stronger nation, but to empower its people."

Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain acknowledged slipping from the top tier of candidates while addressing accusations of sexual harassment and confusion about his policy stands. "Obviously false accusations and confusion about some of my positions has contributed" to the downturn in the polls, he said. The Georgia businessman said his campaign is sound and supporters remain onboard what he called the "Cain train." Cain denied the accusations and said "nothing has gone wrong" in terms of the campaign's mechanics. He told CNN's "State of the Union" that some people "are heavily influenced by perception more so than reality." Cain also said he supports "targeted identification" in identifying potential terrorists. He said "if you take a look at the people who have tried to kill us, it would be easy to figure out exactly what that identification profile looks like."

On Wednesday night, the official MSNBC Twitter account posted a tweet celebrating General Mills' decision to air a biracial commercial touting Cheerios during this Sunday's Super Bowl. The commercial titled "Gracie" is part two of last year's "Just Checking" commercial for Cheerios, in which the father uses Cheerios to explain to "Gracie" she will soon have a younger sibling. Last month, MSNBC host Melissa Harris Perry criticized former Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney and his adopted biracial grandson, which led to her later issuing an apology.

White House counselor Kellyanne Conway said Monday that President Donald Trump disclosed details of a conversation he had with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2017 because he had a "great concern" of leaking at the time. Conway said on "Fox & Friends" that there were tremendous leaks, including from when the president would have meetings in the Oval Office. She said she can recall early on two calls with foreign leaders, she believe Mexico and Australia, the contents of which leaked almost immediately. Conway said there was great suspicion that some people were leaking this. Conway also pointed out the president's actions on Russia, citing expulsions and sanctions as proof of Trump not colluding with Russia, though she said there is still no evidence.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said Monday he would not sign the version of an immigrant tuition bill passed by the state Senate. Christie said the Senate bill grants richer benefits than the federal Dream Act and could make New Jersey a magnet for students in the country illegally who want to go to college. The Senate bill allows state residents who were brought to the United States illegally as children to pay the cheaper in-state rate for college and allows them to apply for financial aid. The version of the bill that passed the Assembly does not address financial aid. The possible 2016 presidential candidate said Monday on Townsquare Media's monthly call-in program that he hopes to reach a compromise with the Legislature during the lame-duck session. Latino groups who endorsed Christie's re-election widely support the in-state tuition measure.

On Sunday's broadcast of NBC's "Meet the Press," House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA) said Congress would get access to President Donald Trump's calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other world leaders. Schiff said, "The paramount need here is to protect the national security of the United States and see whether in the conversations with other world leaders and in particular with Putin that the president was also undermining our security in a way that he thought would personally benefit his campaign." He added, "If those conversations with Putin or with other world leaders are sequestered in that same electronic file that is meant for covert action, not meant for this, if there's an effort to hide those and cover those up, yes we're determined to find out."

Congress approved $6 billion in spending cuts as part of legislation to keep the government running for three more weeks and give President Obama and congressional leaders time to negotiate a package of reductions demanded by Republicans. The bill passed the Senate by an 87-13 vote. The White House and Capitol Hill Republicans remain far apart on larger legislation to cover the day-to-day operations of the government until the 2012 fiscal year begins in October. Government agencies have generally been operating at last year's levels for almost half of the budget year. Thursday's measure combined with $4 billion in cuts from a two-week extension passed earlier this month means that Congress has cut $10 billion since Republicans took control of the House in January.

Florida Governor Rick Scott (R) said Friday that it is time to destroy ISIS, not the Second Amendment. When asked about President Barack Obama's renewed demands for more gun control, Scott said, "The Second Amendment didn't kill anybody. Let's have a conversation about how we destroy ISIS." He added, "This is ISIS. This is evil. This is radical Islam. When are we going to say to ourselves as a country, 'Let's focus on destroying ISIS?'" He also said, "The Second Amendment's been around for 200 years." ISIS is the name of the Islamic army based in northern Syria. The Orlando murderer claimed he murdered the 49 people at the Pulse nightclub out of loyalty to ISIS.

Hours after former Navy SEAL Chris Kyle was shot to death at a gun range last weekend in Texas, former Texas Rep. Ron Paul issued a Facebook statement clarifying his earlier remarks. Paul had tweeted, "Chris Kyle's death seems to confirm that 'he who lives by the sword dies by the sword.' Treating PTSD at a firing range doesn't make sense." In a Facebook post meant to clarify the tweet, Paul wrote, "As a veteran, I certainly recognize that this weekend's violence and killing of Chris Kyle were a tragic and sad event." In the post, Paul wrote, "My condolences and prayers go out to Mr. Kyle's family. Unconstitutional and unnecessary wars have endless unintended consequences. A policy of non-violence, as Christ preached, would have prevented this and similar tragedies."

Rep. Heath Shuler, D-N.C., refused to commit to a challenge against Nancy Pelosi for Democratic House leader in the next Congress. He was repeatedly pressed on CNN'S State of the Union about his plans and he refused to make an announcement. Shuler said it is "unacceptable" for Pelosi to remain leader of the Democrats and "not get us where we need to go as a party." Shuler said he hopes Pelosi will step aside and that if she does not he WILL challenge her. He said if Pelosi does step down he wants Steny Hoyer and James Clyburn to be the party's leaders. "I don't see that happening if she's at the top of the leadership," Shuler said about Democrats chances of regaining the House majority in 2012.

Charles Krauthammer, a syndicated columnist and Fox News contributor, said Wednesday on "Special Report with Bret Baier" that Jeb Bush's attacks on Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump at Tuesday's GOP debate in Las Vegas will not help his campaign. Krauthammer said he was happy to see Bush stand up and get tough, and that he had a really tough campaign, but he did not think it would move the needle one iota. Bush had called Trump a "chaos candidate" who "will be a chaos president." Krauthammer said: "The problem is this: had [Jeb] done that in the first debate, or the second, at a time when Trump was rising...I think it might have had an effect."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Tuesday in a video message produced on a hilltop in the Golan Heights region that all Israelis were deeply moved when President Trump made his historic decision to recognize Israel's sovereignty over the Golan Heights. Netanyahu said he intends to bring to the government resolution calling for a new community in the Golan Heights named after President Donald J. Trump. Trump officially recognized Israel's sovereignty over the Syrian territory on March 25. The mountainous area — a 690-square mile region which Israel annexed following the 1967 Six-Day War with Syria — is currently home to some 20,000 Israelis.

Palestinian factions in the West Bank are calling for "A Day of Rage" to coincide with US President Donald Trump's visit to Bethlehem on Tuesday, where he is expected to meet with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. Trump is currently in Saudi Arabia for his first international trip since taking office in January. He will arrive in Israel on Monday and meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, where the two are expected to discuss prospects for peace negotiations and security issues. One Palestinian organization, the Islamic and National Forces, initiated the "Rage Day" call in a statement in conjunction with other West Bank factions, saying that they want to send a message to the American president that "the Palestinian people insist on their right to self-determination and national independence with east Jerusalem as its sovereign capital."

Twitter experienced an outage Thursday as users were unable to access the platform for over an hour. A message appeared on the company's status page: "We are currently investigating issues people are having accessing Twitter. We will keep you updated on whats happening." Twitter later said "an internal configuration change" was responsible for the disruption. Down Detector, a website that tracks outages, reported the outage began just after 2:45 p.m. ET. The disruption affected Twitter's mobile and web-based platforms. A message appeared when users tried accessing the site. The site returned online around 3:50 p.m. The outage occurred as President Trump was hosting a social media summit with right-wing personalities and tech industry critics who have accused Twitter and other websites of having an anti-conservative bias.

Donald Trump will nominate Steve Mnuchin, who has ties to both Wall Street and Hollywood, to be treasury secretary, according to a report Tuesday. The 53-year-old, who also served as finance director for the presidential campaign, was at Trump Tower on Tuesday to meet with the transition team. The New York Times reported Tuesday evening that he would be the Treasury pick. Democrats said his ties to Wall Street were a betrayal of Trump's campaign promises. Democratic National Committee spokesman Adam Hodge said: "So much for draining the swamp. Nominating Steve Mnuchin to be Treasury Secretary — a billionaire hedge fund manager and Goldman Sachs alumnus who preyed on homeowners struggling during the recession — is a slap in the face to voters who hoped he would shake up Washington."

Over two days of questioning in Congress, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed that he did not know key details of a 2011 consent decree with the Federal Trade Commission that requires Facebook to protect user privacy. Zuckerberg repeatedly assured lawmakers Tuesday and Wednesday that Facebook is in compliance with that agreement. He also declined to answer factual questions about it. At one point, he told Colorado Rep. Diana DeGette that he did not know if Facebook had received a financial penalty in that settlement. It did not. At another point, he acknowledged that he was not familiar with "all of the things the FTC said." The FTC announced in March that it is investigating Facebook. Violations of the 2011 agreement could subject Facebook to fines of $41,484 per violation per user per day.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-SC) said on this week's broadcast of "Fox News Sunday" that the articles of impeachment against President Trump would not be dismissed without a trial. Host Chris Wallace said, "Have you given up on the idea that the majority will vote to dismiss case right away?" Graham said, "That's dead for practical purposes. There are a lot of senators who I think will wind up acquitting the president but believe we need to hear the House's case and the president's case in answer to the House's case." He added, "The idea of dismissing the case early on is not going to happen, We don't have the votes for that."

Hundreds gathered in Southeast Texas on Sunday for a vigil and march in memory of Sandra Bland, the Illinois woman found dead in a jail days after her arrest during a traffic stop. Houston TV station KPRC reported attendees met at a Prairie View church and marched across Prairie View A&M University, which Bland attended. Some carried signs that said "Justice for Sandra." Others called for a Justice Department investigation into her death. Authorities said Bland hanged herself, a finding her family disputes. Also on Sunday, The Houston Chronicle reported dozens protested outside a residence in Katy, west of Houston, that they believed belongs to the state trooper who arrested Bland. Protesters criticized his actions, which were captured on dashcam video, and called for him to be fired and criminally charged. The trooper is on administrative leave pending an investigation.

A Marist College Institute for Public Opinion poll conducted for NBC News shows Republican Joni Ernst and Democrat Bruce Braley at 43 percent each and 14 percent undecided. One-third of respondents say they are unsure of their opinion about the candidates or have never heard of them. Ernst leads Braley by two points in the favor/unfavorable rating category. Braley receives 36 percent positive and 32 percent negative ratings. Ernst receives 38 percent favorable and 33 percent unfavorable ratings.

Mexican immigration authorities initiated the deportation process for 98 Central American caravan migrants who recently entered an international port of entry in Tijuana, triggering crowd control tactics by U.S. authorities. The Mexican government said some migrants tried to attack police officers. In a statement, Mexico's National Migration Institute (INM) announced that 98 migrants arrested during the clash are being deported. Authorities continue to investigate the incident to locate additional migrants to charge under immigration laws for eventual removal. Mexican authorities said that during the rush for the border, some migrants tried to attack and injure several police officers securing the Chaparral/San Ysidro Port of Entry. The statement by INM revealed those actions violate various Mexican laws regarding criminal behavior by foreigners. The 98 deportations are fewer than the original 500 the Mexican government previously promised.

President Obama commented on Bruce Jenner's transformation into Caitlyn Jenner on the Vanity Fair cover on Monday. Obama said Jenner had the "courage" to share publicly. The official Barack Obama account tweeted Monday: "It takes courage to share your story." Jenner came out as transgender in last month's 20/20 interview with Diane Sawyer. On Monday, Jenner broke Obama's record for the fastest Twitter follower count, reaching 1 million followers in four hours, surpassing Obama's five. Obama also asked followers to share their stories at Obama's Organizing for Action website. Obama joins other celebrities and family members who have tweeted support for Jenner since the Vanity Fair cover hit the Internet Monday.

President Obama's speech at the Brookings Institution will not take place until 11:15 a.m. Fox News and Fox Business have detailed details. Major Garrett reports that Obama will announce an effort to boost the nation's infrastructure, including roads and bridges, as well as an injection of money for small businesses. FBN's Peter Barnes breaks down the numbers. His contacts tell him the goal is to appropriate $20-40 billion to increase small business lending, to come from unused TARP funds, and another $25-30 billion for tax credits for small business hiring to create new jobs. TARP, also known as the Troubled Asset Relief Program, was designed to pull the nation out of its financial difficulties. The program has a surplus of funds now, which the administration wants to tap into to create jobs.

Just before midnight, Mr. Alvarez conceded in a tweet reported by NBC: "I want to congratulate Kevin Faulconer. It's clear that he will be the next mayor of San Diego. I look forward to working with him." The winning candidate said during a last-minute speech while votes were still being counted that his leadership would bring San Diegans together, and his administration would "invest where we need the help," NBC reported. The special election was held to replace Mr. Filner, who resigned from his office in August following sexual harassment accusations. Mr. Filner was later sentenced to house arrest for felony false imprisonment and for two misdemeanor charges of battery against three different women, NBC said.

Potential jurors at Cook County Commissioner William Beavers' trial began filling out questionnaires Monday. The lead defense attorney, Victor Henderson, has become ill. The request for a delay in one-on-one questioning of panelists was scheduled to begin later Monday. U.S. District Judge James Zagel said they will reconvene Tuesday morning. Jury selection typically takes a day or two. Attorneys had earlier talked about being ready for openings by Tuesday. Openings may not occur until later this week. Beavers, 77, has denied diverting money from his campaign funds without reporting it.

The U.N. Security Council is set to hold an emergency meeting about Iran on Friday afternoon, the U.S. requested, according to a U.S. request. Members are divided in their views of the protests and could call a vote on whether to address the topic. U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley praised the demonstrators, stating "the U.N. must speak out" on their behalf. Russia warned against "external interference" in what it sees as Iran's internal affairs. At least 21 people have been killed and hundreds arrested in a week of anti-government protests and unrest. Thousands of people took part in pro-government rallies Wednesday and Thursday.

Senator John McCain (R-AZ) told KFYI-AM host Barry Young he is seriously considering running for re-election in 2016. "I'm seriously thinking about maybe giving another opportunity for you to vote for or against me in a few years from now," McCain said. "I'm seriously giving that a lot of thought." Young asked again if it would be correct to say McCain would be running for re-election and McCain said, "that it would not be wrong." McCain would be 80 years old in 2016 when he runs for re-election. The Arizona Republican previously said in a September Hill article he was probably in his last term but would decide on running again in two years and did not "want to be one of these old guys that should've shoved off."

During a press conference on Wednesday, President Trump said that Republicans who stayed away from him "did very poorly." He stated, "On the other hand, you had some that decided to — let's stay away, let's stay away. They did very poorly. I'm not sure that I should be happy or sad, but I feel just fine about it." He specifically cited Carlos Curbelo, Mike Coffman, and Mia Love. Trump then cited Barbara Comstock but said he did not blame her for not embracing him. Trump also cited Peter Roskam, Erik Paulsen, Bob Hugin, and John Faso.

Gallup reported Romney at 49 percent and Obama at 47 percent among national voters. The Gallup poll is in line with other polls, including Rasmussen Reports, that have shown Romney with a similar lead among national voters in the last week. Immediately after the first presidential debate, Romney surged to leads in key swing states including Florida, Virginia, and Colorado. The price of gold has slumped over the past several months while the Federal Reserve and other central banks have accelerated expansion of the money supply. Gold is down about 20 percent so far this year, while silver is down almost 30 percent. The adage "don't fight the Fed" is cited as a factor in the U.S. equity markets reaching new highs during the same period. All of these gains are nominal.

President Obama will speak in primetime Thursday regarding his planned executive action on immigration reform. The major network television stations will not televise the speech. CNN's Brian Stelter reported that ABC, NBC, and CBS will not televise Obama's speech. Stelter noted that the White House did not explicitly request airtime for the address before announcing it. Univision is expected to air Obama's speech. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest said the president opted for a prime-time address to "talk to as many as Americans as possible." Earnest added that 8:00 p.m. was when people were either "sitting in front of their televisions" or "sitting in front of their tablets or their smartphones."

A chemical spill that contaminated drinking water for some 300,000 people in West Virginia has led to scrutiny of the company responsible. The U.S. attorney is investigating the spill. Numerous businesses have sued Freedom Industries because they were forced to close and lost money until the water was safe again. Company officials have repeatedly declined to comment. Court and financial documents provide a window into the firm's history. Freedom Industries traces its start back to 1992, when it was founded by Carl Kennedy II and Dennis Farrell. Kennedy later pleaded guilty to tax fraud. Prosecutors accused Kennedy of withholding more than $1 million from employees' paychecks between 2000 and 2003 and diverting some of that money for his personal use.

New York is joining California and 14 other states in a lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump's national emergency declaration. New York Attorney General Letitia James said in the lawsuit Monday that Trump is threatening public safety with his move to divert funding from military construction and other programs to pay for a U.S.-Mexico border wall. All the states involved in the lawsuit have Democratic attorneys general. Trump declared an emergency on Friday to shift billions of dollars to the wall after Congress would not approve the amount he wanted. Trump, a Republican, considers a wall a national security necessity. The lawsuit alleges he is manufacturing a crisis and that his declaration is an "unconstitutional and unlawful scheme." This year's defense budget includes $194 million for construction at military installations in New York.

President Obama said in an interview with ABC News' George Stephanopoulos on Monday that he is the "underdog" in the 2012 race. Stephanopoulos asked about a new ABC/Washington Post poll showing 55 percent of Americans believe Obama will be a one-term president. Stephanopoulos asked if that makes Obama the underdog. Obama responded "absolutely." He added, "[G]iven the economy, there's no doubt that, you know, whatever happens on your watch." Obama said, "I don't mind. I'm used to being an underdog. And -- and I think that, at the end of the day, though, what people are going to say is, who's got a vision for the future that can actually help ordinary families recapture that American dream?"

Herman Cain is inviting his top supporters and donors to Atlanta on Saturday for a meeting in which he will give them advance word of whether he intends to continue his campaign, sources close to the campaign said Friday. One supporter who has been summoned to the private session said he believes Cain is likely to announce he is ending his candidacy. Another who has been invited to the morning meeting said attendees have been told he has made no decision but wanted to meet with some of the supporters to express his gratitude. Several sources indicated that Cain is likely to announce his plans publicly at a news conference after the meeting. Cain had already scheduled an event on Saturday — the grand opening of his national headquarters in his hometown of Atlanta, as well as the announcement of his campaign's senior leadership team for the state of Georgia.

Trump also cited Peter Roskam, Erik Paulsen, Bob Hugin, and John Faso.

President Donald Trump said Monday he would not visit the Capitol Hill rotunda this week to honor the late Rep. John Lewis. "I won't be going. No," Trump told reporters when asked about whether he would make a trip to honor Lewis. Lewis's body will lie in state at Capitol Hill on Monday and Tuesday following the arrival ceremony in the Capitol Rotunda. The public viewing will take place outside the Capitol building to prevent the spread of the coronavirus. Vice President Mike Pence and Second Lady Karen Pence are expected to pay their respects on Monday evening, and former Vice President Joe Biden will travel from Deleware to make a Monday appearance with former Second Lady Jill Biden. It is unclear whether former President Barack Obama or former First Lady Michelle Obama will pay their respects at the Capitol building.

Viewership for the second presidential debate between Donald Trump and Joe Biden fell to 63 million viewers. The first debate last month was seen by 73.1 million people. The second debate was canceled after Trump's coronavirus infection and replaced by dueling town halls on ABC and NBC. The Biden town hall reached 14.1 million people, while Trump had 13.5 million. On Thursday, the candidates debated mostly over health care, energy policy and how Trump handled the coronavirus pandemic. Both candidates also had an exchange over the business endeavors of Biden's son. In 2016, the first debate between Trump and Hillary Clinton garnered 84 million viewers, which is the most-watched debate ever. Their final debate had slightly less than 71.6 million viewers, which was higher than their second matchup.

Liz Cheney, the elder daughter of former Vice President Dick Cheney, is running for Congress. She has filed federal election documents showing she is running for Wyoming's lone seat in the House. Campaign officials said Cheney plans to formally announce Monday in Gillette, Wyoming. She could not immediately be reached for comment. Cheney ran a brief Senate campaign in 2013. She tried to unseat Wyoming's senior U.S. Sen. Mike Enzi, a fellow Republican, but failed to gain traction among Wyoming's political establishment. She quit her campaign seven months before the 2014 primary. This time, Cheney seeks to replace Republican Rep. Cynthia Lummis, who plans to retire at the end of her term. Cheney faces a field of eight Republican competitors including two experienced Wyoming state legislators.

Former Rep. Jesse L. Jackson Jr. pleaded guilty Wednesday to a conspiracy charge involving more than $750,000 in campaign funds at a hearing before a federal judge in Washington. "I am guilty, your honor," he said, according to a report in the Chicago Tribune. As part of the plea agreement, Jackson could face a jail sentence of 46 to 57 months, the Tribune reported. Both sides reserved the right to argue for more or less jail time. His sentencing hearing is set for this summer. "I used money I shouldn't have ... for personal reasons," Jackson said, according to the Tribune. "I acknowledge that." While leaving the courtroom, Jackson also told reporters, according to the Tribune: "Tell everybody back home I'm sorry I let 'em down, OK?"

Nordstrom shares fell after President Donald Trump tweeted that the department store chain had treated his daughter "so unfairly." The company announced last week it would stop selling Ivanka Trump's clothing and accessory line, stating the decision was based on the sales performance of the first daughter's brand. The tweet said: "My daughter Ivanka has been treated so unfairly by @Nordstrom. She is a great person — always pushing me to do the right thing! Terrible!" It was re-tweeted more than 4,000 times in less than 30 minutes. Shares in Seattle-based Nordstrom traded around $42.70 before the tweet, then fell to $42.48 afterward at around 10:50 a.m. Trump's tweets have in the past also affected shares in U.S. automakers Boeing and Carrier.

Dean Heller, a Nevada Republican, said he would uphold gun rights after the Las Vegas shooting on Sunday night. "You show me the law that would stop that, not only will I support it, I will be an advocate for that law," he said. The shooting left 58 people dead and 489 injured. The gunman, Stephen Paddock, had a cache of 23 guns in his room at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino. Police found another 19 at his Mesquite, Nevada, home and seven at a Reno property. Heller also revealed details about the gunman saying he was on "depressants" and that police believe others may have been involved in planning the event. The Nevada senator thanked President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump for their visit and said he was touched by how the president took the time to speak with survivors of the event.

U.S. Sen. Rand Paul's attorneys said in a court filing that he plans to undergo hernia surgery in Canada because of injuries he suffered when a neighbor attacked Paul while he was doing yard work at his Kentucky home. The filing in Paul's lawsuit against Rene Boucher says the senator will travel to Ontario, Canada, for outpatient surgery scheduled later this month. The document says the surgery is related to the 2017 attack. Boucher pleaded guilty to assaulting a member of Congress and was sentenced to 30 days in prison. Federal prosecutors are appealing the sentence. A Paul spokeswoman did not immediately explain why Paul is having the surgery in Canada, where medical care is publicly funded and universally provided. Paul touts private-market approaches for U.S. health care problems.

An Air Force officer who led the branch's Sexual Assault Prevention and Response unit has been charged with groping a woman in a parking lot in Arlington County, Virginia. Arlington County Police said Monday that Lt. Col. Jeffrey Krusinski of Arlington charged with misdemeanor sexual battery after an alleged assault about 12:30 a.m. Sunday in the Crystal City section of the county. A police report says Krusinski was drunk and grabbed a woman's breast and buttocks. Police say the woman fought him off and called police. Police spokesman Dustin Sternbeck says Krusinski did not know the woman involved. An arraignment is scheduled for Thursday. Air Force spokeswoman Natasha Waggoner said Krusinski was removed from his position after the Air Force learned of his arrest.

Supporters and campaign staff for presidential candidates Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump watched election results roll in minutes from each other in Manhattan. As of 10PM Eastern time, The New York Times live presidential forecast projected a 72 percent chance of a Donald Trump win. This number differed significantly from the initial projections before polls closed, predicting an 85 percent chance that Hillary Clinton would be the United States' next president. The projection changes, centered largely on the battleground states of Michigan, Florida, Ohio, and Virginia, affected the mood at both campaign headquarters. At the Jacob Javits Center, the Democratic headquarters, Clinton supporters appeared tense and dismayed. Meanwhile, some Manhattan blocks away at the New York Hilton Midtown, photos from inside Trump's election night party indicated the mood changed from cautious to increasingly optimistic.

A picture of U.S. President Donald Trump and German Chancellor Angela Merkel displaying body language at the G-7 summit in Frankfurt, Germany, was snapped by German government photographer Jesco Denzel. The picture shows a standing Merkel with hands firmly planted on a table staring down at Trump, who is seated with his arms folded and eyes glaring. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe stands next to Trump as French President Emmanuel Macron leans in next to Merkel. The photo was tweeted by Merkel spokesman Steffen Seibert. Shortly afterward, the White House issued a photo showing Trump speaking as Merkel, Abe and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau listen.

Former First Lady Barbara Bush, the mother of potential 2016 presidential candidate Jeb Bush, spoke in an interview with CSPAN. She said she hoped her son would not run for president because "there are other families. I refuse to accept that this great country isn't raising other wonderful people." She also said she believed Jeb was the best qualified for the job. Jeb Bush may be considering a run for president more after Republican New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie's "Bridgegate" scandal, which may have helped Bush the most. Bush posted on Twitter: "What date is Mother's Day this year? Asking for a friend."

A Quinnipiac University poll released Tuesday shows the race for U.S. Senate in New Jersey has tightened. The poll shows 53 percent support Democratic Newark Mayor Booker, while 41 percent support former Bogota Mayor Mark "Steve" Lonegan. The special election is scheduled for Oct. 16. A poll of registered votes in August showed Booker with a 25-percentage-point lead over the Republican. Booker receives the majority of his backing from women, who support him 60 percent to 34 percent. Men and independents are split. Pollster Maurice Carroll says the results could be driven by bad news about Newark crime and publicity about Booker's business ventures. The telephone survey of 948 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 19-22 and has an error margin of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

Rep. Peter King, a New York Republican, tweeted Wednesday that the Republican Party must distance itself from Steve Bannon after losing the Alabama Senate seat to Democrat Doug Jones. King wrote: "After Alabama disaster GOP must do right thing and DUMP Steve Bannon. His act is tired, inane and morally vacuous. If we are to Make America Great Again for all Americans, Bannon must go! And go NOW!!" Bannon, who was President Trump's former White House chief strategist, was one of the first people to back Republican candidate Roy Moore in the race and continued to sustain his campaign even after allegations of sexual misconduct became public. Moore was accused by multiple women of trying to pursue physical relationships with them when they were teens and he was an adult.

Memphis police said no charges will be filed against a kindergartener after a gun discharged inside the child's backpack in a school cafeteria. Police spokeswoman Karen Rudolph said the 5-year-old student and the child's mother were released from custody Thursday night, hours after the kindergartner was detained by police at Westside Elementary School. Officials said the child was waiting for the opening bell in the cafeteria when the gun went off. No one was hurt, and security officers took control of the backpack. Investigators determined the child obtained the gun from a closet at home and placed it in the backpack. Rudolph said Friday that the information was presented to the attorney general's office, which decided not to file charges. Police are not releasing the identity of the child and mother.

A picture of U.S. President Donald Trump and German Chancellor Angela Merkel displaying body language at the G-7 summit in Frankfurt, Germany, was snapped by German government photographer Jesco Denzel. The picture shows a standing Merkel with hands firmly planted on a table staring down at Trump, who is seated with his arms folded and eyes glaring. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe stands next to Trump as French President Emmanuel Macron leans in next to Merkel. The photo was tweeted by Merkel spokesman Steffen Seibert. Shortly afterward, the White House issued a photo showing Trump speaking as Merkel, Abe and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau listen.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Tuesday shows the race for U.S. Senate in New Jersey has tightened. The poll shows 53 percent support Democratic Newark Mayor Booker, while 41 percent support former Bogota Mayor Mark "Steve" Lonegan. The special election is scheduled for Oct. 16. A poll of registered votes in August showed Booker with a 25-percentage-point lead over the Republican. Booker receives the majority of his backing from women, who support him 60 percent to 34 percent. Men and independents are split. Pollster Maurice Carroll says the results could be driven by bad news about Newark crime and publicity about Booker's business ventures. The telephone survey of 948 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 19-22 and has an error margin of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

Republican Sen. Rand Paul said he is filing a class-action lawsuit against the Obama administration over data-collection policies of the National Security Agency. On his website, he urged Americans to join the lawsuit, describing it as "to stop Barack Obama's NSA from snooping on the American people." In an interview airing Friday night on Fox News, the Kentucky Republican told host Sean Hannity that he believes everyone in the U.S. with a cellphone would be eligible to join the class-action suit. Paul said that people who want to join the suit are telling the government it cannot have access to emails and phone records without permission or without a specific warrant. Paul said the lead lawyer in the suit is Virginia's former attorney general, Ken Cuccinelli.

During a town hall on guns with President Obama, CNN showed a clip of him crying at the White House and asked for a reaction. While the clip played, CNN cameras showed Obama's reaction to the video. CNN's Anderson Cooper described the moment as an "obviously emotional ceremony" and said people who watched were "surprised by that." Obama said, "I was, too, actually," and reminded the audience that he visited families who lost children at Newtown Elementary and it was "still very raw." Obama said, "It's the only time I've ever seen Secret Service cry on duty." Obama recalled the details of the event to emphasize that more needed to be done on gun control.

Republican presidential candidate and likely Republican nominee Donald Trump responded to Speaker of the House Paul Ryan's statement earlier Thursday that he is "not ready" to support Trump. In an emailed statement, Trump said: "I am not ready to support Speaker Ryan's agenda. Perhaps in the future we can work together and come to an agreement about what is best for the American people. They have been treated so badly for so long that it is about time for politicians to put them first!" Trump's comment mirrored Ryan's earlier statement: "I'm just not ready to do that at this point. I'm not there right now." Ryan made the statement earlier Thursday during an appearance on CNN about whether he will support Trump.

The New York City Council passed expanded paid sick days legislation. The bill has the support of Mayor Bill de Blasio, a Democrat, and will give the right to have paid sick days to 355,000 workers. The bill will be the first that de Blasio signs into law. He said Wednesday that the council "made history" with the legislation. Combined with previous legislation, more than a half-million New Yorkers will now be entitled to take up to five sick days without fear of losing their job. The bill passed in a 46-5 vote. It is the first major piece of legislation enacted by the council led by speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito. Some small business owners have voiced concerns that the legislation creates a financial burden.

A letter to the editor from the editor stated that Hillary Clinton and President Obama are examples of politicians who lie to the majority of voters to get elected and revert to their core ideology to govern. The letter stated that Clinton was inept as secretary of state and would do little to nothing to resolve Obama's foreign-policy disaster. It said she particularly did Obama's bidding when she pushed the "reset button" with Russia, and when she exacerbated matters in Libya by mishandling the Benghazi terrorist attacks that cost the lives of four Americans, including the ambassador. The letter said Clinton's recent criticism of the president's foreign policy is hypocritically political at the height of the Islamic State crisis in Iraq. The letter also stated that if elected president, Clinton would still embrace Obamacare, as evidenced by her failed attempt at national health care during the Clinton administration.

Secret Service agent Timothy McCarthy and District of Columbia police officer Thomas Delahanty each took a bullet to protect President Ronald Reagan. McCarthy served five years protecting the president and is now a police chief in Illinois. Delahanty retired on disability after the shooting and lives quietly in a Pittsburgh suburb. McCarthy told The Associated Press he respects the judge's decision to release Hinckley from a psychiatric hospital to live with his mother. He said what Hinckley did is "unforgivable." Delahanty told AP he is "not too enthused" about Hinckley's release.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi on Monday called for Labor Secretary Alex Acosta's resignation after details of the deal he struck as a U.S. attorney with Jeffrey Epstein resurfaced after the financier's latest arrest. Pelosi said Acosta made an "unconscionable" deal with Epstein and alleged that President Trump was aware of this deal when he brought him into his administration. Pelosi tweeted: "@SecretaryAcosta must step down. As US Attorney, he engaged in an unconscionable agreement w/ Jeffrey Epstein kept secret from courageous, young victims preventing them from seeking justice. This was known by [Mr. Trump] when he appointed him to the cabinet. #AcostaResign."

An aide to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, Mohammed Ishtayeh, said Thursday that gaps between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators have widened since talks began seven months ago. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry wants both sides to agree to a framework for a peace deal — effectively ground rules for future negotiations — by April 29. Ishtayeh said the U.S. might seek an extension but that he doubts this will happen because of lack of common ground. Ishtayeh said a key obstacle is Israel's demand that the Palestinians accept it as a Jewish state. He said Abbas cannot do so "under any circumstance" because it would restrict rights of Palestinian refugees and Israeli Arabs. Abbas is meeting March 17 with U.S. President Barack Obama.

I'm not there right now." Ryan made the statement earlier Thursday during an appearance on CNN about whether he will support Trump.

Republican candidate Donald Trump spoke at a rally in Pennsylvania on Wednesday, speaking to about 8,000 attendees. He made a reference to former Penn State coach Joe Paterno. Trump said: "I know a lot about Pennsylvania, and it's great. How's Joe Paterno. We're gonna bring that back? Right?...How 'bout that whole deal?" Paterno, who died in 2012, was criticized for his handling of former Penn State coach Jerry Sandusky, who was later convicted of child sex abuse. Sandusky was sentenced to 30-60 years in prison, and Paterno was fired in 2011. Paterno died two months after being fired. The Trump campaign clarified the comments, saying he was referencing the bronze statue of Paterno that was torn down in 2012 amid the controversy.

The U.S. Senate is moving toward a vote on Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback's nomination for an ambassador's post. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell filed a motion Monday to cut off debate on President Donald Trump's nomination of the conservative Republican governor to serve as U.S. ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom. McConnell communications director David Popp said in an email that a vote on the motion would occur Friday unless minority Democrats agree to have a vote sooner. Ending debate would clear the way for a second vote on Brownback's nomination. Trump first nominated Brownback for the ambassador's post in July, but his appointment has faced opposition from Democrats and LGBT groups. Brownback would resign if confirmed. Fellow Republican Lt. Gov. Jeff Colyer would be elevated to governor.

House Republicans are discussing the possibility of a short-term increase in the debt ceiling, Fox News has learned. Lawmakers are going through various scenarios at their annual retreat in Williamsburg, Va. One senior leadership aide said "many" at the retreat want a debate over a long-term extension of the debt ceiling to be delayed. The aide said they think "the House and Senate should first move budgets and debate about how to responsibly address the debt crisis." The first step could include passing some new spending cuts. President Obama, still smarting over the 2011 debt ceiling fight, has urged Republicans not to use the debt ceiling to extract concessions like spending cuts. Republicans see the debt ceiling as important leverage to pass deficit-reduction measures.

A Tennessee National Guardsman is facing prosecution in the shooting of two superiors at an armory outside Naval Support Activity Mid-South in Millington, Tennessee. The sergeant's first appearance in federal court could come Friday. Maj. Gen. Max Haston, head of the Tennessee Guard, said a major and a sergeant major were wounded in Thursday's attack at the armory just outside Naval Support Activity Mid-South in Millington. Both were expected to be out of the hospital soon. A law enforcement official briefed on the case said the sergeant — whose name was not released — had been disciplined before he opened fire. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss the case publicly. Other Guard members detained the shooter before police arrived.

The Daily Caller revealed that Martha Raddatz attended Obama's wedding to Julius Genachowski in 1991. Raddatz is no longer married to Genachowski. Information has come to light that Raddatz visited Vice President Joe Biden at his official residence earlier this year, on March 26, 2012. Biden was hosting a "Women's History Month Reception." Raddatz visited the White House on December 18, 2009. The reason for that visit is not clear. Raddatz is not the innocent non-partisan journalist she was made out to be. Her performance last night in attacking Paul Ryan consistently betrayed that fact.

President Donald Trump criticized talking heads on CNN for telling him not to campaign on border security and stopping illegal immigration Saturday at a campaign rally at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport in Belgrade, Montana. "Like they're doing me favors right?" Trump said. "CNN, doing me a favor, telling me what to say, right?" The crowd booed. "CNN is telling me how to run the campaign, but in the meantime, I'm president and they're not," he said. The crowd cheered. Trump added, "And their ratings aren't very good either." He said the economy was doing great, but that he wanted to talk about fixing problems that still needed to be addressed.

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern has moved into hospice care near his home in South Dakota. His daughter, Ann McGovern, told The Associated Press on Monday that the longtime South Dakota senator is "coming to the end of his life." Ann McGovern declined to elaborate but noted her 90-year-old father's recent health problems. She said he has moved in the Dougherty Hospice House in Sioux Falls. George McGovern lost to President Richard Nixon in a historic landslide in 1972. Most of his work in recent years has focused on world hunger. Last October, he was treated for exhaustion after a lecture tour. Two months later, he fell and hit his head just before a scheduled interview for a C-SPAN program about failed presidential candidates who have had a lasting impact on American politics.

"CNN is telling me how to run the campaign, but in the meantime, I'm president and they're not," he said. The crowd cheered. Trump added, "And their ratings aren't very good either." He said the economy was doing great, but that he wanted to talk about fixing problems that still needed to be addressed.

Evangelist Billy Graham has returned to his home in North Carolina after being hospitalized for observation and lung tests. Dr. William R. Hathaway, chief medical officer at Mission Hospital in Asheville, said the 95-year-old Graham was released Thursday and that he was alert and in good spirits during his two-day stay. Hathaway said doctors are pleased with the results of Graham's evaluation. Graham also spent two nights in the hospital for pulmonary testing last month after he had gone in for a regularly scheduled hospital visit. Graham uses a wheelchair and has been hospitalized for several health-related issues over the past few years. On Nov. 7, Graham celebrated his birthday surrounded by hundreds of guests including former vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin and real estate mogul Donald Trump.

The Senate approved the nomination of Sen. Max Baucus as the next U.S. ambassador to China on Thursday by a vote of 96-0. Baucus, 72, serves as chairman of the Senate Finance Committee. He has experience in U.S. trade policy but has limited expertise on military and other issues. Baucus was a leading author of President Barack Obama's health care law. He has also helped Republicans pass bills like President George W. Bush's 2001 tax cuts. Baucus' early Senate departure could help Democrats retain his seat. His state's Democratic governor is expected to appoint a Democrat to replace him, potentially giving that person a leg up in November's elections.

The author wrote that most arguments on Twitter in favor of the HHS Mandate and against Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties betray an extreme misunderstanding of the issues involved. The Supreme Court is deciding in the Sebelius v. Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties v. Sebelius cases whether the rights of business owners to operate their family companies without violating their religious convictions are Constitutionally protected. The author wrote that whether a business chooses to pay for an employee's contraception needs, contraception is inexpensive and widely available. The author wrote that an employee's access to the pill is not contingent upon whether or not their insurance covers it. The author wrote that it is hard to tell if these arguments are purposefully deceptive or are just seriously obtuse.

Fox TV planned to produce the upcoming NBC miniseries based on the political life of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. That was before the Republican National Committee vowed not to let NBC handle any 2016 presidential primary debates until the network dropped the project. Fox TV is out of the picture, although The Hollywood Reporter says the deal died due to point squabbles, not political fallout. Some within Team NBC may be relieved over the news, assuming it damaged its chances of bringing the miniseries to the public in the end. The NBC project, first announced by entertainment chairman Bob Greenblatt at the Television Critics Association confab in July, has caused internal strife at the network. NBC White House correspondent Chuck Todd and others have raised concern that the drama could damage the news division's reputation.

A chemical company controlled by Morocco's King Mohammed VI is funding a May 5-7 conference in Marrakech to be hosted by the Bill, Hillary and Chelsea Clinton Foundation's Clinton Global Initiative. Former Secretary of State and 2016 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton will not attend. Phosphate exporter OCP is owned by Morocco's King Mohammed VI and is providing funding of at least $1 million for the Clinton Global Initiative Middle East and Africa Meeting expected to attract other prominent Middle Eastern and North African officials. Hillary Clinton announced the meeting last September. A Clinton Foundation source told Politico Wednesday that she likely will not attend the gathering. The foundation has faced criticism for accepting millions of dollars in contributions from foreign governments, corporations, and individuals. Observers across political spectrum have raised questions about conflicts of interest.

President Obama said in an interview with VICE News that he is "embarrassed for them." He said: "For them to address a letter to the ayatollah — the supreme leader of Iran, who they claim is our mortal enemy — and their basic argument to them is: don't deal with our president, because you can't trust him to follow through on an agreement... That's close to unprecedented." VICE News released a "trailer" of its interview with Obama, which it conducted Thursday, but will not release the full interview until Monday. The trailer included Obama's comments on the letter.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security agent conducting surveillance in Texas was shot twice in the abdomen early Tuesday, according to an agency spokeswoman Nina Pruñeda. The agent, whose name has not been released, is expected to survive. The special agent was transported to a local hospital where he is undergoing surgery for a gunshot wound, Pruñeda said in a statement. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the special agent and his family," she said. An officer at the scene told Themonitor.com that the agent was in an unmarked SUV when he was shot. The circumstances of the shooting are still unclear. The Border Patrol, FBI, and U.S. Marshals Service are assisting ICE in the investigation.

Kathleen Sebelius, who resigned last week as President Barack Obama's Health and Human Services Secretary, will not challenge Sen. Pat Roberts (R-KS) for a Senate seat this year. A spokesperson told the New York Times on Thursday that Sebelius is continuing her important work at H.H.S. and is not considering a run for the Senate. Sebelius has said she would stay on at the department until her replacement is confirmed. Obama nominated Office of Management and Budget chief Sylvia Burwell to take over for Sebelius last week. Some Democrats wanted Sebelius, who was governor of Kansas, to run for Senate. Critics of the move said her candidacy would nationalize Obamacare and the rollout that may have led to her resignation, and hurt Democrats across the board this year.

Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci appeared Sunday on ABC's "This Week." He addressed violence Saturday at a Charlottesville, Virginia protest that left three dead and 19 injured. Scaramucci said President Donald Trump "needed to be much harsher" to white supremacists. He said, "I wouldn't have recommended that statement. I think he needed to be much harsher relating to the white supremacists and the nature of that. I applaud General McMaster for calling it out for what it is. It's actually terrorism. Whether it's domestic of international terrorism, with the moral authority of the presidency, you have to call that stuff out."

Opening statements are scheduled in the corruption trial of former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell and his wife Maureen. Prosecutors and defense attorneys will lay out their case for an eight-man, four-woman jury Tuesday. Jury selection took all day Monday. The McDonnells are charged in a 14-count indictment with accepting more than $165,000 in gifts and loans from Jonnie Williams, the CEO of dietary supplements maker Star Scientific, in exchange for helping promote his products. Their trial is expected to last at least five weeks. The prosecution will begin presenting its case after opening statements. At some point, Williams is expected to testify under immunity as the government's star witness. Among the possible defense witnesses are former Gov. Doug Wilder and former state Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli.

In a debate with President Barack Obama in Madrid on Thursday, U.S. Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney said he does not want the United States to become the equivalent of Spain, which has unemployment of nearly 25 percent and a deep recession. Most Spaniards were asleep at the time. Some Spaniards criticized Romney for singling out Spain. Others said the country is a poster child for economic gloom. Romney said 42 percent of Spain's gross domestic product is government spending. The Eurostat statistics agency said it was 43.6 percent in 2011, lower than the 49.1 percent average for the European Union's 27 countries.

Republican senators questioned Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano on Tuesday before the Senate Judiciary Committee at its third hearing on a bipartisan immigration bill that aims to strengthen border security, improve legal immigration, and create a path to citizenship for approximately 11 million people in the United States illegally. Napolitano had originally been scheduled to appear last Friday but was canceled because of the Boston Marathon bombings. The hearing followed a daylong hearing on Monday. Republicans said the bill does too little on border security and some said the measure should be re-examined in light of the events in Boston.

The Libyan government denied prior knowledge of the U.S. capture of Ahmed Abu Khattala, the top suspect in the 2012 attack on Americans in Benghazi, and demanded his return. In a statement read on television Wednesday, the interim government condemned the seizure. The U.S. accuses Abu Khattala of involvement in the attack on its consulate in Benghazi that left four Americans dead, including Ambassador Chris Stevens. Abu Khattala is headed for the United States to face what President Barak Obama called "the full weight of the American justice system." Obama called the Libyan an "alleged key leader" of the attack. The Libyan statement said: "The government stresses its right to try Abu Khattala on its territories and according to its laws."

A North Carolina textile entrepreneur, Keith Crisco, who is 71, died in a Democratic primary against former "American Idol" singer Clay Aiken on Tuesday. AEC Narrow Fabrics President Robert Lawson said Crisco died at home on Monday after an accident. Lawson said Crisco's son notified company employees of the death. There were less than 400 votes separating Crisco and Aiken after Tuesday's primary. The winner faces Republican incumbent Renee Ellmers in November. Crisco had been North Carolina's top business recruiter for four years under former Gov. Beverly Perdue, who left office in 2013.

President Donald Trump posted on Twitter Monday: "The White House Correspondents' Dinner is DEAD as we know it. This was a total disaster and an embarrassment to our great Country and all that it stands for. FAKE NEWS is alive and well and beautifully represented on Saturday night!" For the second consecutive year, Trump did not attend the dinner, instead holding a rally in Michigan. The annual event drew criticism after comedian Michelle Wolf performed a routine criticizing Sarah Huckabee Sanders. Some of Wolf's jokes about Sanders drew criticism. WHCA President Margaret Talev said she will work with the next president on the format of the dinner going forward.

Iran's President Hassan Rouhani has donated $170,000 to the country's only Jewish hospital, the Dr. Sapir charity hospital, his second such donation since taking office. The official IRNA news agency said Thursday that Rouhani has given the same amount from government funds as he did last year to the hospital, established in 1942 in the capital, Tehran. The donation is seen as part of Rouhani's pledge to pay more attention to the country's minorities. It contrasts with Rouhani's predecessor, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who prompted international criticism by denying the Holocaust took place while also calling for the destruction of Israel. Iran's Jews number about 25,000, making it the largest Jewish community in any country in the Middle East outside of Israel.

Illinois state Sen. James Meeks announced Sunday at the University of Illinois at Chicago that he is running for mayor of Chicago. Meeks is pastor of a megachurch on the South Side. He is the third candidate to officially join the race this weekend. Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel announced his candidacy Saturday. U.S. Rep. Danny Davis made his run official earlier Sunday. They are running to replace Mayor Richard Daley, who announced in September he would not seek a seventh term. The election is Feb. 22. The field also includes City Clerk Miguel del Valle and former Chicago school board president Gery Chico, who have already declared. Former U.S. Sen. Carol Moseley Braun plans an official announcement soon.
