On Thursday, MSNBC's "The Cycle" added political pundit Touré to its program. During the program, Touré agreed with Breitbart News' take on Barbara Walters' interview of potential presidential candidates Chris Christie and Hillary Clinton. Walters said, "you would never ask a man that." Touré asked why he was asking her that and whether he recognized the sexism he was activating and commenting on. Touré said, "No, you don't. They say even a broken clock is right twice a day."

Friends of Tamerlan Tsarnaev's wife, Katherine Russell, describe the suspected Boston Marathon bomber who was killed in a Thursday evening shootout as someone who radically changed around 2008, believing Islam "was under attack." According to NPR's Laura Sullivan, Russell's friends said Tamerlan would party with them, but his behavior started to change in 2008; he became "very religious, and he stopped smoking, and he stopped drinking, and he stopped going out with them." Sullivan reports that Russell's friends said this is when Tamerlan started having "an extremist point of view, that he started talking about being angry with the government, and he said that he felt that Islam was under attack."

Former Vice President Joseph R. Biden said Thursday he would not commit to running for a second term in the White House if he wins the November election. "No, I'm not willing to commit one way or another," Biden said at the Democratic presidential debate in Los Angeles. "Here's the deal - I'm not even elected one term yet, and let's see where we are. Let's see what happens." Moderator Tim Alberta pointed out that Biden would turn 82 years old at the end of his first term and be the oldest president in "American history."

Rudolph W. Giuliani, President Trump's personal lawyer, spoke at a press conference Thursday. A dark substance dripped down both sides of his face while he spoke. The substance, which social media users assumed to be hair dye, was dripping from near each of Giuliani's ears and running down his cheeks while he addressed reporters. Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City, effectively grew wet sideburns while he spoke. The substance left a dark, narrow line on the sides of his face as gravity dragged it down to his jaw.

Law enforcement agents intercepted a package addressed to the White House containing ricin earlier this week, according to CNN and the New York Times. The package was addressed to President Donald Trump. A facility outside the White House typically screens all mail before delivery to the White House. An official speaking to the New York Times said the letter is believed to have been sent from Canada. An attempt to mail ricin to President Trump was also intercepted in October 2018. William Clyde Allen, a former Naval officer, was arrested by the FBI for mailing ricin filled letters to Secretary of Defense James Mattis, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. John Richardson, and FBI Director Chris Wray.

A proposal by Central American businessmen to build a natural gas pipeline from Mexico to Panama will be presented during a weekend meeting between U.S. President Barack Obama and Central American presidents. Nicaraguan businessman Jose Aguerri said Tuesday that the project would lower energy costs in the region and make its economies more competitive. Aguerri said the idea was first proposed by Nicaraguan businessmen and has since gained support across Central America's private sector. He said he hopes Obama will back the idea because the pipeline would make the region more self-sufficient. After a two-day visit to Mexico, Obama will be in Costa Rica on Friday to meet with Central American presidents.

Reclaim America, Sen. Marco Rubio's (R-FL) leadership PAC, will air a new television advertisement for Iowa GOP Senate candidate Joni Ernst, according to Terry Sullivan, the PAC's director. Rubio, who shares a consultant, Todd Harris, with Ernst, endorsed her on May 5. Ernst holds a lead against businessman Mark Jacobs. Her first television advertisement began with the words, "I grew up castrating hogs on an Iowa farm." Former Gov. Mitt Romney and former Gov. Sarah Palin have also backed Ernst.

President Donald Trump said he thinks former national security adviser Susan Rice committed a crime when she unmasked American citizens involved with his campaign. "I think it's going to be the biggest story," Trump said to the New York Times. "It's such an important story for our country and the world. It is one of the big stories of our time." Trump's remarks are his first public statement on the subject since reports claimed Rice was responsible. Trump did not reveal new details to the New York Times but said he would explain himself "at the right time."

White House chief of staff Denis McDonough said on CBS's Face The Nation on Sunday that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad was a liar for denying that he used chemical weapons against his people. McDonough said Assad's statements, which were reported by CBS's Charlie Rose, who interviewed Assad in Damascus, were "misleading" and that his claim not to have authorized chemical weapons use "does appear to me to be a lie." McDonough said, "What we need is to communicate very clearly what is expected of him." Assad reportedly told Rose that there was no evidence that chemical weapons were used to attack Syrians in an interview that CBS will reportedly air on Monday.

Hackers blocked access to Indiana's state government website Friday afternoon in response to the state's religious freedom bill being signed into law this week. Some users were unable to access the state's website, www.in.gov, the Indianapolis Star reported. Indiana Office of Technology spokesman Graig Lubsen said the website was not hacked. A denial of service attack consists of sending many traffic requests at the same time to overwhelm a website and have it not be able to load. The denial of service interruption began at approximately 2:00, but the site has not been continuously down.

President Donald Trump said his reimbursement of a 2016 payment to porn actress Stormy Daniels had nothing to do with his election campaign. The revelation of the president's payment clashed with his past statements and created legal challenges in the West Wing. White House aides were blindsided when Trump's attorney, Rudy Giuliani, said Wednesday night that the president had repaid Michael Cohen for $130,000 that was given to Daniels to keep her quiet before the 2016 election about her allegations of an affair with Trump. Giuliani's revelation contradicted Trump's past statements.

The House extended disaster assistance to livestock producers affected by rising feed prices caused by the drought that has affected much of the nation. The vote to revive expired disaster relief programs for cattle and sheep producers was one of the House's last before lawmakers left for their five-week August recess. It was uncertain whether the Senate would act on the bill before it adjourns for the summer break. Democratic opponents characterized the legislation as cover for Republicans having to explain to rural constituents why they put off action on a comprehensive five-year farm policy bill. Many crop farmers have insurance that provides some protection from the effects of the drought, but livestock producers are vulnerable to sharp increases in feed prices resulting from the dry weather.

Democrat J.D. Scholten announced Monday he is running to unseat Rep. Steve King in Iowa's 4th Congressional District after he faced a stronger than expected challenge last year. Scholten, a former professional baseball player, made the announcement in a video narrated by actor Kevin Costner. "This time, we're going to get the job done," Scholten said in a statement. "Too many Iowan families feel like they're getting kicked in the dirt, suffering from an economy and a government that just doesn't have their interests at heart."

Democratic U.S. Rep. Deb Haaland of New Mexico called for an impeachment inquiry of President Donald Trump on Wednesday. The first-term lawmaker from Albuquerque said Trump "has proven he's unfit to serve as president" and that Congress needs to "shed light on what his administration is hiding and hold the president accountable." Haaland previously said she favored more aggressive oversight of Trump that might lead to impeachment hearings. A tally by The Associated Press indicates more than half of House Democrats support launching an impeachment inquiry.

Three potential nominees for President Obama's administration, including CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta, withdrew Thursday. None had been officially nominated. A White House official confirmed to The Washington Times that Dr. Gupta had been under serious consideration for surgeon general but withdrew his name. Separately Thursday, several news outlets reported that former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission member Annette Nazareth withdrew her name from consideration for deputy secretary at the Treasury Department. Additionally, Caroline Atkinson withdrew her name from consideration for undersecretary of Treasury for international affairs.

China and the United States introduced new sanctions against North Korea at the United Nations on March 5. The resolution tightens existing sanctions against ballistic missile and nuclear tests and contains sanctions on "the import and export of nuclear and ballistic-missile related material." Embargoes on luxury items, arms imports and exports, and financial and travel sanctions are also included. The newest aspect of these measures is believed to broaden financial and travel sanctions. China will not support the embargo because it fears North Korea would collapse, negatively impacting China's economy.

President Obama said Afghanistan will no longer "be a source of terrorist attacks again," a week before the United States ends its combat mission in the Middle Eastern nation. "We've been in continuous war now for over 13 years. Next week we will be ending our combat mission in Afghanistan," Obama told troops in Hawaii late Thursday, celebrating Christmas. "Because of the extraordinary service of the men and women in the armed forces, Afghanistan has a chance to rebuild its own country. We are safer. It's not going to be a source of terrorist attacks again."

Former Vice President Joe Biden (D) won the state of Missouri's Democratic primary on Tuesday evening, according to the Associated Press. Missouri is one of six states holding a Democratic primary on Tuesday offering 68 pledged delegates. In 2016, Bernie Sanders lost the Democratic primary by less than half a percentage point, or 1,531 votes. The margin of Biden's victory is not yet known. Michigan's final polls close at 9:00 p.m. ET.

The number of people applying for unemployment benefits fell 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000 last week, the lowest since late September. The Labor Department said the four-week average fell for the third straight week to 338,500. Both figures are near pre-recession levels. Applications are a proxy for layoffs. They spiked in early October because of the partial government shutdown and processing backlogs in California. First-time applications have fallen in five of the past six weeks. The decline indicates that employers are laying off fewer workers.

President Obama said former Secretary of Defense Robert Gates did an outstanding job while at the Pentagon and called him a good friend. Obama responded to Gates' book, "Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary of War," saying that his administration's policy in Afghanistan was the right one. In the book, Gates questions Obama's commitment to his war policy and details discord among the team that made key decisions about the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Obama said that part of his job as commander in chief is to, quote, "sweat the details" on policies that send men and women into harms' way. Obama spoke Monday as he concluded a meeting with Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy.

The Senate is attempting to pass an extension of the 1994 Violence Against Women Act that would protect women from domestic abuse while broadening protections for Native Americans, gays and lesbians. The Democratic-led Senate and Republican-led House last year passed extensions of the Violence Against Women Act, but the two chambers were unable to bridge a partisan divide and reach a compromise. Republican losses among women voters in the November election were noted. Senate advocates hope the bill will be easier this year to find common ground with House Republicans. The Senate bill coming up for test vote on Monday essentially is the same as the measure that passed the Senate last April.

Officials in Washington and Oregon confirmed Tuesday that 37 people have taken ill with the E. coli bacteria, up from 22 confirmed illnesses on Monday. Chipotle restaurants are a suspected source of the bacteria, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention praised the restaurant chain for closing 43 of its restaurants in the I-5 region between Portland, Ore. and Seattle, Wash. The CDC had little additional information to share about the exact cause on Tuesday. Dr. Tom Frieden, director of the CDC, said Tuesday: "We don't yet know of a vehicle, which food caused it, or even with certainty that all of the cases that are identified there are related to each other."

Sen. Bernard Sanders of Vermont said at the Democratic presidential debate in Los Angeles that while the North American trade pact the House passed Thursday is a "modest improvement" over the status quo, he would not vote for it. "It is not going to stop outsourcing. It is not going to stop corporations from moving to Mexico," Sanders said. "The word climate change, to the best of my knowledge, is not discussed in this new NAFTA agreement at all, which is an outrage." On an overwhelming bipartisan vote, the House approved President Trump's rewrite of the North American Free Trade Agreement on Thursday.

President Obama is reportedly giving serious consideration to a speedy withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan, leaving no troops there after 2014, The New York Times reported. Obama is considering the "zero option," instead of leaving a residual force, because of his deteriorating relationship with Afghan President Hamid Karzai, The Times said. Karzai was upset with American peace talks with the Taliban in Qatar, The Times said. He accused the U.S. government of leaving the country exposed to its enemies. A June 27 video conference between Obama and Karzai ended badly, lending credence to the withdrawal plan, The Times reported.

During a speech on Tuesday, President Trump called for the death penalty for criminals who kill police officers. Trump said, "We're not going to let bad things happen to our police. So we must show appreciation, gratitude, and respect for those who police our streets and patrol our communities. In 2016, an officer was assaulted in America on an average of every ten minutes. Can you believe that? It's outrageous and it's unacceptable. We must end the attacks on our police, and we must end them right now. We believe criminals who kill our police should get the death penalty. Bring it forth."

A former adviser to Barack Obama's presidential campaign, Samantha Power, is working on the transition team for the agency that Clinton may lead. State Department officials said Friday that Power is among foreign policy experts the president-elect's office selected to help the incoming administration prepare for Clinton's anticipated nomination as secretary of state. The Obama transition team's Web site includes Power's name as one of 14 members of the "Agency Review Team" for the State Department. During the Democratic primary campaign, Power called Clinton "a monster" in an interview. She then resigned, calling her remarks inexcusable and contradictory to her admiration for Clinton.

President Obama visited the DC Central Kitchen, a soup kitchen located a few minutes from the White House, on Monday. He accompanied his wife Michelle and daughters Malia and Sasha. The facility serves thousands of meals daily for distribution to local shelters. Obama said he came to help mark its 25th anniversary. He said the facility is honoring Martin Luther King Jr.'s legacy of service. He said he came to help the facility mark the meal preparation.

Sen. Joni Ernst, the first Republican female to address President Trump's Supreme Court nominee Judge Amy Coney Barrett at Monday's confirmation hearing, expressed excitement for another woman to serve on the high court. If confirmed, Judge Barrett would be the fifth woman ever to serve on the Supreme Court but she would be the first to be a working mother with school-age children. "As a fellow woman, a fellow mom, a fellow Midwesterner, I see you for who you are, and I am glad the American people have the opportunity to get to know Amy Coney Barrett," the Iowa Republican said.

Former pizza executive Herman Cain is reportedly expected to withdraw his name from consideration for the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors following lackluster support from Republican senators, according to an ABC News report. President Trump announced Cain last week as his pick, with economist and author Stephen Moore as his second choice. Moore is a columnist for The Washington Times. Cain, the former CEO of Godfather Pizza, ran for the GOP presidential nomination in 2012 on his "9-9-9" tax plan that would eliminate tax laws in favor of a 9 percent tax on sales, individual income and corporate income across the United States.

The White House announced the creation of a team of digital experts tasked with upgrading the government's technology infrastructure and making its websites more consumer friendly. The move is aimed at avoiding a repeat of the website issue that affected the rollout of President Barack Obama's signature health care legislation last year. The administration ultimately surpassed enrollment targets, but the opening weeks of sign-ups experienced website troubles that raised questions about the administration's competence. The new digital team will be overseen by Mikey Dickerson, an engineer who took leave from Google to supervise fixes to the HealthCare.gov site.

Allies are growing concerned about President Donald Trump's legal situation, as his lawyers offer an optimistic view. The shifting explanations for why Trump fired national security adviser Michael Flynn have revived questions about whether the president may have obstructed an ongoing investigation of potential contacts between his campaign and Russia. Pressure on the administration has mounted since Flynn last week pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his conversations with the Russian ambassador, with prosecutors revealing that he is now cooperating with special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation. A muddled White House response, including a presidential tweet, has left some Trump confidants worried that the president is not being well-served by his legal team.

On Wednesday, during NBC's "Nightly News," 2020 Democratic presidential hopeful Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) said he has no plans to slow his presidential campaign after he suffered a heart attack last week. Sanders said, "I misspoke the other day. I said a word I should not have said and media drives me a little bit nuts to make a big deal about it." He added, "We're going to get back into the groove of a very vigorous campaign, I love doing rallies and I love doing town meetings."

On Sunday, former White House Senior Adviser David Axelrod appeared on NBC's "Meet the Press." He said it was a "mistake" for President Barack Obama to say his policies are on the ballot this fall in a speech on Thursday. The line "I'm not on the ballot this fall … but make no mistake, these policies are on the ballot — every single one of them" is already being used in advertisement by Republicans seeking to run against the president. In reaction, Axelrod said, "It was a mistake."

A secret intelligence court has decided to continue an order that requires Verizon Communications to turn over hundreds of millions of telephone records to the government each day in its search for foreign terror or espionage suspects. The longstanding Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order must be renewed every three months. It had been set to expire Friday. National Intelligence Director James Clapper announced the new order. The surveillance program has been under scrutiny since June, when former CIA employee and National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden leaked details of two top secret U.S. surveillance programs that critics say violate privacy rights. Snowden has been charged with espionage and is seeking asylum from several countries, including Russia.

The White House defended President Donald Trump's failure to acknowledge the women who accused former staff secretary Rob Porter of domestic violence. White House spokeswoman Sarah Huckabee Sanders told reporters that Trump and the entire administration take domestic violence very seriously and that the president believes all allegations need to be investigated thoroughly. Sanders said she spoke directly with the president and he had "relayed that message directly to me." Trump posted on Twitter over the weekend that, "Peoples lives are being shattered and destroyed by a mere allegation. Some are true and some are false." He also said he wished Porter well in his future career.

Gov. Lincoln Chafee said Monday that Rhode Island will be "in good shape" despite a change in legislative leadership following law enforcement raids of former House Speaker Gordon Fox's home and office. The Democratic governor said he had been briefed on the investigation related to the raids but declined to comment and referred all questions to federal authorities. Fox has resigned his leadership position and the House is expected to pick a new Speaker Tuesday. Chafee said he looks forward to working with whoever succeeds Fox and said he is confident state leaders can remain focused on their work.

President Barack Obama said the detention center at Guantanamo Bay undermines America's national security and needs to be closed. Obama said the detention center is counterproductive in the fight against terrorism because it is used as propaganda to recruit terrorists and drains military resources. The White House released Obama's plan to close the facility on Tuesday. The plan faces opposition from the GOP-led Congress. The plan calls for transferring remaining detainees to the United States and seeks up to $475 million in construction costs that would ultimately be offset by as much as $180 million per year in operating cost savings. It does not specify where in the United States the detainees would go.

Gov. Scott Walker said Wednesday he is optimistic that President Donald Trump's administration will make "meaningful reforms" to the Medicaid program. Other Republican governors oppose a proposal that would drastically cut payments to the states. Walker released a letter that U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price sent to governors pledging to improve the program, which is jointly funded by states and the federal government. The letter comes as Congress is considering a Republican-backed bill that would cut payments to states for Medicaid, the program that provides health care to the poor and lower-income workers.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV) said Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) "stands for everything America doesn't" and that the Republican Party would end if the GOP nominated Cruz to be their candidate for president in 2016. In an interview with MSNBC's Rachel Maddow that aired Wednesday, Reid said, "If I didn't care so much about our country, I would hope he would get the Republican nomination for president, because that would mean the end of the Republican Party." Reid also said the Republican Party "is staggering right now" and that he did not "know who they can expect to have a vote for them."

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton spoke to the crowd in Durham, North Carolina, and said, "I know you have a favorite, but everyone takes a second look, maybe a third or fourth look. And I hope you give me one of those looks over the next few days." She added, "Of course I still hope to persuade those who are looking at Senator Sanders, but I want you to know that I am truly happy that you are involved in this election and the Democratic Party." The remarks came 24 hours after Clinton and Sanders argued on the debate stage in Durham. Clinton beat Sanders by .2 percent in the Iowa caucus. Sanders currently leads Clinton by twenty points in some New Hampshire polls.

Congressional bargainers are working toward a border security deal amid indications that the White House is preparing to accept a bipartisan agreement that would give President Donald Trump a fraction of the money he has demanded for his proposed southern border wall. Participants said they expect money for physical barriers to end up well below the $5.7 billion that Trump has sought to begin construction of the wall, which has received significant attention from him and his conservative supporters. The amount seems likely to fall closer to $1.6 billion, the participants said, a figure that was in a bipartisan Senate bill last year. An agreement would also avert a new partial federal shutdown next weekend.

At least 80 demonstrators were arrested Monday in House and Senate office buildings on Capitol Hill, according to the U.S. Capitol Police. Most were demonstrating against proposed changes to federal health care law, which includes congressional Republicans' efforts to make changes to ObamaCare. Police officials said those arrested were first told to cease and desist their unlawful demonstration and that those who refused were arrested and charged with "crowding, obstructing or incommoding." Officials said 21 adults — 10 males and 11 females — were arrested in House office buildings, and 59 adults — 22 males and 37 females — were arrested in Senate office buildings.

The Delaware Republican Senate primary proved that nobody voting on Capitol Hill, regardless of party, is safe. There were conflicts about whether Christine O'Donnell can win in the November election. Conservative movement leaders reacted. Kerry Picket, a former Opinion Blogger/Editor of The Watercooler, was associate producer for the Media Research Center, a content producer for Robin Quivers of "The Howard Stern Show" on Sirius satellite radio, and a production assistant and copy writer at MTV.

During an online Q&A, Michelle Obama was asked by Obama impersonator Iman Crosson how many calories could be burned just by dancing. Crosson said, "On average, how many calories do you burn every time you 'turn up'?!" In response, the First Lady posted a Vine holding a turnip and dancing to the song "Turn Down For What." The meme was not original, as the pun had surfaced on the internet in response to the song by DJ Snake and Lil Jon. The White House Vine is already approaching 6 million "loops."

Chinese state media reported that President Xi Jinping called for restraint when dealing with North Korea during a telephone call with President Donald Trump. The official broadcaster CCTV quoted Xi as telling Trump that China strongly opposed North Korea's nuclear weapons program and hoped "all parties will exercise restraint and avoid aggravating the situation" on the Korean Peninsula. The Trump administration warned that all options, including a military strike, are "on the table" ahead of a possible sixth nuclear test by Pyongyang, which could come as early as this week. The call is the second time the two leaders have spoken directly since meeting in Florida earlier this month as tensions mounted.

U.S. Sen. Mark Kirk said in a Chicago Sun-Times column posted Monday that he "looks forward" to President Barack Obama nominating a replacement for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. Kirk said the constitution gives the president, Republican or Democrat, the right to send a nominee to the Senate. He said he swore an oath to uphold the constitution, "not to a party or any one individual." Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and other Republicans said the next president should choose Scalia's successor.

Gallup conducted a survey of congressional leaders on September 5-8 with a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points. The survey was conducted days before Reid is scheduled to attempt to amend the continuing resolution the House passed last week that would fund the government except for the Affordable Care Act. Reid has said he will use a 51-vote threshold to add an amendment that would fund the Affordable Care Act and send the bill back to the House. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and other conservatives including Mike Lee (R-UT) have said Republicans need to unite to oppose a cloture vote on moving the bill forward so Reid is unable to insert funding for the Affordable Care Act.

On October 30, Hillary Clinton, a former Secretary of State from New York, will travel to Los Angeles to support Virginia gubernatorial candidate Terry McAuliffe. The event will be hosted by Hollywood billionaire Haim Saban. Tickets to the event will cost $15,000 per person and $25,000 per couple. Hillary Clinton is expected to endorse McAuliffe formally this week. Her husband, former President Bill Clinton, has also been doing fundraisers for him. McAuliffe currently leads in polls in his race for Virginia governor over current state attorney general Ken Cuccinelli.

President Barack Obama said that in an interconnected world, outbreaks of deadly viruses like Ebola have the potential to affect every nation. Obama spoke to representatives of more than 40 countries attending a global health summit at the White House. He said that while the United States is taking "an opportunity to lead" the response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, it must also be a global priority. Obama announced last week that the United States was dispatching 3,000 military personnel to the region to help contain the outbreak.

Donald Trump Jr., son of President Donald Trump, said on this week's broadcast of Fox News Sunday's "Sunday Morning Futures" that Democrats and the media hate him more than they love America. Trump said, "They will double down. Any opportunity to hurt Trump, and that is the reality." He continued, "Democrats and media hate Trump much more than they love America because you can't dispute the numbers. You can't dispute all-time low unemployment for every group in this country, every demographic."

On Sunday, President Donald Trump appeared on NBC's "Meet the Press" and said his administration would speak with Iranian officials without preconditions. Trump said, "I'm not looking for war, and if there is, it'll be obliteration like you've never seen before. But I'm not looking to do that. But you can't have a nuclear weapon. You want to talk good." When host Chuck Todd asked if talks would include preconditions, Trump said, "Not as far as I'm concerned. No preconditions."

On Tuesday at an event in New York City hosted by Cornell University's Institute of Politics & Global Affairs, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) said President Donald Trump was "goading" Democrats to impeach him. Pelosi said, "Trump is goading us to impeach him. That's what he's doing. Every single day, he's just like taunting, taunting, taunting because he knows that it would be very divisive in the country, but he doesn't really care. He just wants to solidify his base."

On Thursday, after the House of Representatives passed the revised version of the American Health Care Act (AHCA), Planned Parenthood President Cecile Richards released a video on Twitter urging voters to call their senators to stop the bill. She described the bill as the "worst bill for women and women's health in a generation." She said, "we have got to stop it in the Senate, but it's going to take every single one of us. We have one job in this moment. Call you senators, and tell them that you oppose the American Health Care Act. This is the fight of our lives."

Twenty or 21 women were brought back to the hotel in Colombia by U.S. Secret Service agents and members of the U.S. military in an incident last week involving alleged misconduct with prostitutes, U.S. Senator Susan Collins said on Tuesday. Collins was briefed by the director of the Secret Service, Mark Sullivan, on Monday evening. "There are 11 agents involved. Twenty or 21 women foreign nationals were brought to the hotel, but allegedly Marines were involved with the rest," the Republican senator said in comments emailed to Reuters by her spokesman.

Twenty or 21 women foreign nationals were brought to the hotel, but allegedly Marines were involved with the rest," the Republican senator said in comments emailed to Reuters by her spokesman.

Republican Sen. John McCain said he is considering running for a sixth term in 2016, the year he turns 80. In an interview Tuesday with radio station KFYI-AM in Phoenix, the Arizona Republican said he is seriously giving a lot of thought to another bid for re-election. McCain said he is getting encouragement from businesses that are upset with the recent partial government shutdown. He had opposed the tea party tactic of linking gutting the health care law to keeping the government operating. McCain unsuccessfully sought the presidency in 2008 and won another Senate term in 2010. He has challenged President Barack Obama on foreign policy but has worked with Democrats on immigration legislation.

Gov. Rick Scott said Friday he has not seen the letter sent to Florida Secretary of State Ken Detzner on Wednesday. A spokeswoman for Detzner said the agency was reviewing the request. The Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity asked election officials across the country for voter information, including names, political party affiliation and voter history. The request included asking for the last four digits of voters' Social Security numbers. Democratic officials in some states said they will not comply with the request because it is based on false fraud accusations. Trump has claimed without evidence that between 3 million and 5 million people voted illegally last year.

President Obama spoke Saturday before the Global Entrepreneurship Summit in Kenya, where he is conducting his first presidential visit to the country. He said entrepreneurship offers a positive alternative to ideologies of violence and division that can all too often fill the void when young people do not see a future for themselves. Obama noted Africa is on the move and that it is "one of the fastest-growing regions in the world," according to Reuters. China has overtaken the United States as the continent's biggest trading partner. Obama urged the Kenyan government to do more to protect businesspeople from corruption.

White House spokesman Robert Gibbs said President Obama will travel to Manitowoc, Wisconsin, on Wednesday regardless of the outcome. The announcement prompted speculation this week that Obama would attend the Super Bowl if the Bears win. When asked about his plans for the game, Obama said with a laugh: "Oh, if the Bears are in the Super Bowl, we're going." Gibbs said that as a superstitious fan, it was too soon to be making Super Bowl plans.

President Barack Obama entered the White House Correspondents Dinner on Saturday and commented on conservative talk radio host Rush Limbaugh's entrance music. "How do you like my new entrance music?" Obama said, smirking. "Rush Limbaugh warned you about this. Second term, baby." Obama entered "All I Do is Win," a DJ Khaled song featuring Ludacris, who once rapped about wanting to paint the White House black. The president also joked, in reference to Limbaugh, "We're changing things" in the second term.

President Barack Obama told reporters he had "no reaction" to reports that Donald Trump would address the situation today. Obama said he was "shocked" that the media was covering the issue, adding he finds it "typical." "I was pretty confident about where I was born, I think people were as well," he said. "And my hope would be that the presidential election reflects more serious things than that."

Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg said Tuesday he is concerned that marijuana is damaging the brains of the nation's youth. Bloomberg said he supports decriminalizing the possession of marijuana but said the federal government should go slow when it comes to all-out legalization. "They haven't done enough research and the evidence so far is worrisome," Bloomberg said in the Democratic presidential debate in South Carolina. "Until we know the science, it is not sensible to push ahead."

Vietnam's foreign minister Pham Binh Minh arrived in North Korea on Tuesday ahead of a planned summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Vietnam's capital, Hanoi, on Feb. 27-28. No further details of his schedule have been released by his North Korean hosts. The two leaders held their first summit last June in Singapore. The United States is seeking a firm commitment on denuclearization from Kim.

The campaign of former Israeli military chief Gantz, who is a leading challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the race for re-election, says the candidate has been targeted by an Iranian hacking attack. A statement from Gantz's campaign said his opponents leaked the news to damage his political bid, and that the timing of the report weeks before Israel's April 9 elections "raises important questions." A campaign official said the security breach happened several months ago, before Gantz entered politics. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to media.

The Senate Armed Services Committee will hold a confirmation hearing on the nomination of Chuck Hagel to be the next defense secretary on January 31. The panel announced the hearing in a statement issued Wednesday. Committee Chairman Sen. Carl Levin of Michigan has expressed support for Hagel, President Barack Obama's pick to replace Leon Panetta as Pentagon chief. The panel's top Republican, Sen. Jim Inhofe of Oklahoma, said in a statement late Tuesday that he would oppose the nomination. Inhofe is one of a handful of Republicans who have expressed opposition to Hagel, a Republican who served two terms as senator from Nebraska.

Prosecutors are resting their case against Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan, who is accused of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan is acting as his own attorney. The U.S.-born Muslim began the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman who killed and wounded the others. He also has leaked documents during the trial that seek to justify the shooting as a defending his faith.

Republican nominee Donald Trump's speech at the Republican National Convention drew at least two million more viewers than Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton's speech at the Democratic National Convention (DNC). According to Nielsen television ratings, just under 28 million viewers tuned in for Clinton's speech, while 30 million viewers tuned in for Trump's speech. Although Trump had a bigger audience than Clinton, more people watched the DNC over the RNC earlier in the week. CNN reported that the second night of the DNC had 25 percent more viewers than the second night at the RNC.

The Senate voted on Wednesday to save the FCC's Obama-era net neutrality rules, which are set to expire on June 11. Democrats used a legislative mechanism known as the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to force a vote. Three Republican senators — Susan Collins (R-ME), John Kennedy (R-MS), and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) — voted for the measure. The bill has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House. The Commission, now chaired by Ajit Pai, repealed the order in April.

The European Union banned arms sales to Venezuela and established a system for asset freezes and travel restrictions on some Venezuelan officials. The EU foreign ministers announced the measures at talks in Brussels on Monday. The weapons ban would stop sales of military equipment that could be used for repression or surveillance of Venezuelans. The EU said in a statement that the measures can be reversed depending on Maduro's reaction to demands for more democracy in the South American nation. The United States last Thursday imposed financial sanctions on another 10 current and former Venezuelan officials over corruption and abuse of power allegations related to Maduro's crackdown on the opposition.

First Lady Michelle Obama retired President Barack Obama's mom jeans. The jeans will not be immortalized in Cooperstown. President Barack Obama told an audience at the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Thursday. According to pool reports, Obama said, "At the Hall's request, I contributed something of my own, which was the jacket I wore when I threw out the first pitch at the 2009 All-Star Game." He added, "I hear that with all the media attention about it, there was also some interest in the jeans I wore that night. But Michelle retired those jeans quite a while back."

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi has named six Democrats to a special panel formed by Republicans to investigate Planned Parenthood. Rep. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois will act as ranking member of the 13-member special committee, which will be housed within the Energy and Commerce Committee and given broad authority to investigate alleged wrongdoing by the women's health and abortion provider. The provider has come under criticism for supplying aborted fetal tissue to human tissue companies. The other five Democrats on the panel will include Reps. Jerry Nadler of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Suzan DelBene of Washington, Jack Speier of California and Bonnie Watson of New Jersey.

BP agreed to put $20 billion into an escrow account for victims' claims. That amount does not include cleanup costs. A White House official said the $20 billion is not a cap, meaning if costs exceed $20 billion, they may go to BP for more. Kenneth Feinberg, the same attorney who oversaw payments to victims of the 9/11 attacks, oversaw payments to victims of the 9/11 attacks. President Obama is expected to announce more details soon.

President Barack Obama nominated Loretta Lynch as his attorney general nominee. At a White House ceremony Saturday, Obama said Lynch has a commitment to equal justice and a solid record as a tough, fair federal prosecutor. Obama said it is "pretty hard to be more qualified" for the job. The 55-year-old Lynch would be the first African-American woman to serve as attorney general. She is currently the top federal prosecutor in Brooklyn, New York. Outgoing Attorney General Eric Holder also attended Saturday's announcement. Holder was the first black head of the Justice Department.

The Senate Judiciary Committee will begin its immigration hearings this year with testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano next week. Napolitano has overseen the administration's immigration efforts for the last four years and is currently traveling through the Southwest. She says the border is finally secure and has urged lawmakers to turn their attention to legalizing illegal immigrants and overhauling the broader immigration system. Both the House and Senate are holding hearings ahead of a legislative fight. The House Judiciary Committee held its first hearings Tuesday, with testimony from advocates and former government experts, but no from the Obama administration.

The Obama administration on Wednesday offered a parting gift to its longest-standing ally in the Middle East. The administration abstained from a United Nations vote to end Jewish settlement building on occupied Palestinian territory. Secretary of State John Kerry delivered a 72-minute address from Foggy Bottom addressing Israeli leaders about the importance of peace and a two-state solution. "If the choice is one state, Israel can either be Jewish or democratic, it cannot be both, and it won't ever really be at peace," he said.

President Trump said Tuesday he would prefer to let Russia back into the G-7 group of top industrialized nations, doubling down on his view days before this year's round of talks begins in France. "I think it's much more appropriate to have Russia in," Mr. Trump said in the Oval Office during a visit with the president of Romania. Russia's participation in the Group of Eight was suspended in 2014 after its annexation of the Crimean peninsula from Ukraine. The country announced its permanent withdrawal in 2017.

Former NBA player and Celebrity Apprentice contestant Dennis Rodman tweeted to Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) that Donald Trump is "about to fire your ass." Cruz mentioned Rodman during the CNN Republican presidential debate on Thursday in Houston. Cruz said that while Cruz was fighting amnesty, Trump was busy "firing Dennis Rodman on Celebrity Apprentice." Rodman endorsed Trump in July, saying that Trump "has been a great friend for many years. We don't need another politician, we need a businessman like Mr. Trump!"

International envoy Kofi Annan announced that permanent members of the U.N. Security Council will hold a conference on Syria on Saturday in Geneva. Annan said the council members — Britain, China, France, Russia, and the United States — plus Turkey — are invited. The invitations included the U.N. secretary-general and representatives of the League of Arab States, including diplomats from Iraq, Kuwait, and Qatar. The conference aims at finding ways to stop violence in Syria.

The public corruption case against former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell and his wife Maureen is before a federal jury. The seven-man, five-woman jury left the courtroom to begin deliberations Tuesday after hearing nearly two hours of instructions from U.S. District Judge James Spencer. The jury heard from dozens of witnesses over a five-week trial. The McDonnells are charged with doing special favors for Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the former CEO of dietary supplements maker Star Scientific Inc., in exchange for more than $165,000 in gifts and loans.

FOX confirmed the Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor at 10:15 a.m. The program included a bio information section with analysis of the decision. The program also noted that North Korea conducted missile testing. Two more missiles were tested. The program asked what the United States would do about the testing and whether the UN would make an impact. Peter Brooks will join the program at 12 PM.

President Obama signed legislation Wednesday canceling furloughs of air-traffic controllers that had resulted in airport delays. The bill had been passed by Congress last week after flight delays nationwide caused complaints. The Federal Aviation Administration said it instituted the furloughs due to automatic "sequester" budget cuts that took effect March 1. The law allows the agency to transfer as much as $253 million from other accounts through September, action the agency said it did not have flexibility to do under the budget cuts.

A Bloomberg National Poll shows Hillary Clinton's favorability rating at 70 percent and 58 percent among Americans, a decline from December's 70 percent. Twenty-two percent view her unfavorably, compared to 11 percent in December. Forty-one percent of Americans say they would vote for her for president, while roughly 33 percent say they would not. Forty-three percent of women would vote for her. Among Democrats, three-quarters would back her, while 33 percent of independent voters would not. 47 percent disapprove of how Clinton handled Benghazi, while 34 percent approve.

President Obama signed legislation Wednesday canceling furloughs of air-traffic controllers that had resulted in airport delays. The bill had been passed by Congress last week after flight delays nationwide caused complaints. The Federal Aviation Administration said it instituted the furloughs due to automatic "sequester" budget cuts that took effect March 1. The law allows the agency to transfer as much as $253 million from other accounts through September, action the agency said it did not have flexibility to do under the budget cuts.

Rabbi Jeffrey Myers said Saturday's shooting attack on his synagogue was an "attack upon America." Speaking on "Good Morning America," Myers said, "Many will just see this as an attack upon the Jewish community. It's not." The shooting suspect, Robert Gregory Bowers, was arrested and is accused of killing 11 individuals at the Tree of Life Synagogue. Six more victims were injured, including four police officers. The suspected gunman is due in court on Monday.

Hillary Clinton raised $45 million dollars in donations from supporters during the first quarter of her campaign, according to early numbers released by her staff. The mid-April to June 30 haul was a record for a candidate in their first quarter, with the previous record being held by President Obama, who raised $41.9 million in the first quarter of his re-election campaign. Ninety-one percent of all donations were $100 or less, according to Hillary for America Chairman John Podesta. Clinton said that this was a number she and the campaign are "especially proud of."

Bob Dylan turned down an invitation to meet President Obama at the White House on Wednesday. The singer-songwriter will not be among a group of U.S. Nobel Prize winners meeting with Obama in the Oval Office. The president invited the winners to congratulate them before they travel to Sweden to receive their prizes on Dec. 10. Dylan, awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature, is not traveling to Stockholm for the ceremony.

House Speaker Rep. Paul Ryan, R-Wis., said on Thursday that the United States was too soon to say whether the mass shooting in San Bernadino, Calif., was an act of terrorism. Ryan argued that the proper response to mass shootings is to overhaul the nation's mental health system rather than changing gun laws. "If your stomach isn't turned when you see these acts of violence on TV, there's something wrong with you," Ryan said on MSNBC's "Morning Joe." "The question is, can we address these issues without violating a citizen's rights?"

On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi said she was "really excited about the prospect of a woman president of the United States" and that she thinks it would be well, especially a woman as well qualified as Hillary Clinton. Pelosi said she "makes a habit of not endorsing people until they make a decision to run," but added, "But I think there are many people who are waiting to see if Secretary Clinton runs." She also said, "I'm really excited about the prospect of a woman president of the United States. I think it would be well, especially a woman as well qualified as Hillary Clinton."

Former Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole saluted President George H.W. Bush at the casket of the late president. Dole is a World War II veteran who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate. He arrived in the Capitol rotunda Tuesday in a wheelchair pushed by an aide. At the casket's side, the aide lifted Dole, 95, into a standing position. Once Dole steadied, Dole saluted. Bush achieved the office that Dole sought in 1996 as the Republican presidential nominee.

U.S. services firms expanded in August at the fastest pace on record. The Institute for Supply Management says its services index rose to 59.6 last month from 58.7 in July. The August figure is the highest recorded since the measure was introduced in January 2008. Fifteen of 17 industries reported growth last month. Only mining and arts, entertainment and recreation contracted in August. The ISM is a trade group of purchasing managers. Its services survey covers businesses that employ 90 percent of the American workforce, including retail, construction, health care and financial services firms.

The White House has named Hope Hicks as communications director. Hicks, 28, is a longtime aide of President Donald Trump who served as his presidential campaign's lead spokeswoman. She has been interim communications director for the past few weeks. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday that Hicks has been named permanently. Hicks is the third White House communications director in the administration's nearly eight months. Her predecessor, Anthony Scaramucci, served in the role for less than two weeks after being removed over language he used about two then White House advisers.

President Obama visited activists fasting to protest House inaction on immigration legislation. On the day after Thanksgiving, the president stopped by a white tent on the National Mall where some activists have shunned all food except water for the past 18 days. A top labor organizer is among them. Obama told the activists he appreciated their efforts. He also reiterated his view that there is still time this year for the House to pass legislation. House Speaker John Boehner has refused to schedule votes on a comprehensive immigration measure the Senate passed this summer. Boehner has opted for a piecemeal approach. That process has moved too slowly to satisfy immigration advocates.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said "very real gaps" persist between world powers and Iraq over the contours of a nuclear agreement as a Sunday deadline for a deal approaches. Kerry cited some progress after two days of nuclear talks with Iran and America's European partners in Vienna. He said much work remains. Kerry said he is returning to Washington on Tuesday to consult with President Barack Obama and Congress about the state of negotiations. He said he will also discuss the possibility of extending the talks past the deadline so negotiations can continue.

A poll released Monday by Chegg, an online textbook rental and tutoring company, shows a plurality of college students think billionaire businessman Donald Trump won the first Republican presidential debate. Twenty-six percent of college or college-bound students said Trump won the debate. Sixteen percent said former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush won, 14 percent thought Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) won, and 10 percent went for Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.).

A super PAC supporting Ted Cruz's presidential campaign released two new ads on Wednesday. One video shows Sean Hannity and pollster Frank Luntz saying Cruz had the line of the night during CNBC's debate, and former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin arguing that Cruz "schooled the media." Cruz is shown saying: "The questions that have been asked so far in this debate illustrate why the American people don't trust the media. The questions that are being asked shouldn't be trying to get people to tear into one another. ... This is not a cage match."

The head of the Transportation Security Administration, TSA administrator John Pistole, acknowledged that the new pat-downs are more invasive than what travelers were used to in the past. Pistole said he has received the new pat-down, as has Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano. Some travelers complain that the new inspections target sensitive body areas. Pistole said he understands those privacy concerns but says the government must provide the best possible security for air travelers. Pistole was testifying before a Senate committee about TSA policies and procedures. The hearing was scheduled before recent criticism of airport security pat-downs.

On Monday, Bo, President Barack Obama's family's dog, received a sister named Sunny. Sunny, who was born in Michigan in June 2012, is also a Portuguese Water Dog, which helps because Malia Obama has allergies. The White House said Sunny is the perfect little sister for Bo – full of energy and very affectionate – and the First Family picked her name because it fit her cheerful personality. In October, Michelle Obama reportedly said Bo did not have enough doggie interaction. The Obamas reportedly first got the idea of getting a Portuguese Water Dog from the late Sen. Ted Kennedy (D-MA).

On Monday, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA) said President Donald Trump's tweet about a video showing him wrestling a man with a CNN logo as his face was "suggesting violence against journalists." Lieu said, "Donald Trump has had a series of highly disturbing tweets, but his tweet yesterday morning was beyond inappropriate. It was suggesting violence against journalists, and that's going to increase the risk of harm to journalists. The president of the United States should never be inciting violence against any human being."

Heavy rain and lightning early Wednesday morning forced dozens of Girl Scouts camping on the South Lawn of the White House to shelter inside the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. First Lady Michelle Obama hosted the scouts for a camp-out to promote her "Let's Move" campaign designed to get young people exercising more outdoors. Early in the evening, the first lady told the girls they were making history with their South Lawn sleepover — that no one had ever camped out in tents on the White House grounds before. The president also made an appearance and spoke to the young scouts.

President Obama spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in person but on the phone. The call followed Netanyahu's public demand for red lines on Iran during his speech at the UN. In the phone call, Obama reiterated his earlier position that no red lines will be set. The two leaders discussed a broad array of issues. The Obama administration stated they are in full agreement on the shared goal of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Obama told Netanyahu there will be no red lines for you.

White House press secretary Jay Carney said, "Congressman Cummings, in our view, is always the smartest guy in the room. If he wants to speak, he should be allowed to speak." Cummings attempted to ask a procedural question Wednesday during a hearing with former IRS official Lois Lerner when Issa, chairman of the House Oversight Committee, ended the session. Cummings shouted that he deserved the right to speak and told Issa, "you cannot run a committee like this."

Rep. Dennis Kucinich, R-Ohio, has offered an amendment to defund the Libya operation. The amendment was voted down by a vote of 229 to 199. Several other Libya efforts failed in the House last month. The Chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, Bill Young, R-Fla., told Kucinich on the floor that he "is persistent" and expressed concern that Kucinich introduced the amendment after multiple days of debate on the bill.

U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions said one of his top priorities is investigating and prosecuting sex crimes against children, even though technology has made it easier for criminals to avoid detection. Sessions spoke to law enforcement agencies on Tuesday at a conference in Atlanta, where he warned predators that they will be found and prosecuted. Sessions, a former prosecutor, said predators have an easier path to reach children through phones and tablets. Sessions did not address President Donald Trump's criticism of the Department of Justice's legal strategy to defend a travel ban before the Supreme Court. Trump made the comments Monday on Twitter.

Vice President Mike Pence addressed young Republican supporters at the Young America Foundation's fall college retreat on Friday. Pence said President Donald Trump remains committed to pursuing legal challenges to overturn his election loss to President-elect Joe Biden. Pence said: "We're going to fight for an outcome in this election that wins us four more years." Pence offered the conservative group a pep talk as Trump continues to refuse to concede. On Friday, Trump again pressed allegations of widespread voter fraud. His administration has said there is no evidence to support the claims.

On Tuesday night in an interview with CBS's Charlie Rose, Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said there was "no doubt" sexism played a role in former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton's loss. When asked if sexism played a role in 2016, Ginsburg said, "I have no doubt that it did." When asked if it was "decisive," Ginsburg added, "There are so many things that might have been decisive, but that was a major, major factor."

On Sunday morning, President Donald Trump tweeted a video showing him wrestling a CNN logo. CNN responded with a statement. The statement read: "It is a sad day when the president of the United States encourages violence against reporters. Cleary Sarah Huckabee Sanders lied when she said the president had never done so. Instead of preparing for his overseas trip, his first meeting with Vladimir Putin, North Korea and working on the health care bill he is involved in juvenile behavior far below the dignity of his office. We'll keep doing our jobs. he should start doing his."

Twitter suspended President Trump's account @realDonaldTrump on Wednesday evening and threatened to permanently ban him from the platform. The suspension followed an unprecedented and ongoing violent situation in Washington, D.C. Twitter stated it had required the removal of three tweets posted earlier that day for repeated and severe violations of its Civic Integrity Policy. Twitter said the account would be locked for 12 hours following the removal of these Tweets. If the Tweets are not removed, the account would remain locked.

President Trump said he "fell asleep" trying to watch President Obama's 2018 election speech Friday and bristled at his predecessor's claim of credit for the surging economy. "He's very good, very good for sleeping," Trump said as he kicked off a campaign rally in North Dakota. He spoke just after Obama accused Trump of pandering to radicals, losing control of the White House, squandering international good will, and dividing the United States.

Two weeks ago, Hillary Clinton tweeted that "every survivor of sexual assault deserves to be heard, believed and supported." At a campaign event in New Hampshire on Thursday, a woman in the audience asked Hillary if believing all "survivors" meant believing Bill's accusers as well, including Juanita Broaddrick, Kathleen Willey and Paula Jones. Hillary Clinton responded: "I would say that everybody should be believed at first until they are disbelieved based on evidence."

German Chancellor Angela Merkel said Friday that meetings between U.S. and Russian presidents should become "normal" again. Merkel's comments came after President Donald Trump invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the White House. Earlier this week, the two had a meeting in Finland. Merkel said that "in principle it's always good for everyone when there are talks, particularly when there are talks between these two countries." She said: "I think it must once again become normal for Russian and American presidents to meet."

"He's very good, very good for sleeping," Trump said as he kicked off a campaign rally in North Dakota. He spoke just after Obama accused Trump of pandering to radicals, losing control of the White House, squandering international good will, and dividing the United States.

The Republican presidential candidate is expected to visit Virginia, North Carolina and Florida, although the schedule may change in the coming days. Romney returned from an overseas trip late Tuesday and spent Wednesday in meetings at his Boston campaign headquarters. He is scheduled to campaign in the Denver area on Thursday. Aides report that he will attend a Republican Governors Association fundraiser in Aspen later that night. A handful of governors often mentioned as possible Romney running mates are scheduled to attend. Next week's bus tour could be part of the rollout for a running mate. Republican officials are expecting that announcement any day.

Former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe faces the prospect of an indictment after his attorneys were unable to persuade senior Justice Department officials not to pursue charges. Two people familiar with the matter said the deputy attorney general declined an appeal from McCabe's lawyers aimed at preventing a prosecution. The attorneys argued that McCabe, a frequent target of President Trump's criticism, should not face charges on accusations he lied during an internal investigation. The people were not authorized to discuss the issue by name and spoke on condition of anonymity.

CBS News reported that President Donald Trump has bolstered his White House communications staff to fight impeachment. Reporter Paula Reid cited a Senior Administration Official confirming that former Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi and former Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs Tony Sayegh were expected to join the White House team to work on "proactive impeachment messaging." The official said their roles would be temporary as special government employees. Both Sayegh and Bondi have experience defending the president on television, increasing the president's defense in the establishment media.

Colombian police arrested a sixth suspect in the slaying of a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent, Metropolitan Bogota police commander Luis Edwardo Martinez announced Wednesday. Martinez said officials believe the June 20 killing occurred during a robbery and was not related to work done by 43-year-old James Watson, who was known as Terry. Officials say the gang attacked Watson on June 20 after he got into a taxi outside a restaurant and stabbed him to death. They say the group apparently had carried out similar robberies using taxis.

Saudi state TV reported that King Abdullah, a longtime U.S. ally who joined Washington's fight against al-Qaida and sought to modernize the kingdom, died at age 90. The station said Abdullah died Friday. His expected successor is his 79-year-old half-brother Prince Salman, who recently took on Abdullah's responsibilities. The announcement came in a statement read by a presenter on Saudi state TV, which aired video of worshippers at the Kaaba in Mecca.

President Trump's prime-time plea to Americans to support his plans for a border wall fell flat, with opposition to the idea still running strong and public criticism blaming Mr. Trump for the government shutdown. A Quinnipiac University Poll released Monday shows 43 percent of Americans back building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, exactly the same percentage as in December, just before the shutdown hit.

Iranian official news agency Fars News Agency ran a piece from The Onion today as news. The piece, a parody, suggested that a Gallup poll released Monday showed rural whites favored Ahmadinejad over Obama. The Onion stated: "According to the results of a Gallup poll released Monday, the overwhelming majority of rural white Americans said they would rather vote for Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad than US President Barack Obama."

On Monday before leaving for a meeting with President Donald Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he and Trump see "eye-to-eye" on a lot of issues. Netanyahu said, "The alliance between Israel and America has always been extremely strong, it's about to get even stronger. President Trump and I see eye-to-eye on the dangers emanating from the region, but also on the opportunities. And we will talk about both as well as upgrading the relations between Israel and the United States in many many fields."

A Washington restaurant, The Bird DC, is offering a special $5 "Moscow Mueller" drink every time special counsel Robert Mueller indicts an associate of President Donald Trump. The restaurant promoted the offer on Twitter Wednesday and added the hashtag "#muellertime." The drink's name is a play on the popular Moscow Mule, a beverage made with vodka, ginger beer and lime juice. Mueller is investigating potential links between Russia and Trump's presidential campaign.

A poll released by Mercury Analytics, a Democrat-run firm with clients including Fox News and MSNBC, found 19 percent of likely Democratic voters said they would consider voting for Donald Trump and 14 percent for Hillary Clinton. The company also found a higher percentage of Democrats were "100 percent sure" of voting for Trump than Republicans were considering voting for Clinton.

During her weekly press briefing, California Democrat Nancy Pelosi and Maryland Democrat Minority Whip Steny Hoyer exchanged remarks. Pelosi said lawmakers, including Hoyer, were incapable of crafting sound immigration policy because of their color. "The five white guys I call them, you know," Pelosi said. "Are they going to open a hamburger stand next or what?"

US President Barack Obama will announce in his State of the Union address Tuesday that he will pull 34,000 US troops home from Afghanistan in the next year, a source familiar with his speech said. The move will halve the size of the current 66,000 strong US force in Afghanistan, ahead of a final withdrawal of most foreign combat troops by the end of 2014.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) posted a picture of one of the Zodiac Killer's letters on Twitter on Wednesday. The post referenced conspiracy theories that claim Cruz is the serial killer. Cruz posted the letter in response to a post by Sen. Ben Sasse (R-NE), and his reply went viral on the social network ahead of his debate with Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT). Conspiracy theories and memes have often joked that Cruz is the Zodiac Killer, based on old police sketches of the serial killer, who was never caught.

Authorities reported that the number of confirmed dead from the mudslide in Washington state has increased from 18 to 21. Snohomish County Emergency Management Director Jason Biermann said Sunday that 15 victims have been identified by the Snohomish County medical examiner, and six have not been identified. Biermann said another four bodies were found in the debris field on Sunday. About 30 people remain missing after the mudslide in the mountainside community of Oso on March 22.

China said the European Union's decision to stop importing oil from Iran over its nuclear program is not constructive. The official Xinhua News Agency on Thursday quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying, "To blindly pressure and impose sanctions on Iran are not constructive approaches." The EU embargo announced Monday is the latest attempt to pressure Iran over a nuclear program the United States and its allies argue is aimed at developing nuclear weapons but which Iran says is for purely peaceful purposes. China said the dispute should be resolved through dialogue and consultation. The country is a major buyer of Iranian crude oil.

President Donald Trump plans to visit wounded service members at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. It will be Trump's first visit to the facility. Trump tweeted Saturday that he was looking forward to "seeing our bravest and greatest Americans." First lady Melania Trump was expected to join the president. Trump planned to meet with about a dozen service members who are receiving care at the hospital. He is also expected to award at least one Purple Heart, the U.S. military's decoration given to those wounded or killed in action.

Al Hussein said in a formal speech to the Human Rights Council in Geneva that he is deeply concerned by recently adopted policies which punish children for their parents' actions. He called on the United States to end the policy immediately and to ratify the Convention on the Rights of the Child "to ensure that the fundamental rights of all children" will be the focus of all laws. This was Al Hussein's last global update to the Human Rights Council this session.

On Monday, former Secretary of State and presumptive Democratic 2016 presidential frontrunner Hillary Clinton tweeted to swimmer Diana Nyad, who had just swam from Cuba to Florida. Clinton did not comment on Syria. Ben Shapiro is Editor-At-Large of Breitbart News and author of the New York Times bestseller "Bullies: How the Left's Culture of Fear and Intimidation Silences America" (Threshold Editions, January 8, 2013).

Former EPA administrator Gina McCarthy said on CNN that Scott Pruitt needs to be more concerned about the environment. McCarthy said the only thing Pruitt talks about or seems to consider is whether or not it is reducing the cost of business. She said his job is to protect public health and the environment in ways that continue to keep the economy moving. McCarthy said Pruitt, the current EPA administrator, needs to be more transparent in his actions at the agency. He has recently been flagged for possible violations concerning his housing in Washington where he rented from a lobbyist in the energy sector.

Republican leaders said the House will vote Thursday to block President Barack Obama from extending relief from deportation to any more immigrants brought here illegally as children. The move is aimed at persuading conservatives to support an emergency spending bill for the border issue. To secure conservative votes for that legislation, House Republican leaders agreed to a second vote on a measure to prevent Obama from expanding an existing program granting work permits to immigrants brought here illegally as children. The vote will occur as Congress wraps up its work before heading out for a five-week recess.

Attorney General Eric Holder announced Monday that Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and other accused 9/11 conspirators will face a military tribunal at Guantanamo Bay. The announcement reverses a November 2009 decision by President Obama and Holder to try the suspects in a civilian court on U.S. soil.

On Sunday, Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY) said the current government shutdown was a result of President Donald Trump being "dysfunctional." Schumer said, "Americans know why this dysfunction is occurring. Dysfunctional president. We are in a Trump Shutdown, and party leaders who won't act without him have created the chaos and the gridlock we find ourselves in today. It all really stems from the president, whose inability to clinch a deal has created the Trump Shutdown."

The Pentagon announced Wednesday that the top two officials at its Defense Intelligence Agency are retiring. The departure of Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn as director of the DIA and David Shedd as his deputy was announced by Pentagon press secretary Navy Rear Adm. John Kirby. Kirby said the two are retiring this year, but he was not more specific about the timing and offered no reason for their decisions to leave. Kirby said the Flynn and Shedd retirements have been planned for "some time." He said replacements would be announced later.

Police suspect Allison Johnson of Norman was also connected to vandalism at a school and arts center in the city. Johnson was being booked Thursday afternoon into the Cleveland County Detention Center on a complaint of terroristic threats. No criminal charges have been filed, and jail records do not indicate if Johnson has an attorney. The vandalism was discovered Wednesday morning on the windows and sidewalk outside the Cleveland County Democratic Party headquarters in Norman. Similar epithets were found spray-painted March 28 outside the Democratic Party headquarters in Oklahoma City and the Oklahoma City office of the Chickasaw Nation.

Rick Gates testified Tuesday in the tax and bank fraud trial of Paul Manafort. Gates said Manafort's income streams had dried up after his friends in the Ukrainian government lost power, creating financial difficulties for Manafort. "It substantially decreased in terms of income he was accustomed to receiving in prior years," Gates said. Prosecutors alleged that after Manafort's income dropped, he turned to hiding his money in overseas accounts to evade the IRS.

Michelle Obama said her daughters, Sasha, 9, and Malia, 12, have certain restrictions that other children do not have because of Secret Service security issues. During an interview on NBC's "Today Show" on Wednesday, she said she is "not a big fan of young kids having Facebook." Even if the girls were not living in the White House, she said Facebook is "not something they need." Maybe when they get older, she added.
