On Tuesday, House Intelligence Committee chairman Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA) told CNN's senior congressional correspondent Manu Raju that the case for opening impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump was getting stronger. Schiff said, "I think that that the administration is certainly pushing the Congress in that direction by obstructing everything. I expect we'll have a discussion about that today." He added, "I think The case gets stronger the more they stonewall the Congress."

The U.S. Capitol building is on lockdown, with police barring people from entering. The Senate seargant at arms issued a lockdown alert for the building and visitor center, saying police activity has been reported. Capitol office buildings are open. Capitol police say they are searching for an individual but offered no details. House press gallery staff says the building is on lockdown but that the House met briefly and immediately recessed. Voting scheduled to begin at 9:15 a.m. is postponed, gallery staff said.

The Supreme Court ruled Friday making gay marriage legal in all 50 states. Celebrities posted on Twitter celebrating the ruling, including President Obama's #LoveWins hashtag. The tweet read: "Woke up to learn that love is free! Thank you to all those who fought so hard to make this historic moment happen. The Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage in all 50 states today. IT'S ABOUT. FUCKING. TIME. Very happy about the SCOTUS rulings this week! Marriage Equality, Fair Housing and Affordable Health Care!"

Harry Reid underwent cancer surgery. His family said he was in good spirits and resting with his family. They said doctors caught the tumor early during a routine screening and his prognosis was good. The former Senate Democratic leader declined to seek re-election in 2016 after more than three decades in Congress. He suffered an accident in 2015 that left him blind in one eye. Nevada's longest-serving senator helped propel the passage of President Barack Obama's health care law, blocked the development of a nuclear waste dump in Nevada, and built a well-organized Democratic machine in the state.

Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the U.S, Adel Al-Jubeir, said Sunday that the fighting in Yemen is not a proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran. Al-Jubeir said on CBS: "I would describe it as a war of necessity. We had no choice. We tried every possible way to avoid it." Houthi rebels, who are Shiite Muslims backed by Iran, have overrun parts of Yemen. Saudi Arabia, with a coalition of nine other Arab countries, has launched a military campaign against the rebels to restore stability.

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg had surgery Wednesday morning to replace a stent in her right coronary artery. Ginsburg, 81, is resting comfortably and is expected to leave a Washington-area hospital within 48 hours. Court spokeswoman Kathleen Arberg said Ginsburg had the procedure at MedStar Heart & Vascular Institute at MedStar Washington Hospital Center after a coronary blockage was discovered. Ginsburg experienced discomfort Tuesday night during routine exercise and was taken to the hospital. Ginsburg has been on the court since 1993.

On Friday in Nashua, New Hampshire, at the Young America's Foundation Conference, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), a 2016 candidate for the Republican presidential nomination, outlined his vision to repeal and replace ObamaCare. Listing three specific reforms, Cruz said, "Number one, allow people to buy insurance across state lines." He continued, "Number two, we need to expand health saving accounts," and he concluded with, "Number three, we need to de-link health insurance from employment."

Former Vice President Joe Biden appeared on ABC on Thursday night for a town hall in lieu of a debate, opposite a town hall for President Donald Trump on NBC at the same time. Biden said his own crime bill was a mistake, but not at the federal level. Biden said: "Yes, it was. But here's where the mistake. The mistake came in terms of what the states did locally."

The House of Representatives approved a bill by unanimous consent to deny a visa for Hamid Aboutalebi, Iran's Ambassador to the United Nations. Aboutalebi was a participant in the Iranian uprising that seized the US Embassy in Tehran in 1979 and held American hostage for 444 days. The Senate approved by unanimous consent a measure to deny a visa for Aboutalebi earlier this week. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Chuck Schumer (D-NY) crafted the plan.

On Sunday, Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) appeared on ABC's "This Week" and discussed the Republican plan to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. Cotton said GOP House members should "Do not walk the plank and vote for a bill that cannot pass the Senate and then have to face the consequences of that vote." He added, "The bill probably can be fixed, but it's going to take a lot of carpentry on that framework."

Attorney General William Barr left the Justice Department early Saturday evening after spending nearly nine hours reviewing special counsel Robert Mueller's final conclusions on Russian meddling in the 2016 election. Mr. Barr said Friday that he intended to provide Congress with Mr. Mueller's "principal conclusions" as early as this weekend. Congress and the public must wait at least one more day to learn the results of the most significant investigation into the president of the last 20 years.

New York lawmakers have rejected a bill to legalize gay marriage. The Senate decision Wednesday follows months of delays and arm twisting among lawmakers sympathetic to the bill but representing conservative districts. It follows a referendum in Maine earlier this month that struck down a gay marriage law before it took effect. Advocates say they are not surprised by the decision. Most, including Gov. David Paterson, say they at least wanted a floor debate and vote. Gay marriage is legal in Connecticut, Iowa, Massachusetts and Vermont. A New Hampshire law takes effect Jan. 1.

Judges dismissed legal challenges that the president's campaign had launched Wednesday as the presidential election remained unresolved with votes still being tabulated in several battleground states. President Trump's campaign alleged late absentee ballots in one Georgia county were illegally placed alongside on-time ballots instead of being set aside, as required by state law. The issue involved about 53 ballots. The campaign called on the court to separate late-arriving ballots, but a judge dismissed the lawsuit Thursday.

Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, said that Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy was wrong to say what he did about the special committee on Benghazi, and that Chaffetz intends to correct it by challenging McCarthy for the speakership. The House GOP believes this is the only way it can address the committee's political significance, which McCarthy said was his primary target was Hillary Rodham Clinton's presidential run.

President Barack Obama said Thursday from the White House press briefing room that there is no "elaborate strategy" to go "full scale" and defeat ISIS. He said he did not want to "put the cart before the horse." He said the immediate goal is to keep American people and interests safe while the administration is working politically and diplomatically to "cobble together a collation" of allies to create a military, political and economic answer to ISIS.

Police officers in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Thursday morning helped local business owners clean up from damage sustained during riots on Wednesday night. Images shared on social media showed local businesses vandalized, with windows broken and merchandise looted as rioters overshadowed "Black Lives Matter" protests. Demonstrators were marching over the death of Keith Lamont Scott, a black man shot and killed by a black police officer. On Thursday, police officers stood outside looted businesses with weapons drawn and also helped store owners pick up debris.

On Thursday, Secretary of State John Kerry appeared on CNN in an interview with Elise Labott in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Kerry said America is not at war with ISIS. Kerry said, "What we are doing is engaging in a very significant counter-terrorism operation. It's going to go on for some period of time. If somebody wants to think about it as being a war with ISIL, they can do so, but the fact is it's a major counterterrorism operation that will have many different moving parts."

At her weekly press conference on Thursday, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) said she has the votes to become the next speaker of the House. When asked about 17 members currently opposing her and if she could still win, Pelosi said, "Yes." She continued, "I have overwhelming support in my caucus to be speaker of the House." She added, "I happen to think at this point, I'm the best person for that."

President Donald Trump visited US troops stationed in Iraq on Wednesday and declared that "the United States cannot continue to be the policeman of the world." He also defended his decision to pull US troops out of neighboring Syria, saying there would be no delays. "You can't have any more time. You've had enough time," he said he had told his generals.

North Korea has agreed to "actively cooperate" with South Korea in talks to reduce military tensions ahead of next month's Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. Tuesday's trip south of the border by North Korean officials marked the first in-person meeting between countries in nearly two years. The North Koreans agreed at the last minute to open the meeting in the Demilitarized Zone to the press. South Korean media reported both countries agreed to continue discussions about improving conditions along their shared border, AP reported.

Arlen Specter, who has been sent to the Senate five times by Pennsylvania Republicans, announced today that he is switching parties. He will run for reelection to his current post as a Democrat in 2010. The move puts Democrats within one vote of a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate.

The Senate voted 60-40 on Thursday afternoon to end debate on the financial reform bill, making it likely the measure will pass the Senate within days. The vote reversed a closer vote Wednesday in which Republicans joined forces with two liberal Democrats to stall the measure temporarily. President Obama and Democratic leaders made major changes to the legislation during four weeks of Senate debate.

The White House said President Obama's visit with Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko would send a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin that the United States stands with Ukraine. Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Earnest said the photo of the two national leaders together would send a clear message to Putin. Earnest said the visit itself would be "a pretty clear symbol to everybody" that the United States was prepared to stand with Ukraine.

The White House cancelled a Friday event at which Michelle Obama was set observe Earth Day. The event, which was to be held in northwest Washington Park, was called off after rain showers and cool temperatures moved into the D.C. area. The first lady was scheduled to meet with school children and students from the White House Mentorship program and participate in a "habitat improvement project" at Fort Dupont Park. Obama was also slated to present certificates to children who took part in her "Let's Move!" initiative.

The first person diagnosed with the Ebola virus on United States soil is now in a critical condition, health officials said Saturday, having previously described him as seriously ill. The Texas hospital treating Thomas Eric Duncan, who traveled from Liberia to Texas in late September, said in a brief statement: "Mr. Duncan is in critical condition."

Hillary Clinton won the larger portion of the delegates allocated at Saturday's Nevada State Democratic Convention. Clinton took seven delegates, while Sanders received five, according to local reports. As the results were announced, Sanders supporters in attendance shouted in protest, reacting to news that a number of Sanders supporters were barred from participating. One local report showed that by a slim margin, Clinton's 1,695 supporters allowed to participate outnumbered Sanders' 1,662 backers.

The Kremlin said Wednesday it would not participate in "Twitter diplomacy" after US President Donald Trump tweeted that "missiles will be coming" to Syria. Presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in comments reported by news agencies: "We do not take part in Twitter-diplomacy. We support serious approaches. As ever, we believe it is important not to take steps that could damage an already fragile situation."

Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., criticized his congressional colleagues for failing to advance gun control measures following mass shootings such as the one in San Bernardino, California, on Wednesday. Speaking on the Senate floor, Reid said, "We are complicit through our inaction." He added, "When the vicitims turn to us for leadership and help, we will have nothing to show but empty hands and a few empty gestures. It's despicable."

Matt Morgan, general counsel for Trump 2020, said poll workers struggled to operate new voting machines in Maricopa County and improperly pressed and told voters to press a green button to override significant errors. The voting machines disregarded votes cast by voters in person on Election Day. The campaign wants overvoted ballots inspected. The Arizona filing comes as the president also has ongoing litigation in other battleground states, refusing to concede the election.

The House approved a $50.7 billion measure for Superstorm Sandy victims by a vote of 241-180. The measure will be sent to the Senate, which is expected to take it up next Tuesday. Northeast lawmakers from both parties have been pressing for the aid for more than two months. The Oct. 29 storm is blamed for 140 deaths and struck the Atlantic coast from North Carolina to Maine with hurricane-force winds and coastal flooding. New York, New Jersey and Connecticut were the hardest hit.

Lynne Hale, a spokeswoman for Lucasfilm, said President Obama might have created a mash-up of Star Wars friends at Lucasfilm and Star Trek but he might be a lot more savvy with his knowledge of Star Wars than anyone is giving him credit for. Hale said in some of the Star Wars spin-off books there is a "Force Meld." She added: "All of President Obama's friends at Lucasfilm would love to believe that his expertise in Star Wars knowledge runs deep..."

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders criticized Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump on Twitter on Friday, accusing him of trying to divide the nation with fear. Sanders wrote: "We must bring people together to take on the powerful who've hurt the middle class. Trump is trying to play on fears and divide us up." He added: "I believe we stand together to address the real issues facing this country, not allow them to divide us by race or where we come from."

After a loss at the medical board and a lack of progress in the Democrat-controlled Legislature, Project Defending Life gathered enough signatures to place a late-term abortion ban on the municipal ballot. The vote is believed to be the first such referendum of its kind in the country and is being watched as a possible new front for activism in the abortion wars that have typically been waged at the federal and state levels. On Tuesday, Albuquerque voters will decide whether to ban abortions after 20 weeks.

President Obama's executive action protects up to 5 million illegal immigrants from deportation. The White House acknowledges that many of the immigrants spared from deportation under the action will become eligible for Social Security and Medicare benefits once they reach retirement age. The backlash has been swift and will extend into a Republican Congress' deliberations in 2015 over how to limit the reach of the president's immigration blueprint.

Congressional Democrats involved in health care talks at the White House are returning to Capitol Hill for a vote on the House Floor. They will then return to the White House for a second session of talks. Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, and other members of the democratic leadership are meeting with President Obama to discuss health care. Sources told Major Garrett and Mike Emanuel that negotiations are intense but that the President is open to certain changes that House Democrats have requested.

Since Barack Obama was elected president, 10 percent of Americans believe race relations have gotten better, according to a New York Times/CBS Poll published today. The poll found 17 percent of blacks and 8 percent of whites believe race relations have improved under Obama. Thirty-five percent of Americans believe race relations have gotten worse in the Obama era, including 40 percent of whites and 21 percent of blacks. Fifty-two percent of Americans polled said that race relations have stayed about the same.

Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels will deliver the Republican response to President Obama's State of the Union address on Tuesday. House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell made the announcement in a statement Thursday. They said Daniels has a solid record of effective governing and fiscal responsibility. Daniels is in his eighth year as governor of Indiana. He was talked about as a candidate for president until he decided against a White House run. Daniels will speak after Obama's address.

President Obama and his advisers have repeatedly stated that the only way to avoid a default is for Congress to raise the debt ceiling. Each time the clock starts ticking for lawmakers to vote to raise the debt ceiling or face a default, the question arises whether there is another way out. The possibility that the U.S. could fail to make a payment on its bonds or other obligations is described as unthinkable. Other alternatives that would normally be unthinkable become thinkable.

Former President Jimmy Carter, now age 91, told his Sunday school class that he has been declared cancer-free after several months of treatment. Carter underwent radiation treatment and drug treatments beginning in August for melanoma previously found in his liver which had spread to his brain. While teaching a class of about 350 people Sunday morning at Maranatha Baptist Church in the Atlanta area, Carter said a recent scan showed the cancer was gone, attendee Jill Stuckey told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

The Republican governor on Friday announced the state was terminating its Medicaid provider contract with Planned Parenthood. The move followed secretly recorded videos released by an anti-abortion group showing Planned Parenthood officials describing how they provide aborted fetus tissue for medical research. Alabama and Louisiana earlier this month announced they were ending Medicaid payments to Planned Parenthood. Planned Parenthood received more than $51,000 in Medicaid payments in Arkansas over the past fiscal year for family planning and gynecological services. None of the money went toward abortions.

Former professional football player Clint Didier says he will run for Congress. Didier, a former professional football player who ran unsuccessfully as a Republican for the Senate in 2010, announced Monday that he will seek the 4th District seat being vacated by Rep. Doc Hastings. Hastings announced last week he will retire at the end of the year after representing the district in eastern and central Washington for 20 years.

Albanian parliament on Thursday suspended a session on North Macedonia's accession to NATO after an opposition lawmaker threw ink at the prime minister. Lawmakers were scheduled to vote to ratify North Macedonia's NATO accession. The session was disrupted when Lulzim Basha, main opposition center-right Democratic party leader, criticized the leftist government for corruption.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump made a scripted joke in an online video promoting his upcoming appearance on "Saturday Night Live." The video was posted online Wednesday and has since been taken down by NBC. The joke was in an online video promoting Trump's appearance. The video is cut into several segments and includes Trump calling his Republican rival Ben Carson "a complete loser."

The Obama administration stated that Russia violated a 1987 nuclear weapons treaty. A State Department report released Tuesday states that Russia is violating a treaty that bans the possession, production, test-flight of ground-launched cruise missiles with a range of 300 to 3,400 miles. Russia has not officially responded to the report. The administration has not said where and when the alleged violation occurred.

Sean Hannity, the host of Clear Channel's nationally syndicated radio talk show, said on his nationally syndicated radio show that he does not know what the big appeal of Christie, based on the record, is. Hannity said there is hardly an economic boom or a turnaround in the state of New Jersey, and that he can tell you that.

The Washington Times published a poll asking whether gay activists went too far in the ouster of Mozilla CEO Brendan Eich. The publication is switching its third-party commenting system from Disqus to Spot.IM. Users will need to create a Spot.im account or use a Disqus account via a link labeled "Have a Disqus Account?" under the Conversation. Readers are directed to read the Comment Policy before commenting.

Rep. Dave Camp, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, said Monday he will not seek another term. The Michigan Republican said in a statement that he will retire after 12 terms in the House. He was term-limited as chairman. His district is strongly Republican and the GOP is expected to hold the seat. Camp is the second senior Michigan Republican to announce his retirement. Rep. Mike Rogers said Friday he would retire.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that there is "no doubt there are enough seats at play that could cause Republicans to gain control (of the House)." House Minority Leader Steny Hoyer, D-Md., said Tuesday that Democrats are not in danger of losing control of the House.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday vowed to deploy the military to the border with Mexico, describing the move as a "big step." During a White House meeting with Baltic leaders, Trump said "we are going to be guarding our border with our military." He also criticized his predecessor, President Obama, saying "President Obama made changes that basically created no border."

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton criticized President Trump recently for arguing there is a national crisis on the U.S.-Mexico border. In a clip from Showtimes' "The Circus" released Friday, Clinton said: "I just don't think you should call national emergencies unless there truly is a national emergency. There's no national emergency at our border."

The Senate passed a short-term spending bill to keep the government open until Wednesday and give negotiators more time to work out a longer term measure. The Senate approved the bill by voice vote. Lawmakers were seeking a deal on a $1.1 trillion measure financing federal agencies in 2016. Disagreements between Republicans and Democrats over the environment, taxes, and Syrian refugees have stalled the measure. The House is expected to approve the short-term bill on Friday.

Egypt's president-elect Mohammed Morsi said Saturday he would free the blind sheik jailed in the United States for a plot to blow up New York City landmarks. In his first public speech addressing tens of thousands of mostly Islamist supporters, Morsi promised to work to free Omar Abdel-Rahman, the spiritual leader of men convicted in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. He also promised to free detained Egyptian protesters facing military tribunals.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs held his last briefing at the White House on Friday, his 250th since taking the job in January 2009. The news from Egypt dominated the day. President Obama stopped by the White House briefing room to discuss one of his oldest and fondest memories of Gibbs - the story of the 2004 Democratic convention and a tie.

House Speaker John Boehner has floated the idea of suing President Obama over alleged excessive abuse of powers and unconstitutional sidestepping of congressionally passed laws, The Associated Press reported. Boehner has been outspoken in the past about Obama's selective enforcement of laws, especially regarding Obamacare and granting exemptions for certain segments of society but not others, The Associated Press reported. Boehner also accused Obama of doing the same on immigration.

US President Barack Obama said Republicans have failed to agree on a deal to avert the fiscal cliff crisis, stating they cannot bear to raise taxes on the rich. Obama told NBC's Meet the Press in an interview broadcast Sunday that it had been "very hard" for Republicans to accept that "taxes on the wealthiest Americans should go up a little bit, as part of an overall deficit reduction package."

Singapore-based Broadcom said Wednesday it was abandoning efforts to take over US smartphone chipmaker Qualcomm, two days after its bid was blocked by President Donald Trump over national security concerns. "Although we are disappointed with this outcome, Broadcom will comply" with the order blocking its effort to buy Qualcomm, Broadcom said in a statement. Broadcom said it had withdrawn its candidates to sit on the board of directors of Qualcomm.

President Obama said choosing Hillary Clinton to serve as Secretary of State was one of the best decisions he has ever made. Obama continued his tradition of speaking at the event hosted by former President Bill Clinton and said during his speech that he was "proud to come back every year." Obama met with Hillary backstage before the speech and noted that she had the "post-administration glow right now."

Ted Cruz said he is "glad" to support Marco Rubio in his re-election bid. Cruz said, "At this time of great challenges, we very much need strong leaders in the Senate who will fight to restore economic growth, defend our constitutional liberties, and to ensure a strong national security for our nation." Earlier Wednesday, Rubio announced he will run for re-election, reversing his earlier decision not to run for his Senate seat while he was running for president.

US Vice President Mike Pence announced Friday sanctions on 34 vessels of Venezuela's state oil company and two companies that ship crude to Cuba. Another fiscal showdown looms as President Obama will ask Congress to raise the nation's debt ceiling, now at $14.3 trillion, while House Speaker John Boehner warns that Republicans will not vote to raise the cap without serious steps on spending cuts.

A report surfaced early Saturday stating that the address Tashfeen Malik reported on her 2014 fiance visa application to the United States from Pakistan does not exist. The town exists but not the specific address listed. Malik's application was successful, allowing her to emigrate to the U.S. to be with her husband Syed Rizwan Farook and allegedly carry out the murder of 14 people on Wednesday with him in California.

Donald Trump said at a rally Saturday in Las Vegas that Sen. Bernie Sanders refuses to concede to presumptive Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton because he wants to see if the FBI will indict her. "One thing about Bernie, he doesn't give up," Trump said. "He's crazy as a bedbug, but he doesn't quit. And I think Bernie should continue to go forward, folks."

North Korea announced Friday it was voiding non-aggression pacts with South Korea and severing a hotline with Seoul, hours after the UN Security Council adopted new sanctions on Pyongyang. The state-run Committee for the Peaceful Reunification of Korea said in a statement that North Korea "abrogates all agreements on non-aggression reached between the North and the South."
Senator Rob Portman, R-Ohio, announced he will not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate in 2022. Portman said partisanship was one reason for his decision.

Ron DeSantis said Andrew Gillum should be impeached as mayor of Tallahassee. He brought up an ongoing ethics investigation involving Gillum. Gillum has asserted he paid his way on trips to Costa Rica and New York City. Newly released documents contradict Gillum's account. Gillum has denied any wrongdoing in the ethics probe, which is separate from an ongoing FBI investigation into city government.

President Obama called the crew of the Shuttle Atlantis today to congratulate them on their work on repairing the aging Hubble Telescope. Those in the room could only hear the President's portion of the conversation. The White House later provided an audio file to hear the entire conversation. The President was interested to know how his lawn at his home in Chicago is faring.

Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, won a second term on Tuesday, defeating Republican state treasurer Josh Mandel. The Associated Press reported the race with 16 percent of precincts reporting. Brown led Mandel 54 percent to 41 percent.

ABC News San Diego reported that the San Diego City Council was asked to consider a request by Mayor Bob Filner's attorney to cover the cost of Filner's legal fees. The request will be taken up by the City Council at a 5:30 p.m. meeting tomorrow. The meeting will be open to the public.

Pockets of resistance to the Supreme Court's gay marriage ruling have occurred in several states. The court voted 5-4 to guarantee marriage for all same-sex couples. Before Friday's ruling, 13 states outlawed gay marriage. States have largely agreed to comply with the ruling, though some localities have stood their ground.

President Barack Obama announced an executive memorandum that would allow approximately 5 million people to cap their student loan payments at 10 percent of their income. Education Secretary Arne Duncan was briefing reporters on the plan at the White House daily press briefing. NBC's chief White House correspondent Chuck Todd questioned Duncan on the constitutionally of the executive action.

Maine GOP Chairman Mitt Romney won a caucus victory. The former Massachusetts governor defeated Ron Paul, the only other Republican hopeful competing in the state. Rick Santorum and Newt Gingrich did not actively participate. Party leaders announced the results Saturday. The caucuses began February 4 and continued through the week. Some Maine communities have not held their caucuses, though party leaders say they do not plan to count those votes.

US Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke acknowledged risks of the Fed's low interest-rate policy Wednesday but warned that tightening policy now could stall the US recovery. In a statement to Congress, he said: "A premature tightening of monetary policy could lead interest rates to rise temporarily but would also carry a substantial risk of slowing or ending the economic recovery and causing inflation to fall further."
